I would like to cite one more example illustrating the significance that an apparently random childhood memory can acquire through analytical study. In my forty-third year, when I became interested in the remnants of my own childhood memories, I recollected a scene which had come into my mind now and then over a long period — for ever, as it seemed to me — and there were reliable indications that it must date from before the end of my third year of life. I saw myself standing in tears in front of a wardrobe [in Austrian usage: Kasten ] and demanding something, while my half-brother, twenty years older than me, was holding its door open, and then my mother suddenly came in, beautiful and slender, as if just coming home from a walk through the streets. I had used these words to describe the three-dimensional scene, but I could take it no further. I had no idea whether my brother was going to open or close the wardrobe — in the first translation of the image into words I called it a Schrank [‘wardrobe’ in standard German] — or why I was crying, or what my mother’s arrival had to do with it; I was tempted to explain it to myself as a memory of my older brother’s teasing me and being interrupted by our mother. Such misinterpretations of a remembered childhood scene are not at all unusual; we remember a situation, but it is unfocused, and we do not know exactly where the psychic emphasis lies. My analytical investigations led me to an entirely unexpected interpretation of this image. I had been missing my mother, and began to suspect that she might be shut up in the wardrobe — the Schrank or Kasten — so I asked my brother to open it. When he did, and I could see that my mother was not inside, I began screaming; that was the part I remembered, along with my mother’s appearance immediately afterwards, which calmed my fears and longings. But what made me, as a child, think of looking for my absent mother in the wardrobe? Some of my dreams from the same period relate vaguely to a nursemaid of whom I had certain other memories, for instance that she consistently used to make me hand over to her the small change people gave me as presents, a detail which itself could claim to figure as a screen memory for later events. This time, I decided to facilitate the task of interpretation, and I asked my now elderly mother, about the nursemaid. I learned a good deal, including the fact that this clever but dishonest character had stolen from the household on a large scale while my mother was lying in, and my half-brother had insisted on bringing legal charges against her. This information, casting a sudden bright light on my childhood memory, helped me to understand it. The nursemaid’s sudden disappearance had affected me quite deeply, and in fact I had turned to that same brother to ask where she was, probably because I had noticed that he had something to do with her removal from the household. Evasively playing on words, as he commonly did, he had told me that she was ‘in the clink [German: eingekastelt , a colloquial expression for ‘in jail’]’. I understood this answer in a purely childish way [as meaning ‘in the wardrobe’ — Kasten] and asked no more questions, since there seemed no more to learn. When my mother went out a little later I was anxious, fearing that my bad brother had shut her up too, just like the nursemaid, and I made him open the wardrobe for me. And now I also understand why my mother’s slender figure, which seemed to have been just restored, featured so prominently in my visual version of this childhood scene; I am two and a half years older than my sister, who was born at this time, and when I was three years old my half-brother left our household. 4

我想再举一个例子，说明看似随机的童年记忆如何通过分析研究而获得意义。在我四十三岁那年，当我开始对自己的童年记忆残片产生兴趣时，我回忆起一个场景，它在我脑海中时隐时现，仿佛永无止境。种种迹象表明，它一定发生在我三岁之前。我看到自己泪流满面地站在衣柜前（奥地利语：Kasten），向人索要着什么，而比我大二十岁的同父异母的哥哥正为我打开衣柜门，然后我的母亲突然走了进来，她美丽苗条，仿佛刚从街上散步回来。我曾用这些词语来描述这个立体的场景，但我却无法再进一步描述它。我当时完全不知道哥哥是要打开还是关上衣柜——在最初将画面翻译成文字时，我把它称为“Schrank”（德语中“衣柜”的意思）——也不知道我为什么哭，也不知道妈妈的到来和这件事有什么关系；我甚至想把它解释为哥哥捉弄我，然后被妈妈打断的记忆。这种对童年记忆的误解并不罕见；我们记得某个场景，但记忆模糊不清，我们并不清楚当时的心理重心在哪里。我的分析探究最终让我对这幅画面有了完全出乎意料的解读。我一直很想念妈妈，开始怀疑她可能被关在衣柜里——无论是“Schrank”还是“Kasten”——于是我让哥哥打开它。当他打开衣柜，我看到妈妈不在里面时，我开始尖叫；这就是我记得的部分，以及之后妈妈出现的情景，她的出现平息了我的恐惧和思念。但是什么让我在孩提时代就想到在衣橱里寻找失踪的母亲呢？同一时期我的一些梦境模糊地与一位保姆有关，我对她还有一些其他的记忆，比如她总是让我把别人送我的零钱都交给她——这个细节本身或许可以算作是后来事件的某种预兆。这一次，我决定借助一些方法来解读梦境，于是向年迈的母亲询问了关于这位保姆的事。我了解到不少，包括这个聪明却不诚实的女人在我母亲卧床期间大规模地偷窃了家里的东西，而我的同父异母的哥哥坚持要起诉她。这些信息如同拨开云雾见青天，让我对童年的记忆有了更深的理解。保姆的突然消失对我影响很大，事实上，我当时也曾向哥哥询问她的下落，或许是因为我注意到他与保姆的离开有关。他像往常一样玩弄文字游戏，含糊其辞地告诉我，她“在监狱里（德语：eingekastelt，是“在监狱里”的俗语）。”我当时只是幼稚地理解了这个答案（意思是“在衣柜里”——Kasten），并没有再问什么，因为似乎没什么可学的了。过了一会儿，妈妈出门了，我很焦虑，害怕我那坏哥哥也像保姆一样把她关了起来，于是我让他帮我打开衣柜。现在我也明白了，为什么妈妈纤细的身形——似乎刚刚恢复——在我童年记忆中如此突出；我比妹妹大两岁半，妹妹是那时出生的，而我三岁的时候，同父异母的哥哥就离开了家。

Notes

笔记

1 . ‘Enquěue sur les premiers souvenirs de l’enfance’ [‘An Inquiry into Early Childhood Memories’], L’année psychologique III, 1897.

1.《童年记忆的探究》，《心理学 III》，1897 年。

2 . ‘Study of Early Memories’, Psychological Review , 1901.

2.《早期记忆研究》，心理学评论，1901 年。

3 . I state this on the basis of several inquiries I have made.

3. 我根据我所做的几次调查得出此结论。

4 . Anyone with an interest in the mental processes of childhood will easily understand the deeper conditioning of my demand to my big brother. At the age of not quite three, I realized that my recently born sister had grown in my mother’s uterus. I was not at all pleased about the new baby and suspected, gloomily, that my mother’s body might be harbouring yet more children. The wardrobe symbolized the maternal womb to me; I therefore demanded to see inside the cupboard, and to that end I applied to my big brother. As other material shows, an older brother can replace a father as a little boy’s rival. Apart from my well-founded suspicion that this brother was responsible for putting the absent nursemaid in prison, I also feared that he had somehow implanted the new-born child in my mother’s body. My sense of disappointment when the wardrobe proved empty arose from the superficial motivation of my childish demand, and was misplaced in relation to my deeper level of feeling. On the other hand, my great satisfaction at noting my mother’s slender figure on her return is fully comprehensible only on that deeper level.

4. 任何对儿童心理过程感兴趣的人都很容易理解我向哥哥提出要求的深层原因。不到三岁的时候，我意识到刚出生的妹妹是在母亲的子宫里孕育的。我对这个新宝宝一点也不高兴，甚至阴郁地怀疑母亲的身体里可能还怀着其他孩子。衣柜对我来说象征着母体子宫；因此，我要求看看衣柜里面有什么，为此我向哥哥提出了要求。正如其他材料所表明的那样，哥哥可以取代父亲，成为小男孩的竞争对手。除了我理所当然地怀疑哥哥是把不在家的保姆送进监狱的罪魁祸首之外，我还害怕他以某种方式把新生儿植入了母亲的体内。当衣柜空空如也时，我的失望源于我孩童般要求的肤浅动机，与我内心深处的感受并不相符。另一方面，看到母亲回来时苗条的身材，我感到无比欣慰，这种感觉只有在更深层次上才能完全理解。

# ↩

V

V

Slips of the Tongue

口误

While our everyday vocabulary in our mother tongue seems immune to being forgotten, it is all the more prone to another disturbance, familiar to us as a ‘slip of the tongue’. When observed in normal people, such slips give the impression of being a preliminary stage for the phenomenon known as ‘paraphasia’ that occurs under pathological conditions. Here, for once, I am in a position where I can pay tribute to an earlier work. In 1895, Meringer and C. Mayer published a study on ‘Slips of the Tongue and Slips in Reading’, approaching the subject from a standpoint very far from my own. One of the authors, who wrote the major part of the text, is a philological scholar and was led by his linguistic interests to study the rules governing slips of the tongue. He hoped that they would enable him to conclude that there is ‘a certain intellectual mechanism […] in which the sounds of a word or a sentence, and the words themselves, show typical connections and interrelationships’ ( p. 10 ).

虽然我们日常使用的母语词汇似乎不会遗忘，但它却更容易受到另一种干扰，我们称之为“口误”。在正常人身上观察到的口误，给人一种错觉，仿佛是病理状态下发生的“错语症”的前兆。在这里，我难得有机会向一位前辈致敬。1895年，梅林格和C·梅耶发表了一篇题为《口误与阅读失误》的研究论文，他们从与我截然不同的角度探讨了这一主题。其中一位作者撰写了该书的主要部分，他是一位语言学家，出于对语言学的兴趣，他研究了口误的规律。他希望这些规律能让他得出结论：存在一种“特定的认知机制……在这种机制中，单词或句子的发音以及单词本身，都展现出典型的联系和相互关系”（第10页）。

The authors initially classify the examples of their collection of ‘slips of the tongue’ from a purely descriptive viewpoint: as reversals (for instance, the Milo of Venus instead of the Venus of Milo); anticipations or anticipated sounds (for instance, ‘Es war mir auf der Schwest…auf der Brust so schwer [‘I felt it weigh heavy on my breast’ but with Brust replaced by Schwest , echoing schwer and also suggesting Schwester , ‘sister’])’; echoes or resonances (for instance, ‘Ich fordere Sie auf, auf das Wohl unseres Chefs aufzustossen’ instead of anstossen [‘I will ask you to belch to the health of our leader’ instead of ‘drink a toast to the health of our leader’]); contaminations (for instance, ‘Er setzt sich auf den Hinterkopf’, from ‘Er setzt sich einen Kopf auf’ combined with ‘Er stellt sich auf die Hinterbeine’ [‘He stands up on the back of his head’, from ‘He is headstrong’ combined with ‘He gets up on his hind legs’]); and substitutions (for instance, ‘Ich gebe die Präparate in den Briefkasten’ for Brütkasten [‘I will put the specimens in the letterbox’ for ‘incubator’]), adding to these main categories some that are less important or less significant for our purposes here. It makes no difference to this system of classification whether the distortion, transposition, disfigurement, amalgamation or any other slip affects the separate sounds in a word, or syllables, or whole words of the intended sentence.

作者最初从纯粹描述的角度对他们收集的“口误”示例进行分类：颠倒（例如，维纳斯的米洛而不是米洛的维纳斯）；预期或预期的声音（例如，“Es war mir auf der Schwest…auf der Brust so schwer”[“我感到它沉重地压在我的胸口”，但 Brust 被 Schwest 取代，呼应了 schwer，也暗示了 Schwester，即“姐姐”]）；回声或共鸣（例如，“Ich fortdere Sie auf, auf das Wohl unserem Chefs aufgestossen”而不是 anstossen[“我会请你打嗝来祝我们的领导健康”而不是“为我们的领导的健康干杯”]）。混杂（例如，“Ersetzt sich auf den Hinterkopf”，由“Ersetzt sich einen Kopf auf”与“Er stellt sich auf die Hinterbeine”组合而成）和替换（例如，“I will put the specimens in the letterbox”代替“incubator”），此外还有一些不太重要或与我们此处讨论的目的关系不大的类别。对于这套分类系统而言，无论变形、移位、变形、合并或其他任何错误影响的是单词、音节还是整个句子中的单个音素，都无关紧要。

In order to explain the slips of the tongue he has observed, Meringer suggests that spoken sounds have different psychic strengths. If we give innervation to the first sound of a word or the first word of a sentence, that stimulatory process immediately affects subsequent sounds and words, and in so far as these innervations are simultaneous they can modify each other. Stimulation of the psychically more intense sound anticipates or echoes other sounds, thus disturbing the weaker process of innervation. It is then a question of determining which sounds in a word are the strongest. Meringer thinks that: ‘If we want to know which is the most intense sound in a word, we should observe ourselves trying to remember a forgotten word, for instance a name. Whatever comes back to the conscious mind first had the greatest intensity before it was forgotten’ ( p. 160 ). ‘Sounds of high value are therefore the initial sound of the root syllable, the initial sound of the word, and the stressed vowel or vowels’ ( p. 162 ).

为了解释他观察到的口误现象，梅林格提出，口语中的声音具有不同的心理强度。如果我们对一个词的第一个音或一个句子的第一个词进行神经刺激，这种刺激过程会立即影响后续的声音和词语，并且由于这些刺激是同时发生的，它们可以相互影响。对心理强度更高的声音的刺激会预先或回响其他声音，从而干扰较弱的声音的神经刺激过程。因此，问题在于确定一个词中哪些声音的心理强度最高。梅林格认为：“如果我们想知道一个词中最强烈的声音是什么，我们应该观察自己试图回忆一个遗忘的词，例如一个名字。最先回到意识中的，是它在被遗忘之前心理强度最高的声音”（第160页）。“因此，具有高价值的声音是词根音节的首音、词的首音以及重读元音”（第162页）。

Here I cannot help disagreeing. Whether the initial sound of a name is one of the strongest elements in the word or not, it is certainly wrong to claim that it will be the first sound of a forgotten word to be recalled to mind, so the rule Meringer gives above will not hold good. When we observe ourselves trying to remember a forgotten name we are relatively often convinced that it begins with a certain letter, but as often as not there turns out to be no basis for that conviction. Indeed, I would even say that we claim the wrong initial letter for the name in the majority of cases. In my own example of Signorelli the initial sound and the most important syllables were lost in the substitute name; only the weaker couple of syllables, elli , came back to my mind in the substitute name Botticelli. The following case may serve to show how few substitute names respect the initial sound of the forgotten name:

对此我不得不表示异议。无论名字的首音是否是该词最强的组成部分之一，断言它会是遗忘词最先被回忆起来的音肯定是错误的，因此梅林格上面提到的规则并不适用。当我们试图回忆一个遗忘的名字时，我们常常会确信它以某个字母开头，但这种确信往往毫无根据。事实上，我甚至可以说，在大多数情况下，我们认定的首字母都是错误的。以我自己的例子“Signorelli”为例，它的首音和最重要的音节在替代名中都丢失了；在替代名“Botticelli”中，我只能想起较弱的几个音节“elli”。以下案例或许可以说明，有多少替代名能够保留被遗忘名字的首音：

One day I could not remember the name of the small country whose capital is Monte Carlo. The substitutes I thought of were:

有一天，我突然想不起首都是蒙特卡洛的那个小国的名字。我能想到的替代词有：

Piedmont, Albania, Montevideo, Colico.

皮埃蒙特、阿尔巴尼亚、蒙得维的亚、科利科。

I soon replaced Albania by Montenegro , and it then struck me that the syllable mont (pronounced mon ) occurred in all my substitute names except the last. That made it easier for me to make my way from the name of Prince Albert to the name of the country I had forgotten, Monaco. Colico more or less follows the syllabic sequence and rhythm of the forgotten name.

我很快用黑山（Montenegro）替换了阿尔巴尼亚（Albania），这时我突然意识到，除了最后一个名字之外，我所有替换的名字里都出现了音节“mont”（发音为“mon”）。这让我更容易从阿尔贝亲王（Prince Albert）的名字联想到我遗忘的那个国家——摩纳哥（Monaco）。“Colico”这个名字的音节顺序和韵律也大致与我遗忘的那个名字相同。

Assuming that a mechanism similar to the mechanism already demonstrated in the forgetting of names may also operate to some extent in causing slips of the tongue, one is led to assess such phenomena on a more firmly established basis. Verbal disturbance in the form of a slip of the tongue can be caused, first, by the influence of another component in the same word or set of words — through an anticipation or echo of sound — or by another version within the sentence or its context that we intend to express (all the examples cited above from Meringer and Mayer belong in this category). Second, however, the disturbance can be caused, in a way analogous to the process in the Signorelli case, by influences outside the word, the sentence or the context, deriving from elements that we do not intend to express, and only the disturbance itself makes us aware of their arousal. The common factor in the mechanisms causing these two kinds of slips of the tongue would lie in the simultaneity of the arousal, and the distinguishing factor would be in its position within or outside the same sentence or context. At first the difference does not seem to be very great, deriving as it does from certain deductions drawn from the symptomatology of slips of the tongue. However, it is clear that only in the first instance is there any prospect that such slips of the tongue will allow us to draw conclusions from them about a mechanism linking sounds and words so that they will influence each other — conclusions, that is to say, such as a linguistic scholar would hope to gain from studying the phenomenon. In the case of disturbance by influences outside the same sentence or linguistic context, discovering the disturbing elements would be the main concern, and we would then have to look at the question of whether the mechanism of this disturbance can, in itself, tell us anything about the laws of linguistic construction that we may assume to be operating.

假设类似于遗忘姓名机制的某种机制也可能在一定程度上导致口误，那么我们就能以更坚实的基础来评估这类现象。口误这种言语干扰，首先可能由同一词语或词组中其他成分的影响引起——例如通过声音的预判或回响——或者由句子或其语境中我们想要表达的另一个版本引起（以上引用的梅林格和梅耶的例子均属于此类）。其次，口误也可能以类似于西尼奥雷利案例的方式，由词语、句子或语境之外的影响引起，这些影响源自我们无意表达的元素，而只有口误本身才能让我们意识到它们的出现。导致这两种口误的机制的共同点在于这些影响同时出现，而区别在于它们出现在同一句子或语境中还是之外。起初，这种差异似乎并不显著，因为它源于对口误症状学的某些推论。然而，显而易见的是，只有在第一种情况下，我们才有可能从口误中得出关于声音和词语之间相互影响的机制的结论——也就是说，语言学者希望通过研究这种现象获得的结论。如果干扰因素来自同一句子或语言语境之外，那么发现干扰因素将是主要关注点，然后我们才需要考察这种干扰机制本身是否能够告诉我们一些关于我们假定正在发挥作用的语言结构规律的信息。

It cannot be said that Meringer and Mayer have overlooked the possibility that speech disturbance may arise from ‘complex psychic influences’, elements outside the word, the sentence or the sequence of words themselves. They could hardly help noticing that their theory of the psychic imbalance of strength between sounds is adequate, strictly speaking, only to elucidate disturbances of sound, anticipations of sound and echoes of sound. Where verbal disturbances cannot be reduced to disturbances of sound, for instance in substituted and contaminated words, they themselves, without a second thought, have looked for the cause of a slip of the tongue outside its intended context, demonstrating their point with some good examples. I quote the following passages:

不能说梅林格和梅耶忽略了言语障碍可能源于“复杂的心理影响”，即词语、句子或词序之外的因素。他们几乎不可能不注意到，严格来说，他们关于声音之间心理强度失衡的理论仅足以解释声音障碍、声音预判和声音回响。当言语障碍无法归结为声音障碍时，例如在词语替换和词语污染的情况下，他们毫不犹豫地从语境之外寻找口误的原因，并用一些恰当的例子来论证他们的观点。我引用以下段落：

( p. 62 ) ‘Ru. was describing certain things that he privately called Schweinereien [obscenities, filthiness, from Schwein , ‘pig’]. However, trying to find a milder way of putting it, he said, “Dann aber sind Tatsachen zum Vorschwein gekommen [meaning to say Vorschein : ‘But then facts came to light’].” Mayer and I were present, and Ru. admitted that he had indeed been thinking of Schweinereien. The similarity of sound is enough to explain the way in which the presence of this word in his mind suddenly betrayed itself through another word, which ought to have been Vorschein. ’

（第62页）“鲁当时正在描述一些他私下里称之为‘Schweinereien’（污秽之物，源自Schwein，意为‘猪’）的东西。然而，为了找到一种更温和的说法，他说：‘Dann aber sind Tatsachen zum Vorschwein gekommen’（意为‘但后来真相大白了’）。’我和迈耶当时都在场，鲁承认他当时确实想到的是‘Schweinereien’。这两个词发音相似，足以解释为什么他脑海中突然冒出的这个词会通过另一个词——本应是‘Vorschein’——暴露出来。”

( p. 73 ) “‘Hovering” or “wandering” verbal structures play a considerable part in substitutions as well as contaminations, and probably to an even greater degree. Although they may be subliminal they are in operative proximity, and can easily be brought to light by some similarity to the intended spoken complex, producing a slip or disarranging the verbal construction. Such “hovering” or “wandering” verbal structures are often, as we have pointed out, resonances or echoes of something recently said.’

（第73页）“‘徘徊’或‘游移’的语言结构在替代和混淆中都扮演着相当重要的角色，而且可能在混淆中扮演着更为重要的角色。尽管它们可能是潜意识的，但它们在运作上却非常接近，并且很容易通过与预期的口语复合体之间的某种相似性而被揭示出来，从而导致口误或语言结构的紊乱。正如我们所指出的，这种‘徘徊’或‘游移’的语言结构通常是对最近所说的话的回响或回声。”

( p. 97 ) ‘A slip may also be made possible by similarity, when another and similar word lies just beneath the threshold of consciousness but the speaker has no intention of uttering it. This is how substitutions occur. I hope that examination of my rules will confirm their validity. But if they are to be examined (and if someone else is speaking) we have to be clear about everything the speaker was thinking. 1 I add an instructive case. We heard a schoolteacher called Herr Li. saying: “Die Frau würde mir Furcht ein l agen [‘That woman would give me a fright’, but with an incorrect l in the intended verb einjagen ].” I was baffled, since I could not explain the l to myself, and was emboldened to point out the substitution of “ein l agen” for “ein j agen” to the speaker, whereupon he immediately replied: “Oh, that’s because I was thinking: Ich wäre nicht in der Lage [I would not be in a position (to)], etc.”

（第97页）“口误也可能由相似性引起，当另一个相似的词恰好处于意识的临界点，但说话者并没有说出口的意图时。这就是替代发生的方式。我希望对我的规则进行检验能够证实它们的有效性。但如果要检验这些规则（并且说话者是其他人），我们必须清楚地了解说话者当时的想法。 1 我再补充一个有启发性的例子。我们听到一位名叫李先生的教师说：“Die Frau würde mir Furcht einlagen [‘那个女人会吓到我’，但本意是想说动词 einjagen，却把 l 拼错了]。”我感到困惑，因为我无法向自己解释这个 l，于是我大胆地向说话者指出“einlagen”代替了“einjagen”，他立即回答说：“哦，那是因为我当时在想：Ich wäre nicht in der Lage [我不会处于（可以）的位置]，等等。”

‘In another case, I asked R. von Schid. how his sick horse was doing. He replied: “Ja, das draut…dauert vielleicht noch einen Monat [‘Well, it may last another month’, but with an intrusive r in the verb dauert ].” I could make nothing of the r in draut , since it could hardly have been caused by the r towards the end of dauert. I pointed this out to R. von S., who explained that he had been thinking, “Das ist eine traurige Geschichte [It’s a sad story].” The speaker had two answers in mind, and they had mingled.’

“在另一次谈话中，我问R. von Schid他的马情况如何。他回答说：‘Ja, das draut…dauert vielleicht noch einen Monat’（‘嗯，也许还能撑一个月’，但动词dauert中多了一个r音）。’我完全不明白draut中的r是什么意思，因为它不太可能是由dauert末尾的r引起的。我把这一点告诉了R. von S.，他解释说他当时想的是‘Das ist eine traurige Geschichte’（这是一个悲伤的故事）。’说话者脑子里有两个答案，它们混杂在一起了。”

It will be obvious that study of the ‘wandering’ verbal but subliminal structures which were not meant to be uttered, together with a demand to know what the speaker was thinking about, approximate to the conditions of my own ‘analyses’. I too am in search of unconscious material, and indeed I go about it in the same way, except that, using a complex series of associations, I have to trace a longer route from the ideas of the person I am questioning to the discovery of the disruptive element.

显而易见，对那些本不该说出口的、游离的、潜意识的语言结构的研究，以及对说话者内心想法的探究，与我自身的“分析”条件颇为相似。我也在寻找无意识的素材，而且我的方法也与他类似，只不过，我需要运用一系列复杂的联想，从被探究者的思想出发，追溯一条更长的路径，最终发现那个破坏性的因素。

I will dwell briefly on another interesting procedure demonstrated in Meringer’s examples. According to the author himself, it is some similarity of a word in the intended sentence with another word, one not meant to be spoken, which allows the latter to enter the conscious mind by causing a distortion, a mixed construction, or a structural compromise (contamination):

我将简要地探讨梅林格例子中展示的另一个有趣的现象。根据作者本人的说法，这是因为目标句子中的某个词与另一个原本不打算说出口的词存在某种相似性，这种相似性使得后者能够通过造成扭曲、混合结构或结构上的妥协（污染）而进入意识层面：

jagen, dauert, Vorschein

狩猎需要时间，外表

lagen, traurig,…schwein.

它们可怜地躺着……猪。

In my work on The Interpretation of Dreams 2 I showed what part compression played in creating what may be called the manifest content of the dream out of the latent dream ideas. Some similarity of objects or verbal ideas between two elements in the unconscious material causes the creation of a third composite or compromise idea, one representing both components in the content of the dream, and it is because of this origin that the new idea frequently tends to pull in two different directions. The formation of substitutions and contaminations in slips of the tongue is thus the first stage in that process of compression which is most active in the construction of dreams.

在我的著作《梦的解析》中，我阐述了压缩在将潜意识的梦境观念转化为所谓的显性梦境内容的过程中所起的作用。潜意识素材中两个元素之间物体或语言观念的相似性会导致第三个复合或妥协观念的产生，该观念代表了梦境内容中的两个组成部分。正是由于这种起源，新观念常常倾向于向两个不同的方向发展。因此，口误中出现的替代和混淆是压缩过程的第一阶段，也是梦境构建中最活跃的阶段。

In a small article meant for a wide public ( Neue Freie Presse of 23 August 1900: ‘How slips of the tongue occur’), Meringer claimed that there is a particular practical significance in certain cases of verbal confusions, those in which a word is mentally replaced by its opposite. ‘You will probably remember the words of the President of the Austrian Parliament when, some time ago, he opened a session by announcing: “Members of this House! I confirm the presence of such-and-such a number of gentlemen, and hereby declare this session closed. ” Only the general mirth made him realize what he had said, whereupon he corrected his mistake. In this case the explanation may well have been that the President wished he was already in a position to close the session, since nothing very productive could be expected to come of it, but — and this is a frequent phenomenon — his underlying idea made its influence felt, at least in part, and as a result he said the opposite of what he meant to say: “closed” and not “open”. However, many and various observations have taught me that verbal opposites are very often interchanged; they are associated with each other in our verbal awareness, they lie close together, and the wrong word can easily be summoned up by mistake.’

在一篇面向大众的短文（1900年8月23日《新自由报》：“口误是如何发生的”）中，梅林格声称，某些语言混淆的情况具有特殊的实际意义，即人们在脑海中将一个词替换成了它的反义词。“你们或许还记得奥地利议会议长不久前在一次会议上的发言。他宣布：‘各位议员！我确认有某某先生出席，并在此宣布本次会议结束。’只有众人的哄笑才让他意识到自己说错了话，于是他纠正了自己的错误。在这种情况下，解释很可能是议长希望能够立即结束会议，因为预计这次会议不会有什么实质性的成果。但是——这种情况很常见——他原本的想法至少在一定程度上影响了他，结果他说出了与他本意相反的话：‘结束’而不是‘开始’。”然而，许多不同的观察告诉我，词语中的反义词经常被互换使用；它们在我们的语言意识中彼此关联，它们彼此靠近，很容易因为错误而说出错误的词。

In instances of interchanged words, it is not always as easy as it was in the case of the Austrian President to make it seem likely that a slip of the tongue arose from opposition to the intended remark in the speaker’s mind. I found a similar mechanism operating in my analysis of the aliquis case, where internal opposition was expressed by the speaker’s forgetting a word rather than replacing it by its opposite. To level out that difference, however, let me note that the little word aliquis cannot really suggest a contradiction of the kind arising from the ideas of ‘to close’ and ‘to open’, and that the verb ‘to open’, as a common part of everyday vocabulary, is proof against being forgotten.

在词语互换的情况下，并非总能像奥地利总统的例子那样，轻易地让人觉得口误是说话者内心反对原意所致。我在分析“aliquis”一词时也发现了类似的机制，说话者并非用反义词代替，而是通过遗忘某个词来表达内心的反对。不过，为了消除这种差异，需要指出的是，“aliquis”这个词本身并不能暗示“关闭”和“打开”这类概念所引发的矛盾，而且“打开”作为日常用语，本身就足以证明它不会被遗忘。

If these last examples from Meringer and Mayer show us that speech disturbance can equally well originate in the influence of sounds and words intended to be spoken, anticipating or echoing others within the same sentence, or in the influence of words outside the intended sentence, which would not otherwise have given away the fact that they suggested themselves , we shall want to start by finding out whether we can draw any clear distinction between these two categories of slips of the tongue, and how we can tell the two apart. At this point, however, I must mention the comments of Wundt, who discusses instances of slips of the tongue in his comprehensive work on the development of language ( Völkerpsychologie , vol. I, part 1, pp. 371ff, 1900). A constant characteristic of these and related instances, according to Wundt, is the presence of certain psychic influences. ‘First, as a positive requirement, is the uninhibited flow of verbal and tonal associations aroused by the sounds uttered. This is accompanied, as a negative factor, by the suspension or remission of those operations of the will which inhibit that flow, and of the careful attention which is also a function of the will. Whether the play of association is expressed in anticipation of a coming sound or reproduction of the sound that has just been uttered, or in the insertion of what is usually a very familiar sound among others, or finally whether it is expressed in entirely different words that have an associative relationship with the spoken sounds and bring influence to bear on them — all this merely describes differences in the tendency and above all in the scope of the associations entering the mind, not in their general nature. In many cases, moreover, it is hard to decide in which category a certain disturbance belongs, and perhaps it would have been more correct to derive it from a combination of several reasons, on the principle of the complexity of causes’ 3 (pp. 380 and 381).

如果梅林格和梅耶的最后这些例子表明，言语障碍既可能源于预期说出的声音和词语的影响（这些声音和词语在同一句子中预先发出或重复其他声音和词语），也可能源于预期句子之外的词语的影响（这些词语本身并不会暴露它们是无意中产生的），那么我们首先需要弄清楚能否对这两种口误做出明确的区分，以及如何区分它们。然而，在此我必须提及冯特的评论。冯特在其关于语言发展的著作（《民族心理学》，第一卷，第一部分，第371页及后续页，1900年）中讨论了口误的例子。根据冯特的说法，这些以及相关例子的一个共同特征是存在某些心理因素。“首先，一个积极的要求是，由所发出的声音引起的言语和语调联想能够不受抑制地流动。”伴随这一负面因素的是，抑制这种思维流动的意志活动以及作为意志功能的专注力的暂停或减弱。联想的运作方式，无论是对即将到来的声音的预期，还是对刚刚发出的声音的复述，抑或是在众多声音中插入一个通常非常熟悉的声音，又或是用与口语声音具有联想关系并对其产生影响的完全不同的词语来表达——所有这些都仅仅描述了进入思维的联想倾向，尤其是联想范围的差异，而非联想的本质差异。此外，在许多情况下，很难确定某种干扰属于哪一类，或许根据“原因的复杂性”原则，将其归因于多种原因的综合作用会更为准确（第380页和381页）。

I think these remarks by Wundt are thoroughly justified and very instructive. Perhaps one might lay a little more emphasis than he does on the way in which the positive factor encouraging slips of the tongue — the uninhibited flow of associations — and the negative factor — the suspension of the attention that would inhibit them — regularly operate together, the two factors being only different aspects of the same process. With the suspension of the attention that would inhibit it, the uninhibited flow of associations is activated and may be said, even more definitely, to do so through that suspension.

我认为冯特的这些评论完全合理且极具启发性。或许我们应该比他更强调一下，促使口误发生的积极因素——即联想的自由流动——和消极因素——即抑制联想的注意力被暂停——是如何经常共同作用的，因为这两个因素只是同一过程的不同方面。当抑制联想的注意力被暂停时，联想的自由流动就会被激活，甚至可以说，正是通过这种注意力的暂停才得以激活。

Among the examples of slips of the tongue that I have collected myself I can scarcely find any where I have had to derive the verbal disturbance solely from what Wundt calls the ‘contact effect of sounds’. Almost always, I discover that there is also a disruptive influence from something outside the intended utterance, and that this disruptive element is either a single idea that has remained unconscious, makes itself felt in the slip of the tongue, and can often be brought into the conscious mind only after thorough analysis, or it is a more general psychic motive directed against the intended utterance as a whole.

在我收集的口误例子中，我几乎找不到任何一个仅仅因为冯特所说的“声音接触效应”而导致言语障碍的例子。几乎在所有情况下，我都会发现，除了预期的言语之外，还存在某种干扰因素。这种干扰因素要么是一个潜意识中存在的单一想法，它在口误中显现出来，通常只有经过彻底分析才能被带入意识层面；要么是一种更普遍的心理动机，它针对的是整个预期的言语表达。

1) My daughter bit into an apple and pulled a nasty face; I was going to quote the lines:

1）我女儿咬了一口苹果，做了个鬼脸；我本来想引用那句话：

Der Affe gar possierlich ist.

这只猴子真是太可爱了。

Zumal wenn er vom Apfel frisst.

尤其是当他吃苹果的时候。

[The monkey is very funny, particularly when he’s eating an apple.]

这只猴子非常滑稽，尤其是在它吃苹果的时候。

Instead, I began to say: ‘Der Apfe …’ This seems to be a contamination of Affe by Apfel (a compromise structure), or alternatively it may be seen as anticipation of the word Apfel which I was about to utter. The fact is, however, that I had already begun on the quotation once, and I made no mistake the first time. My slip of the tongue was made only when I repeated it, as I had to because my daughter’s attention was elsewhere when I first quoted her the lines, and she was not listening. This repetition, and my impatience to get my quotation of the lines over and done with, must be included as part of the motivation for my slip of the tongue, which represents a case of compression.

相反，我开始说：“Der Apfe…”这似乎是Affe被Apfel混淆了（一种妥协结构），或者也可以理解为我预想即将说出的Apfel这个词。然而，事实是，我之前已经引用过一遍，而且第一次并没有出错。我的口误只发生在重复的时候，因为我第一次引用时女儿的注意力不在她身上，她根本没在听，所以我不得不重复。这种重复，以及我急于结束引用的心情，必然是我口误的原因之一，这属于一种思维压缩的情况。

2) My daughter told me: ‘I’m writing to Frau Schresinger .’ In fact the lady’s name was Schlesinger . This slip was probably connected with a tendency to make articulation easier, since it is difficult to say the letter l after a repetition of r . However, I must add that my daughter’s slip of the tongue came a few minutes after I had said Apfe instead of Affe. Slips of the tongue are very infectious, in the same way as the forgetting of names, as noted by Meringer and Mayer. However, I can give no reason for this psychic tendency to contagion.

2）我女儿告诉我：“我要写信给施雷辛格夫人。”实际上，那位女士的名字是施莱辛格。这种口误可能与她为了方便发音而采取的习惯有关，因为在重复发完r音后，很难再发出l音。不过，我必须补充一点，我女儿的口误发生在我把Affe说成Apfe几分钟之后。正如梅林格和迈耶所指出的，口误和忘记名字一样，都具有很强的传染性。然而，我无法解释这种心理上的传染倾向。

3) ‘Ich klappe zusammen wie ein Tassenmescher — Taschenmesser [‘I’m folding up like a — penknife’, with Taschenmesser mispronounced as Tassenmescher ],’ a woman patient told me at the beginning of her session of treatment, and, again, this could be put down to the difficulty of articulation (as in tongue-twisters such as Wiener Weiber Wäscherinnen waschen weisse Wäsche [Viennese washerwomen wash white washing] and Fischflosse [fish fin]). When I pointed out her slip of the tongue she immediately replied: ‘Yes, but that was only because you said Ernscht today.’ Sure enough, I actually had greeted her by saying: ‘ Heute wird es also Ernst [We’re in earnest today, then],’ because it was to be our last session before the holiday, and I had jokingly drawn out the pronunciation of Ernst to make it Ernscht. However, she kept making more slips of the tongue, and at last I realized that she was not just imitating me but had a particular reason to linger on the word ernst [earnest] in her unconscious mind, since it can also be a proper name, Ernst [Ernest]. 4

3) “Ich klappe zusammen wie ein Tassenmescher — Taschenmesser [‘我像一把小刀一样折叠起来’，Taschenmesser 被误读为 Tassenmescher]，”一位女性患者在治疗开始时告诉我，这又可以归因于发音困难（如 Wiener Weiber 等绕口令） Wäscherinnen waschen weisse Wäsche [维也纳洗衣女工洗白水] 和 Fischflosse [鱼翅])。当我指出她口误时，她立刻回答说：“是的，但那是因为你今天说了‘Ernscht’。” 确实，我当时跟她打招呼时说的是：“Heute wird es also Ernst [那么，我们今天认真起来了]”，因为那是假期前的最后一次课，我开玩笑地把“Ernst”的发音拉长，说成了“Ernscht”。然而，她继续口误，最后我意识到她不仅仅是在模仿我，而是在潜意识里特别在意“ernst”（认真）这个词，因为它也可以是一个专有名词，Ernst（欧内斯特）。

4) ‘Ich bin so verschnupft, ich kann nicht durch die Ase natmen — Nase atmen [‘I have such a bad cold I can’t breathe through my nose’, with Nase atmen mispronounced as Ase natmen , in a spoonerism],’ said the same patient on another occasion. She immediately realized how she had come to make that slip of the tongue, ‘I catch the tram every day in Hasenauerstrasse, and this morning, as I was waiting for it, I thought that if I were a Frenchwoman I would call the street Asenauerstrasse , because the French never pronounce an initial H .’ She then embarked on a series of reminiscences about French people she had met, and after going a long way round the subject she came up with a memory of herself at the age of fourteen, when she took the part of Picarde, in which she had to speak broken German, in the little play Kurmärker und Picarde. By a coincidence, there was a guest from Paris in her lodgings at present, a fact that had aroused this whole series of memories. The transposition of the sounds was therefore the result of disturbance by an unconscious idea in an entirely different context.

4）“Ich bin so verschnupft, ich kann nicht durch die Ase natmen — Nase atmen [‘我感冒太严重了，鼻子都喘不过气来’，这里把 Nase atmen 误读成了 Ase natmen，犯了音位混淆的错误]，”这位病人在另一次谈话中说道。她立刻意识到自己为什么会说错话，“我每天都在 Hasenauerstrasse 坐电车，今天早上等车的时候，我想如果我是个法国人，我就会把这条街叫做 Asenauerstrasse，因为法国人从来不发 H 的音。” 然后，她开始回忆起自己遇到的法国人，绕了好大弯子之后，她想起了自己十四岁时在小剧《库尔马克和皮卡德》中扮演皮卡德的经历，当时她需要说一口蹩脚的德语。巧合的是，她当时的住处正好有一位来自巴黎的客人，这件事唤起了她所有的回忆。因此，声音的错位是由于潜意识中一个完全不同情境下的想法所干扰造成的。

5) I observed a slip of the tongue operating similarly in another woman patient, whose power of recollection forsook her while she was telling me about a long-forgotten event in her childhood. Her memory refused to tell her what part of her body it was that a certain intrusive and lustful hand had touched. Directly afterwards she visited a woman friend, and was discussing summer holiday cottages with her. Asked about the location of her cottage in M. she said: an der Berglende [on the loin of the mountain] instead of Berglehne [on the side of the mountain].

5）我观察到另一位女病人也出现了类似的口误。她在向我讲述一段早已被遗忘的童年往事时，突然失去了记忆。她完全想不起来究竟是哪只充满欲望的手触碰了她身体的哪个部位。事后，她去拜访了一位女性朋友，两人正在讨论度假小屋。当被问及她在M.的小屋具体位置时，她脱口而出“an der Berglende”（山腰），而不是“Berglehne”（山坡）。

6) When I asked another patient at the end of her session how her uncle was, she replied: ‘I don’t know; these days I see him only in flagranti .’ Next day she began: ‘I felt really ashamed of myself, giving you such a silly answer. You must have thought me a very uneducated person, always getting foreign words mixed up. What I meant to say was en passant .’ At this point we did not know where she had found the incorrectly used foreign phrase. In the same session, however, and going on from what we had been discussing the day before, she came up with a reminiscence to which being caught in flagranti was central. The previous day’s slip of the tongue, therefore, anticipated the memory of which she was not yet consciously thinking.

6）在一次治疗结束时，我问另一位病人她叔叔的情况，她回答说：“我不知道；最近我只能看到他被当场抓获。”第二天，她开始说：“我真为自己感到羞愧，竟然给了你这么愚蠢的答案。你肯定觉得我很没文化，总是把外语搞混。我本来想说的是‘en passant’（顺便一提）。”当时我们并不知道她是在哪里听到这个用错的外语短语的。然而，在同一次治疗中，基于我们前一天的讨论，她回忆起一件与被当场抓获有关的往事。因此，前一天的口误预示了她尚未意识到的那段记忆。

7) With another patient, a point in her analysis came where I had to express my suspicion that at the time we were discussing she felt ashamed of her family, and had blamed her father for something, we were not yet sure what. She did not remember this, and said that anyway it was unlikely. However, she went on to talk about her family: ‘You have to say one thing for them; they’re not part of the common herd, they’re all well known for their Geiz [avarice] — I meant to say Geist [intellect, wit].’ So now we knew the real accusation that her memory had suppressed. It is quite common for the idea one is trying to keep at bay to emerge in a slip of the tongue (cf. Meringer’s case of zum Vorschwein gekommen ). The only difference is that in Meringer’s example the subject was trying to suppress something he knew, whereas my patient did not know what she was suppressing, or one might say that she did not know either that she was keeping any idea at bay, or what idea it was.

7）在另一位病人身上，分析过程中，我不得不表达我的怀疑：在我们讨论的时候，她可能对自己的家庭感到羞耻，并且责怪过她的父亲，但我们当时还不确定是什么事。她不记得这件事了，并说无论如何都不太可能。然而，她接着谈到她的家人：“你得说他们有一点很了不起；他们不属于普通人，他们都以他们的‘Geiz’（贪婪）而闻名——我本想说的是‘Geist’（智慧、机智）。” 所以现在我们知道了她记忆中被压抑的真正指责。人们试图隐藏的想法在口误中流露出来是很常见的（参见梅林格的案例，即“zum Vorschwein gekommen”）。唯一的区别在于，梅林格的例子中，受试者试图压制他所知道的事情，而我的病人不知道她压制的是什么，或者可以说，她既不知道自己压制了什么想法，也不知道那是什么想法。

8) The following example of a slip of the tongue was also the result of an intentional suppression of an idea. One day in the Dolomites I meet two ladies in walking dress. I accompanied them for a little way, and we talked about the pleasures and pains of a walking holiday. One of the ladies admitted that there were a number of disadvantages to a day spent out walking. ‘The fact is,’ she said, ‘it’s not at all comfortable to be out in the sun all day until your blouse and under-vest are drenched in sweat.’ At one point in bringing out this sentence she had to overcome a small hesitation. Then she went on: ‘But when you get nach Hose [ Hose , ‘knickers’, substituted for nach House , ‘home’] and you can change your clothes …’ I imagine that this slip of the tongue hardly needs much study to explain it. The lady had obviously begun by intending to enumerate her items of underwear in full, ‘blouse, under-vest and knickers’, but for reasons of decorum refrained from naming the third garment. However, in the next sentence, which was quite independent in content, the suppressed word Hose involuntarily emerged as a distortion of the similar phrase nach Hause.

8）下面这个口误的例子也是有意压抑某种想法的结果。有一天在多洛米蒂山脉，我遇到两位穿着徒步装的女士。我陪她们走了一小段路，我们聊起了徒步旅行的酸甜苦辣。其中一位女士承认，徒步旅行也有不少缺点。“事实上，”她说，“整天待在阳光下，直到衬衫和背心都被汗水浸透，一点也不舒服。” 她说这句话的时候，似乎有点犹豫。然后她接着说：“但是当你回到家（nach House，用“nach House”代替“nach Hose”，指内裤）之后，就可以换衣服了……” 我想，这个口误应该不用费什么心思去研究就能明白。这位女士显然一开始打算把她的内衣全部列举出来：“衬衫、背心和内裤”，但出于礼貌，她没有提及第三件衣物。然而，在下一句内容完全独立的句子中，被她省略的“Hose”一词却不由自主地出现了，它似乎是对类似短语“nach Hause”的一种曲解。

9) ‘If you want to buy carpets, try Kaufmann in Matthäusgasse. I think I can safely recommend you to go there,’ a lady told me. I repeated what she had said: ‘Oh, so you really think I should try Matthäus … I mean Kaufmann.’ My giving one name instead of another looks like the result of mere inattention, and the lady’s remark had in fact distracted me, turning my attention to something else, of far more importance to me than carpets. As it happens, the building where my wife lived before we were married was in Matthäusgasse, but its main entrance was in another street, and I realized that I had forgotten the name of that street and could only recall it to my mind by a circuitous train of thought. The name Matthäus on which I dwelt was thus a substitute for the forgotten name of the street, and a more suitable one than the name Kaufmann, since Matthäus is exclusively a personal name, but Kaufmann is not [it is not only a surname but also means ‘merchant’, ‘dealer’], and in fact the street I had forgotten also bears a personal name, Radetzky.

9）一位女士告诉我：“如果你想买地毯，可以去马特乌斯街的考夫曼地毯店看看。我觉得我可以放心地推荐你去那里。”我重复了她的话：“哦，所以你真的觉得我应该去马特乌斯……我是说考夫曼地毯店。”我把店名记错，看起来像是一时疏忽，但实际上，那位女士的话分散了我的注意力，让我想到了另一件对我来说比地毯重要得多的事情。碰巧的是，我妻子婚前住的那栋楼就在马特乌斯街，但它的正门在另一条街上，我这才意识到我忘记了那条街的名字，只能通过一番迂回的回忆才想起来。因此，我居住的马特乌斯（Matthäus）这个名字，就成了那条被遗忘的街道名字的替代品，而且比考夫曼（Kaufmann）这个名字更合适，因为马特乌斯（Matthäus）完全是一个人名，而考夫曼（Kaufmann）不是（它不仅是姓氏，还有“商人”、“交易商”的意思），事实上，我忘记的那条街道也有一个人名，叫拉德茨基（Radetzky）。

10) I could equally well include the following case among the ‘Errors’ to be discussed later, but I will cite it here because the phonetic relationships accounting for the compensatory word are particularly clear. A woman patient told me her dream: she dreamed that a child had decided to kill itself by snakebite, and did so. She watched the child writhing in pain, and so forth. I now wanted her to locate what had happened during the day that was connected with her dream. She remembered at once that she had been to hear a popular lecture that evening, on first aid in cases of snakebite. If an adult and a child have been bitten at the same time, the audience was told, the child’s injury must be treated first, and she also remembered the lecturer’s instructions for treatment. It all depended, he had said, on which species of snake bit you. Here I interrupted, asking her: ‘Didn’t he tell you that we have very few poisonous snakes in this country, and which the most dangerous species are?’ ‘Yes, he particularly mentioned the Klapperschlange [rattlesnake].’ My laughter made her realize that she had slipped up. However, instead of simply correcting the name, she returned to her statement. ‘Oh no, of course we don’t have rattlesnakes here; it was the viper he mentioned. However did I come to say rattlesnake?’ I suspected it was through confusing the ideas concealed by her dream. Suicide by snakebite can hardly be anything but a reference to the beautiful Kl eo p at r a [the German spelling of Cleopatra]. The considerable similarity of sound between the two words in German, the coincidence of the letters Kl … p … r , appearing in that order, and the emphasis on the vowel a cannot be overlooked. The strong connection between the noun Klapperschlange and the name of Kleopatra caused her to suspend her judgement for a moment, and as a result she found nothing odd about the idea of the lecturer’s instructing his Viennese audience on the treatment of rattlesnake bites. She normally knows as well as I do that rattlesnakes are not among our native fauna. Nor should she be blamed for so glibly transferring the rattlesnake to Egypt, since we commonly put everything non-European and exotic into the same category in our minds, and I had to stop and think for a moment myself before saying that rattlesnakes are found only in the New World.

10）我完全可以将以下案例列入稍后要讨论的“错误”范畴，但我在此引用，是因为其中解释补偿词的语音关系非常清晰。一位女病人告诉我她的梦：她梦见一个孩子决定被蛇咬死，而且真的这么做了。她看着孩子痛苦地扭动着身体，等等。现在我想让她回忆一下当天发生了什么与这个梦相关的事情。她立刻想起那天晚上她去听了一场关于蛇咬伤急救的讲座。讲座上说，如果一个大人和一个小孩同时被咬伤，必须先处理小孩的伤口，她也记得讲师的指导。讲师说，这一切都取决于咬你的是哪种蛇。我打断了她的话，问道：“他没告诉你我们国家毒蛇很少，最危险的蛇是哪些吗？” “是的，他特别提到了响尾蛇。” 我的笑声让她意识到自己说漏了嘴。然而，她并没有纠正蛇的名字，而是继续说道：“哦，不，我们这里当然没有响尾蛇；他提到的是蝰蛇。我怎么会说响尾蛇呢？” 我怀疑是她把梦境中隐藏的想法混淆了。被蛇咬自杀，除了指代美丽的埃及艳后克利奥帕特拉（德语拼写为Kleopatra）之外，几乎不可能有其他解释。这两个词在德语中的发音非常相似，字母Kl…p…r的顺序也相同，而且都强调了元音a，这些都不能被忽视。 “响尾蛇”这个词与克利奥帕特拉的名字之间强烈的联系，让她一时之间无法做出判断，因此，她觉得讲师向维也纳听众讲解如何处理响尾蛇咬伤这件事并没有什么不妥。她和我一样清楚，响尾蛇并非我们本土的动物。她也不应该因为如此轻易地将响尾蛇与埃及联系起来而受到责备，因为我们通常会将所有非欧洲的、外来的事物归为一类，而我自己也需要停下来思考片刻，才能说出响尾蛇只生活在新大陆。

More confirmation came to light in the further course of her analysis. The day before, the dreamer had seen Strasser’s statuary group of Mark Antony, which is near her home, for the first time. This was the second cause of her dream (the first being the snakebite lecture). In the later part of the dream she was cradling a child in her arms, and this scene brought Gretchen [of the Faust legend and Goethe’s drama] to mind. Other ideas produced reminiscences of Arria und Messalina [by the dramatist Adolf Wilbrandt]. The emergence in her dream of so many names from stage plays had already made me suspect that in the past the dreamer had cherished a secret wish to be a professional actress. The beginning of the dream, in which a child decided to commit suicide by snakebite, really meant simply that, as a child, she was determined to be a famous actress some day. Finally, the train of thought leading to the subject at the heart of her dream derived from the name Messalina. Certain recent incidents had made her anxious about her only brother, who might be about to contract an unsuitable marriage with a non- Aryan woman — and if he did it would be a mésalliance.

在进一步的分析中，更多线索浮出水面。前一天，做梦者第一次看到了斯特拉瑟创作的马克·安东尼雕像群，它就在她家附近。这是她做梦的第二个原因（第一个原因是关于蛇咬的讲座）。在梦的后半部分，她怀抱着一个孩子，这一幕让她想起了浮士德传说和歌德戏剧中的格雷琴。其他一些想法则让她联想到了阿道夫·维尔布兰特的剧作《阿丽亚与梅萨利娜》。梦中出现这么多舞台剧的名字，让我怀疑做梦者过去曾暗自渴望成为一名职业演员。梦的开头，一个孩子决定用蛇咬自杀，这实际上意味着她小时候就立志要成为一名著名演员。最终，她梦境的核心主题源于梅萨利娜这个名字。最近发生的一些事情让她担心她唯一的弟弟，他可能即将与一位非雅利安女性缔结不合适的婚姻——如果真是这样，那就是一桩不伦不类的婚姻。

11) I will now describe a perfectly innocuous example, or perhaps one with motives only inadequately clear to us, because it illustrates an obvious mechanism:

11）我现在要描述一个完全无害的例子，或者说一个动机我们不太清楚的例子，因为它说明了一种显而易见的机制：

A German travelling in Italy needed a strap to secure his suitcase, which had been damaged. Looking up the German word for strap, Riemen , in the dictionary, he found the Italian version coreggia. I shall remember that easily enough, he told himself, if I think of the painter Correggio. But when he went into a shop he asked for una ribera.

一位德国人在意大利旅行，他的行李箱损坏了，需要一条带子固定。他在字典里查德语“带子”Riemen，发现对应的意大利语是coreggia。他心想，如果想到画家科雷乔，应该很容易记住。但当他走进一家商店时，却说要买una ribera。

Evidently he had not quite managed to replace the German word by its Italian equivalent in his mind, but his efforts had not been entirely unsuccessful. He knew it was a painter’s name that would serve as his aide-mémoire , so he came up not with the name of the painter resembling the Italian word, but with another painter’s name that resembles the German word Riemen. Of course I could just as well have put this example among the instances of forgetting names as in this section on slips of the tongue.

显然，他没能完全在脑海中用意大利语替换掉那个德语单词，但他的努力并非完全徒劳。他知道要用一位画家的名字来做记忆辅助，所以他没有想到一个与那个意大利语单词相似的画家的名字，而是想到了另一个与德语单词“Riemen”相似的画家的名字。当然，我完全可以把这个例子放在忘记名字的例子里，而不是放在口误的章节里。

When I was collecting examples of slips of the tongue for the first edition of this work, I subjected all cases I had observed to analysis, including the less impressive of them. Since then many other people have amused themselves by taking the trouble to collect and analyse such slips, thus allowing me to select from a greater wealth of material.

在为本书第一版收集口误案例时，我分析了所有观察到的案例，包括那些不太引人注目的案例。此后，许多其他人也饶有兴致地收集和分析这类口误，使我得以从更丰富的素材中进行选择。

12) A young man said to his sister: ‘I’ve broken off my acquaintance with the D. family, I don’t even pass the time of day with them now.’ She replied: ‘Oh, what a Lippschaft they are!’ She meant to say Sippschaft [‘clan’, or in this context with the pejorative meaning of ‘gang’], but her slip of the tongue combined two ideas: first, her brother himself had once embarked on a flirtatious relationship with the daughter of this family, and, second, it was said of the same girl that she had recently entered into a serious and illicit Liebschaft [love affair].

12) 一个年轻人对他的妹妹说：“我已经和D家断绝了关系，现在我连看都不看他们一眼。” 她回答说：“哦，他们真是一群混蛋！” 她本想说的是“帮派”（Sippschaft），但她的口误把两个意思混在了一起：首先，她的哥哥曾经和这个家的女儿有过一段暧昧关系；其次，据说这个女孩最近陷入了一段认真的、不正当的恋情。

13) A young man addressed a lady in the street, saying: ‘If you will allow me, Fräulein, I would like to begleit-digen you.’ He was clearly thinking he would like to accompany her ( begleiten ), but feared that the offer might insult her ( beleidigen ). The expression of these two contradictory ideas in a single word — his slip of the tongue — shows that the young man’s real intentions were certainly not as pure as they might have been, and even to himself might seem insulting to the lady. But while he was trying to conceal this from her, his unconscious mind tricked him into betraying his real purpose, also and conversely making him anticipate her conventional answer: What on earth do you take me for? How can you insult [ beleidigen ] me so?’ (Communicated to me by O. Rank.)

13）一位年轻男子在街上对一位女士说：“小姐，如果您不介意的话，我想陪您走走。”他显然是想陪伴她（begleiten），但又担心这个提议会冒犯她（beleidigen）。他一口误地将这两个矛盾的想法表达在一个词里，表明这位年轻人的真实意图肯定不像他想象的那么纯粹，甚至在他自己看来，这番话也可能冒犯了这位女士。然而，当他试图向她掩饰这一点时，他的潜意识却让他泄露了自己的真实意图，同时也让他预料到了她可能会说的话：“你到底把我当什么了？你怎么能这样冒犯我（beleidigen）？”（O. Rank 提供。）

I take a number of examples from an article by W. Stekel in the Berliner Tageblatt of 4 January 1904, entitled ‘Unconscious Confessions’.

我从 W. Stekel 于 1904 年 1 月 4 日在《柏林日报》上发表的题为《无意识的忏悔》的文章中举出了一些例子。

14) ‘The following example reveals a distasteful side to my unconscious thinking. I should begin by saying that as a doctor I have never been concerned for material gain, and have concentrated solely on the interests of the patient, which of course is only natural. I had a woman patient whom I was treating during her convalescence from a severe illness; we had passed some trying days and nights together. I was pleased to find her better one day, painted a picture of the pleasure she would derive from a visit to Abbazia, and added, “That is if, as I hope, you do not leave your bed soon.” Obviously the “not” arose from a selfish wish on the part of my unconscious that I could go on treating this prosperous patient longer, an idea entirely alien to my conscious mind and one which I would reject with horror.’

14）“以下例子揭示了我潜意识思维中令人厌恶的一面。首先我要说明，作为一名医生，我从未谋求过物质利益，始终专注于病人的利益，这当然是理所当然的。我曾治疗过一位重病康复中的女病人；我们一起度过了几个难熬的日日夜夜。有一天，我很高兴地看到她病情好转，便向她描绘了去阿巴齐亚（Abbazia）游玩的美好景象，并补充道：‘当然，前提是，正如我希望的那样，你不要很快下床。’显然，这个‘不要’源于我潜意识中一种自私的愿望，即我可以继续治疗这位富裕的病人更长时间，这种想法与我的意识完全背道而驰，我会对此感到无比厌恶。”

15) Another example (from W. Stekel). ‘My wife was interviewing a Frenchwoman whom she was thinking of employing in the afternoons, and once they had agreed on terms said she would like to keep her references. But the Frenchwoman wanted them back, giving as her reason: “Je cherche encore pour les après-midis, pardon, pour les avant-midis [I am still looking for work in the afternoons — oh, I beg your pardon, in the mornings].” She obviously intended to look elsewhere and perhaps get better terms — and in fact that was just what happened.’

15）另一个例子（来自W. Stekel）。“我妻子面试了一位法国女士，打算让她下午来上班。双方谈妥条件后，妻子说想保留她的推荐信。但这位法国女士想要回推荐信，理由是：‘我还在找下午的工作——哦，抱歉，是上午的工作。’她显然打算另谋出路，或许能找到更好的工作条件——而事实上，事情也正是如此。”

16) Another example from Dr Stekel: ‘I was to read a certain lady a stern lecture at the request of her husband, who was listening on the other side of the door. At the end of my sermon, which obviously made an impression, I said, “Well, goodbye then, gnädiger Herr [instead of gnädige Frau ]!” In doing so I had given away, to anyone who knew the circumstances, the fact that what I had said was on behalf of the husband and was really addressed to him.’

16）斯特克尔博士举的另一个例子：“我应一位女士丈夫的要求，对她进行了一番严厉的训诫。我的丈夫当时就在门外听着。我的训诫显然给那位女士留下了深刻的印象，训诫结束后，我说的是‘好吧，再见，先生（gnädige Herr）’（而不是‘gnädige Frau’）！”这样一来，任何了解情况的人都会明白，我说的话是替她丈夫说的，实际上是对他说的。”

17) Dr Stekel tells us how he himself was once treating two patients from Trieste whom he always used to greet by the wrong names. ‘I would say “Good morning, Herr Peloni,” to Askoli, and: “Good morning, Herr Askoli,” to Peloni.’ At first he was inclined to ascribe no very profound motivation to this switch of their names, and explained it by the fact that the two gentlemen had several things in common. However, he was easily able to convince himself that his confusing the names was really a kind of boastfulness, enabling him to let each of his Italian patients know that he, the patient, was not the only person to have come from Trieste to Vienna to seek Stekel’s medical advice.

17）斯特克尔医生讲述了他自己曾经治疗两位来自的里雅斯特的病人，他总是把他们的名字叫错。“我会对阿斯科利先生说‘早上好，佩洛尼先生’，对佩洛尼先生说‘早上好，阿斯科利先生’。”起初，他并不认为这种名字混淆有什么特别的动机，只是因为这两位先生有很多共同之处。然而，他很快就说服自己，把名字搞混其实是一种炫耀，让他的每一位意大利病人都知道，他并不是唯一一个从的里雅斯特来到维也纳寻求斯特克尔医生诊治的人。

18) Dr Stekel himself, in a heated general meeting, announced: ‘Wir streiten (in error for schreiten ) nun zu Punkt 4 der Tagesordnung [We will now quarrel (in error for proceed ) to point 4 of the agenda].’

18) Stekel 博士本人在一场激烈的股东大会上宣布：“Wirstreiten（错误地表示 schreiten）nun zu Punkt 4 der Tagesordnung [我们现在将争论（错误地继续）议程的第 4 点]。”

19) A professor said, in his inaugural lecture: ‘Ich bin nicht geneigt (for geeignet ), die Verdienste meines sehr geschätzten Vorgängers zu schildern [I am not inclined (for qualified ) to say anything about the merits of my highly esteemed predecessor].’

19）一位教授在他的就职演讲中说：“我不愿（或不具备资格）描述我备受尊敬的前任的优点。”

20) Dr Stekel said to a lady who, he suspected, might have Basedow’s disease: ‘Sie sind um einen Kropf (in error for Kopf ) grösser als Ihre Schwester [You are a goitre (in error for head ) taller than your sister].’

20) 斯特克尔医生对一位他怀疑可能患有巴塞多氏病的女士说：“你是个甲状腺肿（误认为是头），比你姐姐还高。”

21) Another incident reported by Dr Stekel concerns a man trying to describe the relationship of two friends, one of whom was Jewish. “‘They lived together,” he said, “like Castor and Pollak [substituting the Jewish surname Pollak for the name Pollux, one of the Dioscuri in classical myth].” This was not meant as a joke; the speaker failed to notice his own slip of the tongue, and became aware of it only when I pointed it out.’

21）斯特克尔博士报告的另一起事件是一位男士试图描述两位朋友的关系，其中一位是犹太人。“‘他们住在一起，’他说，‘就像卡斯托尔和波拉克（用犹太姓氏波拉克代替古典神话中狄俄斯库里兄弟之一的波吕克斯）’。这并非玩笑；说话者没有意识到自己说漏了嘴，直到我指出来他才明白。”

22) ‘Sometimes a slip of the tongue paints the picture of an entire character. A young lady who wore the trousers in her marriage told me that her husband, who was unwell, had been to the doctor and asked what diet would be best for him. The doctor, however, said diet had nothing to do with it. “He can eat and drink what I like,” said the wife.’

22）“有时候，一句不经意的话语就能勾勒出一个人的全貌。一位在婚姻中占据主导地位的年轻女士告诉我，她生病的丈夫去看医生，问医生什么饮食对他最有益。然而，医生却说饮食与他的病情无关。“他想吃什么就吃什么，想喝什么就喝什么，”妻子说道。”

The following two examples, taken from T. Reik ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse III, 1915), arise from situations where it is particularly easy for a slip of the tongue to occur, because in such cases more must be withheld than can be openly said.

以下两个例子摘自 T. Reik（《国际精神分析杂志》第三卷，1915 年），它们都源于容易口误的情况，因为在这种情况下，必须保留的信息比可以公开说出口的信息要多。

23) A gentleman was condoling with a young lady whose husband had recently died, and added: ‘Sie werden Trost finden, indem Sie sich völlig Ihren Kindern widwen [‘You will find comfort in devoting yourself entirely to your children’, but using the slip widwen , echoing Witwe , ‘widow’, in error for widmen , ‘devote’].’ The suppressed idea is of another kind of comfort: a beautiful young widow would soon be likely to enjoy sexual pleasure again.

23）一位绅士安慰一位丈夫刚刚去世的年轻女士，说道：“Sie werden Trost finden, indem Sie sich völlig Ihren Kindern widwen [‘你会在全心全意照顾孩子中找到慰藉’，但误用了widwen，与Witwe（寡妇）一词混淆，而widmen是widmen（奉献）]。” 这句话隐藏的含义是另一种慰藉：一位年轻貌美的寡妇很可能很快就能再次享受到性爱的乐趣。

24) The same gentleman was talking to the same lady at an evening party about the large-scale Easter preparations being made in Berlin, and asked: ‘Have you seen the display in Wertheim’s windows today? It is all dekolletiert [in error for dekoriert ].’ He had not been able to express his admiration for the beautiful woman’s décolletage explicitly, but the taboo idea surfaced when he referred not to the decoration of a store window but to a décolletage , unconsciously using the word Auslage [display, put on show] with a double meaning.

24）同一位先生在一次晚宴上与同一位女士谈论柏林正在进行的大规模复活节准备工作，并问道：“你今天看到韦特海姆百货公司的橱窗了吗？全是 dekolletiert（误用 dekoriert）。”他无法直接表达对这位美丽女士的胸衣的欣赏，但当他提到胸衣而不是商店橱窗的装饰时，这个禁忌的想法浮现出来，他无意中使用了具有双重含义的单词 Auslage（展示，陈列）。

The same circumstances applied to an observation of which Dr Hanns Sachs has done his best to supply a full account:

同样的情况也适用于汉斯·萨克斯博士尽力详尽描述的一项观察结果：

25) ‘A lady told me that when she last saw a common acquaintance of ours he was as elegantly dressed as ever, and in particular he was wearing remarkably handsome brown flat-heeled shoes ( Halbschuhe ). When I ask where they had met she said: “Oh, he rang my doorbell, and I saw him through the roller blinds, which were pulled down. However, I didn’t open the door or give any other sign of life, because I didn’t want him to know I was back in town.” listening, I suspected that she was hiding something from me, and very likely she didn’t open the door because she was not alone and was improperly dressed to receive visitors. I asked, with some irony: “Oh, so you could admire his Hausschuhe [slippers] — his Halbschuhe through the drawn blinds?’ The idea of her Hauskleid [dressing gown], which I had refrained from expressing, emerged in the word Hausschuhe. I may also have tried not to say Halb [half] because it contained the answer I would not let myself give: “You are telling me only half the truth; you forget to say that you were only half dressed.” The slip of the tongue was also encouraged by the fact that immediately before we had been discussing the conjugal life of the gentleman in question and his häusliches Glück [domestic happiness], a term that probably helped to determine the displacement to his own person. Finally, I must admit that perhaps my own envy played a part in my making this elegant gentleman stand in the street in his slippers, since I myself had recently bought some low-heeled brown shoes which were by no means “remarkably handsome” any more.’

25）一位女士告诉我，她上次见到我们的一位共同熟人时，他一如既往地衣着考究，尤其引人注目的是他那双格外帅气的棕色平底鞋。我问她是在哪里遇到的，她说：“哦，他按了我的门铃，我透过拉下来的卷帘看到了他。但我没有开门，也没有做出任何回应，因为我不想让他知道我已经回到城里了。” 听着，我怀疑她有所隐瞒，很可能她没开门是因为她当时并非独自一人，而且穿着打扮也不适合接待访客。我带着几分讽刺问道：“哦，所以你可以透过拉上的窗帘欣赏他的拖鞋——或者说他的半截拖鞋？”我原本想说的她的晨衣，却在“拖鞋”这个词里浮现了出来。我可能也刻意避免说“半截”，因为它包含了我不想说出口的答案：“你只跟我说了一半的真话；你忘了说你当时只穿了一半的衣服。”我脱口而出，也跟之前我们讨论这位先生的婚姻生活和他所谓的“家庭幸福”有关——这个词可能让我把话题转移到了他身上。最后，我必须承认，或许是出于我自己的嫉妒，我才让这位优雅的先生穿着拖鞋站在街上，因为我自己最近也买了一双棕色的低跟鞋，现在看来，它们再也算不上“特别好看”了。

Times of war like the present give rise to a number of slips of the tongue that are readily comprehensible.

像现在这样的战争时期，难免会出现一些容易理解的口误。

26) ‘What is your son’s regiment?’ a lady was asked. She replied: The 42nd Mörder [‘murderers’, in error for Mörser , ‘mortars’].’

26）有人问一位女士：“你儿子在哪个团？”她回答说：“第42 Mörder（误将 Mörser，即“迫击炮兵”）团。”

27) Lieutenant Henrik Haiman wrote from the front: ‘I was torn away from reading a fascinating book to deputize briefly for the reconnaissance telephonist. When the gun emplacement rang to test the line I reacted by saying: All correct, Ruhe [shut up]. It ought really to have been: All correct, Schluss [over and out]. My lapse can be explained by my annoyance at being disturbed in reading my book’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse IV, 1916/17).

27）亨里克·海曼中尉从前线写道：“我正津津有味地读着一本书，突然被打断，不得不临时代理侦察电话员的工作。当炮位响起测试线路的电话时，我脱口而出：‘一切正常，安静。’其实应该是：‘一切正常，完毕。’我的口误可能是因为读书被打断而感到恼火。”（《国际精神分析杂志》第四卷，1916/17年）

28) A sergeant told his men to send their addresses home accurately so that the Gespeckstücke [a word suggesting ‘pieces of bacon’, Speck , for Gepäckstücke , ‘packages’] would not go astray.

28) 一名军士长告诉他的部下，要准确地把他们的地址寄回家，这样 Gespeckstücke（这个词暗示着“培根片”，Speck，代表 Gepäckstücke，“包裹”）就不会丢失。

29) I owe the following outstandingly fine example, significant for its very unfortunate background, to Dr L. Czeszer, who made this observation while he was in neutral Switzerland during the war and analysed it at length. I reproduce his own account with a few minor cuts:

29）我要感谢L. Czeszer博士，他于战争期间身处中立国瑞士，并在此观察到这一现象，并对其进行了深入分析。以下是他对这一现象的描述，仅作少量删减：

‘Let me permit myself to describe a case of a “slip of the tongue” made by Professor M. N. in O., during one of the lectures he was delivering during the last summer semester on the psychology of the emotions. I must state first that these lectures were held in the great hall of the university, and were well attended by interned French prisoners of war as well as the French-speaking Swiss students, most of whom were very much in favour of the Entente. In O., as in France itself, the word boche is now generally and exclusively used as a term for Germans. In public announcements, however, and in lectures and so forth, senior civil servants, professors and other responsible people try to avoid this unfortunate word for reasons of neutrality.

“请允许我描述一下M. N.教授在O.大学夏季学期的一次关于情绪心理学的讲座中，不小心说漏了嘴的一件事。首先我必须说明，这些讲座是在大学的大礼堂举行的，听众包括被拘禁的法国战俘以及讲法语的瑞士学生，他们中的大多数人都非常支持协约国。在O.大学，就像在法国一样，“boche”一词现在通常且专门用来指代德国人。然而，在公开场合、讲座等场合，高级公务员、教授和其他负责人出于保持中立的考虑，都会尽量避免使用这个不恰当的词。”

‘Professor N. was in the middle of describing the practical significance of affects, and he intended to quote an example of the intentional exploitation of an affect in order to endow intrinsically uninteresting physical labour with pleasurable feelings, thus intensifying its structure. He therefore told the story, in French of course, that at the time had just been reprinted from a German journal in the local Swiss papers, about a German schoolmaster who made his pupils work in the garden, and to encourage them to work harder told them to imagine that instead of every clod of earth they dug they were smashing a French skull. Whenever he mentioned Germans in telling his story of course N. said, quite correctly, allemand , not boche. However, when he reached the point of the story he rendered the schoolmaster’s remarks as follows: Imaginez-vous qu’en cheque moche vous écrasez le crâne d’un Français. He had turned motte [a clod of earth] into moche !

N教授当时正在阐述情感的实际意义，他打算举一个例子，说明如何有意利用情感，使原本枯燥乏味的体力劳动变得令人愉悦，从而强化其结构。于是，他用法语讲述了一个故事——这个故事当时刚从瑞士当地报纸上转载自一份德国期刊——讲的是一位德国教师让学生们在花园里干活，为了鼓励他们更加努力，教师告诉他们，想象自己挖的每一块土不是一团土，而是在砸碎一个法国人的头骨。在讲述这个故事时，N教授每次提到德国人时，都正确地使用了“allemand”（德国人），而不是“boche”（法国佬）。然而，当他讲到故事的关键部分时，他却把教师的话翻译成了这样：“Imaginez-vous qu’en cheque moche vous écrasez le crâne d’un Français.”（想象你挖土时，你砸碎了一个法国人的头骨。）

‘Here we can actually see the impeccable scholar taking care, from the very beginning of his story, not to give way to the usual habit, and perhaps the temptation, of allowing the taboo word (which in fact had been expressly banned by a Swiss decree) to be uttered from the lectern of the university hall! And just as he had successfully pronounced the phrase instituteur allemand for the last time, perfectly correctly, and was making haste, with an inward sigh of relief, towards the inoffensive conclusion of the story, the word he had so laboriously suppressed fastened on the similarity of sound in the word motte — and the mischief was done. Fear of political tactlessness, perhaps a suppressed wish to use the common and indeed expected word after all, and the distaste of a man who had been a republican and democrat from birth for any constraint on freedom of expression all interfered with his main intention of giving a correct account of his example. The speaker was aware of the interfering tendency, and we may well suppose that he was thinking of it directly before his slip of the tongue.

“在这里，我们可以看到这位严谨的学者从一开始就小心翼翼地避免屈服于惯常的习惯，或许也避免了诱惑，在大学讲台上说出那个禁忌的词语（事实上，瑞士的一项法令明确禁止使用这个词！）。就在他最后一次成功地、完全正确地念出‘instituteur allemand’这个词，并带着内心的如释重负的叹息，匆匆走向故事无伤大雅的结尾时，他费尽心思压抑的那个词却因为与‘motte’一词发音相似而脱口而出——祸不单行。或许是出于对政治失礼的恐惧，或许是出于压抑的想要使用这个常用且人们普遍接受的词语的愿望，又或许是出于一个生来就是共和主义者和民主主义者的人对任何限制言论自由的厌恶，所有这些都干扰了他原本想要正确讲述这个例子的初衷。”说话者意识到了这种干扰倾向，我们完全可以推测，他在口误之前就已经想到了这一点。

‘Professor N. did not notice his slip, or at least he did not correct it, as people usually do quite automatically. On the other hand, his lapse was noted with real satisfaction by most of the French in his audience, and had just the same effect as an intentional play on words. Personally, I followed this apparently innocuous process with a genuine sense of internal excitement. Although for obvious reasons I could not ask the professor the questions forcibly suggested by psychoanalytic method, I still saw his slip of the tongue as striking evidence for the accuracy of your theory of the determination of such slips, and the profound analogies and relationships between slips of the tongue and jokes.’

N教授没有注意到自己的口误，或者至少他没有像人们通常那样下意识地纠正。另一方面，他的口误却让在场的大多数法国听众感到十分得意，其效果与故意玩文字游戏无异。就我个人而言，我当时内心充满了兴奋。虽然出于显而易见的原因，我无法向教授提出那些精神分析方法强加的问题，但我仍然认为他的口误有力地证明了您关于口误判定的理论的准确性，以及口误与笑话之间深刻的类比和联系。

30) It was also under the depressing influence of wartime impressions that an Austrian officer, First Lieutenant T., made a slip of the tongue that he described on his return home:

30）也正是在战争带来的压抑印象的影响下，一位奥地利军官，T 中尉，说错了一句话，他在回国后描述了这句话：

‘For several months while I was a prisoner of war in Italy our group of 200 officers was billeted in cramped accommodation in a villa. During this time one of us died of influenza. The impression that this incident made on us was naturally profound, for our present circumstances, the lack of medical aid, and our powerlessness at the time made an epidemic more than likely. We had laid the dead man out in a room in the basement. In the evening, when I went out to walk around the house with a friend, we both thought we would like to look at the corpse. I went first, and when I entered the cellar I saw a sight that greatly alarmed me, since I had not been prepared to find the bier so close to the door or to have to see the face, which seemed to be moving in the flickering candlelight, at such close quarters. Still under the influence of this image, we went on with our walk. At a place where we had a view of the park bathed in full moonlight, and of a brightly illuminated meadow with faint drifts of mist beyond, I expressed the idea it suggested to me, that one could imagine elves dancing among the pines surrounding this place. Next afternoon we buried our dead comrade. We found the way from our prison to the graveyard of the little village near by both bitter and humiliating, since half-grown, yelling lads, mocking, contemptuous locals and people shouting vulgarities at the top of their voices had seized on this occasion to give open expression to their emotions of mingled curiosity and hatred. A sense of inevitable resentment, even in this defenceless situation, and my distaste for such rough behaviour preyed upon my mind until evening. Then, at the same time as the day before and with the same companion, I set out on the gravel path round the villa again, and on passing the grille in front of the cellar behind which the corpse had been lying I was overcome by the memory of the impression the sight had made on me. At the place from which I had seen a view of the moonlit park, and by the light of the same full moon, I stopped and said to my companion: “We could sit down here in the Grab [grave] — I mean Gras [grass], and sinken [‘sink’, in error for singen , ‘sing’] a serenade.” Only when I made my second slip of the tongue did I realize what I had said; the first time I had corrected myself without understanding the reason for my mistake. Now that I thought about it I connected the ideas of “sinking” and “into the grave”. Then these images immediately came into my mind: elves dancing and hovering in the moonlight; our comrade on his bier; his face, apparently moving; various scenes from the funeral; my sense of distaste, the disruption of our mourning; the memory of certain remarks about the onset of an epidemic, expressions of alarm on the part of several of the officers. Later I remembered that it was the anniversary of my father’s death on that day. I found this recollection striking, because I am usually very bad at remembering dates.

“我在意大利当战俘的几个月里，我们200名军官被安置在一栋别墅里狭小的住所中。期间，我们当中有人死于流感。这件事给我们留下了深刻的印象，因为当时的处境、医疗资源的匮乏以及我们的无能为力，使得疫情爆发的可能性极大。我们把死者安放在地下室的一个房间里。一天晚上，我和一位朋友出去散步，我们都想看看尸体。我先去了，当我走进地下室时，眼前的一幕让我大吃一惊，因为我没想到灵柩会离门口这么近，也没想到会在摇曳的烛光下如此近距离地看到那张似乎还在动的脸。我仍然沉浸在刚才的景象中，继续散步。”在一个可以俯瞰沐浴在皎洁月光下的公园，以及远处阳光明媚、薄雾缭绕的草地的地方，我表达了我的感受：仿佛能看到精灵在环绕这片土地的松林间翩翩起舞。第二天下午，我们埋葬了死去的战友。从我们被囚禁的地方到附近小村庄的墓地，这段路程既痛苦又屈辱，因为那些半大不小的喧闹少年、嘲讽轻蔑的当地人，以及那些大声辱骂、满口脏话的人，都趁机肆意地表达着他们既好奇又憎恨的复杂情绪。即使在这种毫无防备的情况下，一种无法避免的怨恨感，以及对这种粗鲁行为的厌恶，一直萦绕在我的心头，直到傍晚。然后，和前一天一样，我和同一位同伴再次沿着别墅周围的碎石路出发。当我经过地窖前的栅栏时——尸体就躺在那里——我被眼前景象的震撼所淹没。在那个我曾眺望月光下的公园的地方，借着那轮满月的光芒，我停了下来，对同伴说：“我们可以坐在这草丛里——我是说，草丛里——唱首小夜曲。”直到我第二次口误，才意识到自己说了什么；第一次我纠正自己时，并没有明白自己错在哪里。现在回想起来，我把“沉入”和“进入坟墓”这两个词联系了起来。于是，这些画面立刻涌入我的脑海：精灵在月光下翩翩起舞；我们的同伴躺在灵柩上；他的脸似乎在动；葬礼上的种种场景；我感到厌恶，哀悼被打断；我记得有人说过一些关于疫情爆发的话，还有几位军官流露出的惊恐神色。后来我才想起来，那天是我父亲的忌日。我发现自己记性很差，因为我通常记不住日期。

‘On thinking it over later I noticed the way in which the external conditions matched each other on the two evenings: the same time of day, the same light, the same place and the same companion. I remembered my uneasiness when concern about the possible spread of influenza was discussed, but also my inner determination not to let fear get the better of me. I also saw the significance of my word order in saying that we could sink into the grave [German: wir könnten ins Grab sinken ] and I realized that the first correction of “grave” to “grass”, which had not been a very emphatic one, was the only reason for my second slip of turning “sing” into “sink”, thus ensuring that the suppressed complex could finally come into the open.

“后来仔细想想，我注意到这两个晚上外部环境的相似之处：相同的时间、相同的光线、相同的地点，还有同一个人。我记得当时讨论流感可能传播时，我感到不安，但也记得我内心决心不让恐惧战胜自己。我还意识到，我说‘我们可以沉入坟墓’（德语：wir könnten ins Grab sinken）时语序的重要性，我意识到，第一次把“grave”（坟墓）改成“grass”（草）时语气并不强烈，而正是那次无意中把“sing”（唱歌）说成“sink”（沉没）的失误，才导致我第二次口误，把“sing”（唱歌）说成“sink”（沉没），从而让压抑已久的复杂情绪最终得以释放。”

‘I will add that at this time I was suffering from anxious dreams in which I repeatedly saw a woman member of my immediate family lying ill, and once even dead. Just before I was taken prisoner, I had heard that the flu was raging particularly virulently in the place where this relation of mine lived, and I had told her of my alarm for her. We had been out of touch since then. Months later I heard that she had indeed fallen victim to the epidemic two weeks before the event I have described!’

“我还要补充一点，当时我经常做噩梦，梦里反复看到一位女性亲属病倒在地，甚至有一次她已经去世了。就在我被俘之前，我听说这位亲属居住的地方流感肆虐，我曾向她表达过我的担忧。从那以后，我们就失去了联系。几个月后，我听说她确实在两周前，也就是我所描述的事件发生之前，感染了这场流感！”

31) The following example of a slip of the tongue casts a revealing light on one of those painful conflicts that doctors are always having to resolve. A man who was probably mortally sick, although his diagnosis was not yet certain, had come to Vienna to await the outcome of his problems, and had asked a friend of his youth, now a well-known doctor, to take on his case. The doctor, not without reluctance, finally agreed. The sick man had to stay somewhere where there was medical help on hand, and the doctor suggested the Hera Sanatorium. Oh no, objected the invalid, that’s only for certain kinds of cases (it was a maternity hospital). No, indeed, the doctor protested: they can umbringen [kill] — I mean unterbringen [accommodate] any kind of patient in the Hera. He then vehemently protested against the obvious interpretation of this slip of the tongue. ‘You surely don’t believe I feel aggressive towards you?’ Quarter of an hour later, the doctor told the lady who had agreed to look after the sick man and was seeing him out: ‘I can’t find anything very bad, and I still don’t believe it will come to the worst, but if it does I’m in favour of a good dose of morphine, and then he’ll be at rest.’ It turned out that his friend had made him promise to cut short his suffering with drugs as soon as it was certain that no more could be done for him, so the doctor had in fact undertaken to kill [ umbringen ] the sick man.

31）下面这个口误的例子揭示了医生们经常要解决的棘手冲突之一。一位可能身患绝症的男子（尽管诊断尚未确定）来到维也纳等待病情结果，并请他年轻时的朋友——如今已是位知名医生——接手他的病例。医生最终勉强答应了。病人必须待在有医疗救助的地方，医生建议去赫拉疗养院。病人反对道：“哦，不，那里只收治特定类型的病人（那是一家妇产医院）。”医生反驳道：“不，的确如此：赫拉疗养院可以收治任何类型的病人。”然后，他强烈反对人们对这句口误的明显解读。 “你肯定不认为我对你怀有敌意吧？”一刻钟后，医生对那位同意照顾病人并送他出院的女士说：“我没发现什么特别严重的问题，我仍然认为情况不会恶化，但如果真的恶化了，我赞成给他注射大剂量吗啡，这样他就能安息了。”原来，他的朋友让他答应，一旦确定无药可救，就用药物结束他的痛苦，所以医生实际上是答应要结束这个病人的生命。

32) I must include here a particularly instructive example of a slip of the tongue, although according to my informant it happened some 20 years ago. ‘A lady once said in company — and the words themselves show that they were uttered with feeling and under the pressure of all kinds of concealed emotions: “Oh yes, a woman must be pretty if she is to please men. It’s much easier for a man: so long as he has his fünf geraden Glieder [five straight limbs] that’s all he needs!” This example provides a good insight into the intimate mechanism at work when a slip of the tongue is caused by compression or contamination (cf. p. 53 ), It seems obvious that two rather similar expressions have been merged:

32）我必须在此举一个特别有启发性的口误例子，尽管据我的线人说，这件事发生在20年前。“一位女士曾在公共场合说过——从字里行间可以看出，她是在各种隐秘情绪的压力下，带着感情说出这句话的：‘哦，是的，女人要想取悦男人，就必须漂亮。男人就容易多了：只要他有五条笔直的腿，就足够了！’”这个例子很好地揭示了口误是由压迫或污染引起的内在机制（参见第53页）。显然，两个非常相似的表达被混淆了：

wenn er seine vier geraden Glieder hat [so long as he has his four straight limbs]

当他四肢伸直的时候

wenn er seine fünf Sinne beisammen hat [so long as he has the use of his five senses].

只要他的五官能够正常运作（只要他的五官能够正常运作）。

Alternatively, the word gerade [straight] may contain the element in common to two intended remarks, running:

或者，单词 gerade（直截了当）可能包含两个预期表达的共同元素，即：

wenn er nur seine geraden Glieder hat [so long as he has his straight limbs]

如果他只有笔直的四肢

alle fünf gerade sein lassen [‘to let all five be even ( gerade ) numbers’, but also, colloquially, ‘to stretch a point, turn a blind eye’].

让这五个都是偶数 [“让这五个都是偶数（偶数）”，但口语中也有“延伸观点，视而不见”的意思]。

There is nothing to prevent us from supposing that both expressions, one turning on the five senses and the other on even numbers, could have introduced into the sentence about straight limbs first a number and then the puzzling five instead of the expected four. However, it is unlikely that they would have merged if the construction arising from the slip of the tongue had not made perfectly good sense in itself, having a double meaning [taking Glied in its sense of male member, penis] which the speaker, being a woman, could not acknowledge openly. Finally, one must point out that the wording of the lady’s remark could just as well have made it an excellent joke as an amusing slip of the tongue, depending on whether she said it intentionally or unintentionally. However, her manner in this case showed that her remarks were unintentional and not meant to be funny.’

我们完全可以假设，这两个表达方式——一个涉及五官，另一个涉及偶数——都可能在关于笔直肢体的句子中先引入一个数字，然后又引入令人费解的“五”，而不是预期的“四”。然而，如果口误产生的结构本身并非完全合理，具有双重含义（Glied 指男性生殖器，阴茎），而说话者作为女性无法公开承认这一点，那么这两个表达方式不太可能融合在一起。最后，必须指出的是，这位女士的措辞既可以是一个绝妙的笑话，也可以是一个有趣的口误，这取决于她是有意还是无意地说出这句话。然而，在这种情况下，她的举止表明，她的话语并非有意为之，也并非意在搞笑。

The close approximation of a slip of the tongue to a joke can go quite a long way, as it does in this case described by O. Rank, where the lady who made the slip of the tongue eventually laughed at it herself:

口误与笑话的近似程度可能相当高，就像 O. Rank 描述的这个例子一样，那位口误的女士最终自己也笑了：

33) ‘A young husband whose wife, wishing to preserve her girlish looks, was reluctant to let him have frequent sexual intercourse, told me the following story, which in retrospect amused both of them very much: the morning after a night when, yet again, he had ignored his wife’s desire for sexual abstinence, he was shaving in the bedroom they shared, and used the powder-puff lying on his wife’s bedside table, as he often did for the sake of convenience, while she was still in bed. The lady, who thought a great deal of her complexion, had asked him several times before not to do it, and now cried out in vexation: “Oh no, there you go powdering me again with your puff!” Alerted to her slip of the tongue by her husband’s laughter (for she had meant to say: powdering yourself with my puff), she finally laughed heartily too. (“To powder” is an expression for sexual intercourse known to any Viennese, and a powder-puff is an obvious phallic symbol)’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse I, 1913).

33）一位年轻丈夫给我讲了这样一个故事，事后回想起来，他们俩都觉得很有趣：一天晚上，他又一次无视了妻子禁欲的意愿，第二天早上，他在他们共用的卧室里刮胡子，像往常一样，为了方便，用了放在妻子床头柜上的粉扑，当时妻子还在床上。妻子很在意自己的肤色，之前已经多次要求他不要这样做，现在她恼火地喊道：“哎呀，你又用粉扑给我扑粉了！”丈夫的笑声让她意识到自己说错了话（她本想说的是：用我的粉扑给自己扑粉），她也跟着哈哈大笑起来。 （“扑粉”是任何维也纳人都知道的性交表达方式，粉扑是明显的阳具象征）”（Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalysis I，1913）。

34) An intentional joke might also be suspected in the following case (from A. J. Storfer):

34）在以下案例中，也可能怀疑是故意开的玩笑（引自 A. J. Storfer）：

Frau B., who was suffering from an ailment of obviously psychogenic origin, was repeatedly urged to consult X. the psychoanalyst. She always refused, objecting that such treatment was never any use, and the doctor, mistakenly, was bound to say her trouble was all due to sexual causes. At last, however, she agreed to take this advice, and asked: ‘Nun gut, wann ordinärt also dieser Dr X. [‘When does this Dr X. have his consultations?’, but confusing the verb ordinieren , ‘to hold consultations’, and the adjective ordinär , ‘vulgar’]?’

B女士患有一种明显由心理因素引起的疾病，人们多次劝她去看精神分析师X。她总是拒绝，认为这种治疗毫无用处，而且医生肯定会错误地认为她的病都是性方面的原因造成的。然而，最终她还是同意接受这个建议，并问道：“Nun gut, wann ordinärt also dieser Dr X. [‘这位X医生什么时候接诊？’，但她混淆了动词ordinieren（接诊）和形容词ordinär（粗俗的）]？”

The relationship between a joke and a slip of the tongue is also obvious in the fact that the slip of the tongue is often simply a short cut:

笑话和口误之间的联系也很明显，因为口误通常只是一种捷径：

35) A young girl left school and, in the contemporary fashion, registered to study medicine, but after a few semesters she changed from medicine to chemistry. A few years later she described the reason for her change by saying: ‘I never felt squeamish about dissection in general, but once, when I had to remove the nails from the fingers of a corpse, I found I had entirely lost my enthusiasm for — chemistry .’

35）一位年轻女孩辍学后，按照当时的潮流报名学习医学，但几个学期后，她转而学习化学。几年后，她这样描述自己转变的原因：“我以前从不害怕解剖，但有一次，当我不得不从一具尸体的手指上拔指甲时，我发现自己对——化学——的热情完全消失了。”

36) Here is another case of an easily interpreted slip of the tongue. ‘A professor of anatomy was speaking about the nasal cavity, which is known to be a very difficult enterological subject. When he asked whether his audience had understood his explanation, there was a general “Yes”. At this the professor, a man notorious for his self-assurance, commented: I doubt whether, even in a city with a population of millions like Vienna, those who really understand the nasal cavity can be counted on one finger — I beg your pardon, I meant on the fingers of one hand.’

36）这里又是一个容易被误解的口误的例子。“一位解剖学教授正在讲解鼻腔，众所周知，鼻腔是肠道学中一个非常复杂的课题。当他问听众是否理解他的解释时，大家普遍回答‘是的’。这位以自信著称的教授随即说道：‘我怀疑，即使在维也纳这样拥有数百万人口的城市，真正了解鼻腔的人也屈指可数——抱歉，我指的是一只手的手指头。’”

37) On another occasion the same anatomist said: The study of the female genitals, despite many Versuchungen [temptations] — I beg your pardon, Versuche [experiments]…’

37）另一次，这位解剖学家说道：“尽管有很多诱惑——请原谅，是实验……”，但对女性生殖器的研究仍然得以进行。

38) I am grateful to Dr A. Robitsek of Vienna for drawing my attention to two cases of slips of the tongue noted by a French author of the past, which I quote in the original French. In the Discours second of his Vies des Dames galantes , Brantôme (1527-1614) writes: ‘Si ay-je cogneu une très belle et honneste dame de par le monde, qui, devisant avec un honneste gentilhomme de la cour des affaires de la guerre durant ces civiles, elle luy dit: “Jay ouy dire que le roy a faict rompre tous les c … de ce pays là.” Elle voulait dire les ponts. Pensez que, venant de coucher d’avec son mary, ou songeant à son amant, elle avoit encor ce nom frais en la bouche; et le gentilhomme s’en eschauffa en amours d’elle pour ce mot [I knew a very beautiful and virtuous society lady who, discussing the war during this time of civil unrest with a gentleman of the court, told him: “I have heard that the king has mounted an assault on all the c … of that part of the country.” She meant “all the bridges” [ ponts , rhyming with cons , ‘cunts’]. Very likely, having just been to bed with her husband or else thinking of her lover, she still had that word on the tip of her tongue, and it inflamed the gentleman with love for her.’

38）我感谢维也纳的A. Robitsek博士，他让我注意到一位法国古代作家记录的两起口误，以下引用原文。布朗托姆（1527-1614）在其《英俊淑女传》第二篇中写道：“如果我认识一位非常美丽诚实的女士，她在与一位诚实的宫廷绅士谈论内战期间的战争事务时，对他说：‘我听说国王已经把这个国家所有的桥都炸毁了。’她指的是桥梁。想想看，她刚刚与丈夫同寝，或者还在想着她的情人，这个名字还历历在目；那位绅士因为这个词爱上了她。[我认识一位非常美丽贤淑的社交名媛，在内战动荡时期，她与一位宫廷绅士谈论战争时，说道：“我听说国王已经对那片地区的所有……发动了进攻。”她指的是“所有的桥”（ponts，与cons，即“cunts”押韵）。很可能，她刚刚和丈夫上过床，或者正在想着她的情人，这个词还萦绕在她耳边，这激起了那位绅士对她的爱慕之情。]

‘Une autre dame que j’ai cogneue, entretenant une autre grand dame plus qu’elle, et luy louant et exaltant ses beautez, elle luy di après: “Non, madame, ce que je vous en dis: ce n’est point pour vous adultérer;” voulant dire adulater, comme elle le rhabilla ainsi: pensez qu’elle songeoit à adultérer [Another lady I knew, speaking to a lady whose rank was higher than hers, praising her and complimenting her on her beauty, finished by remarking: “No, madame, I do not say these things to adulterate you.” She meant to adulate , but the way she put it suggests that she was thinking of adultery ].’
