我认识的另一位女士，在与一位地位比她高的女士交谈时，赞美了她的美貌，最后说道：“不，夫人，我这么说并非想与您发生婚外情。”她本意是奉承，但她的措辞却让人觉得她心里想着婚外情。

39) Of course more modern examples exist of sexual double meanings arising from slips of the tongue: Frau F. said, of her first lesson in a language course she was taking: ‘It’s really interesting; the tutor is a nice young Englishman. In the very first lesson he indicated to me durch die Bluse [through my blouse]’ — and corrects herself: ‘ durch die Blume [literally, ‘through the flower’ but colloquially ‘with veiled hints’] — that he would rather give me private tuition’ (Storfer).

39) 当然，现代也存在因口误而产生性双关含义的例子：F 女士在谈到她参加语言课程的第一堂课时说：“这真有趣；老师是一位和蔼的年轻英国人。在第一堂课上，他就向我暗示 durch die Bluse [透过我的衬衫]”——然后他纠正自己说：“durch die Blume [字面意思是‘透过花朵’，但口语中带有隐晦的暗示’]——他更愿意给我提供私人辅导”（Storfer）。

In the psychotherapeutic methods that I use to resolve and eliminate neurotic symptoms, I very often have to track down the subject of a train of thought from the remarks and ideas which patients bring out as if by chance. They may try to conceal that subject, but cannot help revealing it unintentionally in many different ways. In such circumstances a slip of the tongue often proves very helpful indeed, as I could demonstrate by quoting some very odd but extremely cogent examples. Speaking of an aunt, for instance, patients may consistently call her ‘my mother’ without noticing the slip, or a woman patient may describe her husband as her ‘brother’. This tells me that they are ‘identifying’ these people with each other and have arranged them in a manner which suggests that the same type of character recurs in their emotional lives. Again, a young man of 20 introduced himself to me when he came for a consultation by saying, ‘You treated so and so; I’m his father. Oh, I’m sorry, I meant his brother. He’s four years older than me.’ I realize that his slip of the tongue was intended to convey that it was their father’s fault if both he and his brother were ill, and like his brother he wanted to be cured, but it was their father who needed a cure most urgently. On other occasions an unusual verbal construction or what appears to be a stilted manner of expression is enough to reveal part of a repressed idea in the patient’s differently motivated remarks.

在我用于解决和消除神经症症状的心理治疗方法中，我经常需要从患者看似无意间说出的言语和想法中追溯其思维主题。他们或许试图隐藏这个主题，但却无法避免以各种方式无意间流露出来。在这种情况下，口误往往非常有用，我可以举一些非常奇特但又极具说服力的例子来说明这一点。例如，谈到一位姑姑时，患者可能会一直称她为“我的母亲”，而没有意识到自己说错了；或者一位女患者可能会把她的丈夫描述为她的“兄弟”。这告诉我，他们正在将这些人“认同”在一起，并且以一种暗示同一种性格在他们的情感生活中反复出现的方式将他们联系起来。还有一位20岁的年轻人在来咨询时自我介绍说：“您治疗过某某，我是他的父亲。哦，对不起，我说的是他的父亲。” “他比我大四岁。”我意识到他口误的意思是，如果他和哥哥都生病了，那就是他们父亲的错；他和哥哥一样渴望痊愈，但最迫切需要治疗的是他们的父亲。在其他情况下，不寻常的语言结构或看似生硬的表达方式，就足以揭示患者出于不同动机的言语中隐藏的部分想法。

I do not, therefore, think that those instances of obvious or subtler speech disturbances which can also be subsumed under ‘slips of the tongue’ are mainly due to the influence of phonetic contacts; I believe that such slips derive from ideas outside what the speaker intends to say, which are sufficient to explain the slip. I do not mean to imply any doubt of the phonetic laws causing sounds to modify each other, but they do not seem to me strong enough to impair correct speech by their own influence alone. In those cases that I have studied closely and of which I can claim some understanding, they merely represent an existing mechanism that can easily be used by a more remote psychic motive without its binding itself to the sphere of influence of those connections. In a great many substitutions, a slip of the tongue occurs quite regardless of such laws of phonetics. Here I am completely in agreement with Wundt, who like me assumes that conditions producing slips of the tongue are complex and go far beyond phonetic interaction. On the other hand, while I accept these ‘more remote psychic influences’, as Wundt calls them, I do not see why we should not also admit that when someone is speaking fast, and his attention is to some extent distracted, the conditions for a slip of the tongue can easily be restricted to those defined by Meringer and Mayer. But in some of the examples they collected it seems likely that there is in fact a more complex solution. Let me take the case already mentioned above [ p. 53 ].

因此，我认为那些明显或较为隐晦的言语障碍，也就是所谓的“口误”，并非主要源于语音接触的影响；我相信，这类口误源于说话者意图之外的观念，而这些观念足以解释口误的发生。我并非质疑语音规律对语音相互影响的作用，但这些规律本身似乎不足以影响正确的言语表达。在我仔细研究并有所了解的案例中，它们仅仅代表了一种既有的机制，这种机制很容易被更间接的心理动机所利用，而无需受到语音接触的影响。在许多情况下，口误的发生完全与语音规律无关。在这一点上，我完全同意冯特的观点，他和我一样认为，导致口误的条件十分复杂，远远超出了语音相互作用的范畴。另一方面，虽然我接受冯特所说的这些“更遥远的心理影响”，但我看不出为什么我们不能也承认，当一个人语速很快，注意力有所分散时，口误的条件很容易被限制在梅林格和迈耶所定义的范围内。但在他们收集的一些例子中，似乎实际上存在更复杂的解释。让我以前面提到的案例为例[第53页]。

Es war mir auf der Schwest … Brust so schwer.

它压在我姐姐的胸口，让她感觉很沉重。

Was this really a simple instance of Schwe displacing Bru , a syllable of equal value, as the initial sound? It can hardly be denied that here the sound Schwe could also have superseded Bru because of a special relationship, none other than the associated ideas of Schwester — Bruder [sister — brother], and perhaps also Brust der Schwester [sister’s breast], leading on to other trains of thought. These assistants, invisible backstage, lent the otherwise innocuous Schwe the force to express itself as a slip of the tongue.

这真的仅仅是“Schwe”取代了“Bru”这个同等音节的起始音吗？很难否认，“Schwe”的发音也可能因为某种特殊关系而取代了“Bru”，这种关系正是源于“Schwester — Bruder”（姐妹—兄弟）以及“Brust der Schwester”（姐妹的乳房）等相关概念，进而引申出其他含义。正是这些幕后推手，赋予了原本无害的“Schwe”以口误的形式表达出来的力量。

In other slips of the tongue we may assume that an echo of indecent words or meanings is the really disruptive factor. The sole aim of the intentional distortion and misrepresentation of words and phrases, so popular among the vulgar-minded, is to take something harmless in itself as the occasion for referring to taboo subjects, and such plays on words are so common that it would hardly be surprising for them to emerge unintentionally and against the speaker’s will. Examples that belong in this category probably include Eischeissweibchen [egg-shit-female] for Eiweissscheibchen [small slices of egg white], Apopos Fritz [ Popo , bum] for A propos Fritz , Lokuskapitäl [lavatory capital] for Lotuskapitäl [lotus capital], etc., and perhaps even the transposition of the vowels in St Mary Magdalene’s Alabasterbuchse [alabaster casket] to create Alabüsterbachse [a coinage with the central element suggesting Büste , bosom]. 5 The example quoted above [ p. 53 ] — ‘I will ask you to belch to the health of our leader’ — is little more than an unintentional parody echoing what the speaker intended to say, and had I been the man to whose honours this lapse was contributed, I would probably have thought how wise the Romans were, when an emperor celebrated a triumph, to let the common soldiers express their private reservations about the great man in satirical songs. Meringer ( p. 50 ) tells us that when the oldest man in a certain gathering was addressed by the familiar honorary title of ‘Senexl’ or ‘altes Senexl [‘old man’, using Latin senex with the Austrian diminutive l added]’, he himself had drunk a toast to him saying, ‘Prost, Senex altesl!’ His own slip shocked him, and perhaps we can understand why if we remember how close ‘Altesl [‘old fellow’, again with the Austrian ending]’ comes to insulting someone by calling him ‘alter Esel [old donkey]’. There have always been strong inhibitions against failing to show the veneration due to age (or reduced to childhood ideas, respect for one’s father).

在其他一些口误中，我们可以认为真正造成干扰的因素是无意间说出的不雅词语或含义。故意歪曲和误用词语和短语的做法在庸俗之人中十分盛行，其唯一目的就是借由一些本身无害的事物来指涉禁忌话题。这种文字游戏如此常见，以至于说话者无意间脱口而出也并不奇怪。属于这一类别的例子可能包括 Eischeissweibchen（蛋黄-屎-女人）对应 Eiweissscheibchen（小块蛋清），Apopos Fritz（屁股）对应 A propos Fritz，Lokuskapitäl（厕所柱头）对应 Lotuskapitäl（莲花柱头）等等，甚至可能包括圣玛丽·玛格达琳的 Alabasterbuchse（雪花石膏匣）中元音的颠倒，从而创造出 Alabüsterbachse（一个以 Büste（胸部）为中心元素的造词）。 5 上面引用的例子[p. 53] — “我要请你们打嗝来祝我们的领袖健康” — 只不过是无意中模仿了演讲者想要表达的意思，如果我是因这次失误而获得荣誉的人，我可能会想，罗马人在皇帝庆祝凯旋时，让普通士兵用讽刺歌曲表达他们对这位伟人的私人保留意见，真是明智之举。梅林格（第50页）告诉我们，在一次聚会上，当人们用熟悉的尊称“Senexl”或“altes Senexl”（拉丁语senex加上奥地利语的指小词缀l）称呼最年长的老人时，他自己却举杯向他敬酒，说道：“Prost, Senex altesl!”（干杯，老先生！）。他的口误让他自己都感到震惊，如果我们记住“Altesl”（同样加上奥地利语后缀）与“alter Esel”（老驴）这种侮辱性的说法有多么接近，或许就能理解他的震惊了。人们总是强烈地忌讳不去表达对长者的敬意（或者说，源于孩童时代对父亲的尊重）。

I hope my readers will note the difference of value between those interpretations for which there is no evidence, and the examples I have collected myself and elucidated by analysis. If at heart, however, I still expect to find that even apparently simple cases of slips of the tongue will prove to derive from disruption by a partly suppressed idea from outside the intended context, then I am led to do so by a very interesting remark of Meringer’s. As he says, it is worth noting that no one likes admitting to a slip of the tongue. There are some very clever and honest people whose feelings will be quite injured if they are told they have perpetrated one. I would not venture to make this statement as universal as Meringer’s ‘no one’ suggests, but there is significance in the emotion we feel when faced with the evidence of our slips of the tongue, which is obviously in the nature of shame. It may be equated with our annoyance on being unable to remember a forgotten name and our surprise at the persistence of an apparently insignificant memory, and always indicates that there has been some reason for the disturbance.

我希望读者能注意到，那些缺乏证据支持的解释与我亲自收集并经分析阐明的例证之间存在价值差异。然而，即便我内心深处仍然认为，即使是看似简单的口误，最终也源于某种被部分压抑的、来自语境之外的想法的干扰。梅林格的一句非常有趣的评论促使我得出这样的结论。正如他所说，值得注意的是，没有人喜欢承认自己口误。有些非常聪明诚实的人，如果被告知自己犯了口误，也会感到非常受伤。我不敢断言这句话像梅林格所说的“没有人”那样具有普遍性，但当我们面对自己口误的证据时所感受到的情绪——显然是羞耻感——确实具有重要意义。这可以比作我们记不起一个遗忘的名字时的恼怒，以及我们对一个看似无关紧要的记忆的持久性的惊讶，并且总是表明这种干扰是有原因的。

The intentional distortion of names is taken as insulting, and in a considerable number of cases where it manifests itself as an unintentional slip of the tongue it may well have the same significance. The person who, according to Mayer ( p. 38 ), once said Freuder instead of Freud because just before that he had mentioned the name of Breuer , and on another occasion spoke of a Freuer-Breudian method ( p. 28 ), was no doubt a fellow professional who felt no great sympathy for that method. I will deal later, under the heading of slips of the pen, with a case of the distortion of a name which cannot be explained in any other way. 6

故意歪曲名字会被视为一种侮辱，而且在很多情况下，即使只是无意的口误，也可能具有同样的侮辱意味。据梅耶（第38页）所述，有人曾把弗洛伊德（Freud）说成弗罗伊德（Freuder），因为在此之前他提到了布鲁尔（Breuer）的名字；还有一次，他谈到了一种弗罗伊德-布鲁德式的方法（第28页）。毫无疑问，此人是一位同行，但他对这种方法并不认同。稍后，在“笔误”这一章节中，我将讨论一个无法用其他方式解释的名字歪曲案例。

In these cases, a criticism that has to be dismissed because just at that moment it does not correspond to the speaker’s intention is the disturbing factor.

在这些情况下，令人不安的因素是，由于批评意见与说话者的意图不符，因此必须予以驳回。

Conversely, the substitution of names, the appropriation of another name, and identification by a slip in the name must denote some kind of recognition that at the moment, for one reason or another, has to stay in the background. S. Ferenczi tells us of an experience of this kind from his schooldays:

反之，名字的替换、挪用他人名字以及通过名字上的小错误进行识别，必然意味着某种程度的认可，而这种认可由于某种原因，此刻必须保持低调。S. Ferenczi 向我们讲述了他学生时代就曾有过类似的经历：

‘In my first year at grammar school, I was to recite a poem in public (that is, in front of the whole class) for the first time in my life. I was well prepared, and was dismayed to have my recitation disrupted by roars of laughter at the very beginning. The teacher explained this curious reception: I had given the title of the poem, “Aus der Ferne” [‘From Afar’] perfectly correctly, but as its author I had named not the real poet — but myself. The poet’s name is Alexander (Sándor) Petöfi. The fact that his first name was the same as mine encouraged the confusion, but its real cause was surely my identification at the time in my heart of hearts with that famous and heroic poet. I felt love and deep respect bordering on adoration for him even in my conscious mind, and of course there was also a whole lamentable ambition complex behind my slip.’

“我上文法学校一年级的时候，生平第一次要在全班同学面前公开朗诵诗歌。我做了充分的准备，却没想到朗诵一开始就被哄堂大笑打断，这让我非常沮丧。老师解释了这种奇怪的反应：我把诗的标题“Aus der Ferne”（《来自远方》）说得完全正确，但却把作者写成了我自己的名字，而不是真正的诗人。诗人的名字是亚历山大·佩托菲（Alexander (Sándor) Petöfi）。他的名字和我的名字一样，这加剧了大家的误会，但真正的原因肯定是我当时内心深处对这位著名而英勇的诗人产生了强烈的认同感。即使在我的意识层面，我也对他充满了爱戴和深深的敬意，甚至近乎崇拜。当然，我的口误背后也隐藏着一股令人遗憾的野心。”

I heard of a similar case of identification through the switching of names from a young doctor, who hesitantly and reverently introduced himself to the famous Virchow in the words: Dr Virchow. The professor turned to him in surprise and asked: ‘Oh, is your name Virchow too?’ I don’t know how the ambitious young man justified himself for this slip of the tongue: whether he hit upon the engaging excuse that he had felt so insignificant beside the man who bore this great name that his own was bound to escape him, or whether he was brave enough to confess that he hoped to become as great a man as Virchow himself some day, and trusted that the professor would not despise him for that. One of those two ideas — or perhaps both of them at once — may have cast the young man into confusion when he introduced himself.

我听说过一个类似的误认案例：一位年轻医生怯生生地、毕恭毕敬地向著名的维尔肖教授自我介绍时，脱口而出：“维尔肖医生。”教授惊讶地转向他，问道：“哦，你也叫维尔肖吗？”我不知道这位雄心勃勃的年轻人是如何解释自己口误的：他是否想出了一个令人信服的借口，说自己在这位拥有如此伟大名字的人面前感到渺小，以至于一时想不起自己的名字？或者他是否勇敢地坦白，自己希望有朝一日能像维尔肖一样伟大，并相信教授不会因此而轻视他？这两种想法中的一种——或许两者兼而有之——可能正是这位年轻人自我介绍时感到困惑的原因。

For very personal reasons, I must leave the question of whether a similar interpretation can be applied to the following case open. At the International Congress in Amsterdam in 1907, the theory of hysteria that I had put forward was the subject of lively discussion. In his vehement tirade against me, it appears that one of my most energetic adversaries repeatedly slipped up by putting himself in my place and speaking as if in my name. He said, for instance: ‘As everyone knows, Breuer and I have shown…’ whereas he must have meant to say: ‘Breuer and Freud’. The name of this opponent of my theories is not in the least like my own. This example, and many other cases of names being switched by a slip of the tongue, remind us that such slips can dispense entirely with any resonance to help them come into being, and can emerge purely through concealed associations of content,

出于非常私人的原因，我必须对以下案例是否可以采用类似的解释持开放态度。在1907年阿姆斯特丹举行的国际大会上，我提出的癔症理论引发了热烈的讨论。在我激烈的抨击中，我的一位最有力的对手似乎屡次口误，把自己代入我的位置，以我的名义发言。例如，他说：“众所周知，布鲁尔和我已经证明……”，而他本想说的应该是“布鲁尔和弗洛伊德”。这位理论反对者的名字与我的名字截然不同。这个例子，以及许多其他因口误而混淆名字的例子，提醒我们，这种口误的产生完全不需要任何共鸣，而仅仅是通过隐藏的内容联想而产生的。

In other and much more significant cases a slip of the tongue, or indeed the replacement of an intended remark by its reverse, is caused by self-criticism and internal resistance to what one is saying. We are surprised to find the wording of a statement working against its intention, so that the linguistic slip reveals an internal insincerity. 7 Here the slip of the tongue acts as a mimic means of expression, although often, admittedly, the expression of something unintended; it is a means of giving oneself away. For instance, when a man who does not prefer what might be described as normal intercourse in his relations with women says in conversation, of a girl with a reputation as a coquette: ‘If she had anything to do with me she’d soon stop her Koëttieren ,’ there is no doubt that he can only have meant the word koitieren [to have sexual intercourse], and its effect on the intended word kokettieren [to be coquettish] can be ascribed to this kind of modification. Or take the following case: ‘An uncle of ours was greatly offended for months because we never visited him. When we moved house we took the chance of going to see him again after a long interval. He appeared to be delighted by our visit, and on parting said, with warm feeling: “Well, from now on I hope to see you less frequently than before.”’

在其他一些更为重要的情况下，口误，或者更确切地说，用相反的词语代替原本想说的话，是由自我批评和对所说内容的内在抵触造成的。我们惊讶地发现，某些陈述的措辞反而与本意背道而驰，以至于这种语言上的失误暴露了内心的虚伪。 7 在这里，口误起到了一种模仿表达的作用，尽管它常常表达的是无意之言；它是一种暴露自我的方式。例如，当一个不喜欢与女性进行正常性交的男人在谈话中谈到一位以卖弄风情著称的女孩时说：“如果她跟我在一起，她很快就会停止她的卖弄风情”，毫无疑问，他想表达的只能是“koitieren”（性交），而它对原本想表达的“kokettieren”（卖弄风情）的影响，正是这种语言上的改变造成的。或者举个例子：“我们的一位叔叔几个月来一直很生气，因为我们从未去看望过他。搬家后，我们抓住机会，时隔多年再次去看望他。他似乎对我们的探望非常高兴，临别时热情地说：‘嗯，从今以后，我希望你们能少来几次。’”

Favourable opportunities that the verbal material happens to offer frequently cause slips of the tongue to occur, with the startling effect of a revelation or the full comic effect of a joke.

口头材料恰好提供的有利机会常常导致口误发生，其效果可能是令人震惊的发现，也可能是十足的笑话。

For instance, take the following case, observed and reported by Dr Reitler: ‘One lady said or intended to say admiringly to another: “I expect you trimmed that pretty new hat yourself?” but instead of aufgeputzt [trimmed] said aufgepatzt [echoing the word Patzerei , a clumsy job]. She could not go on praising the hat, as she meant to, since her unfortunate slip of the tongue had expressed her silent criticism of the trimming of the hat as “clumsily done” only too clearly, and no phrases of conventional admiration would now have carried conviction.’

例如，雷特勒博士观察并记录了以下案例：“一位女士本想对另一位女士赞许地说：‘我想这顶漂亮的新帽子是你自己修剪的吧？’但她却把‘aufgeputzt’（修剪）说成了‘aufgepatzt’（与Patzerei一词相似，意为笨拙的工作）。她无法继续像原本打算的那样赞美这顶帽子，因为她无意间的口误已经清楚地表达了她对帽子修剪‘笨拙’的无声批评，任何惯常的赞美之词都无法令人信服。”

Milder but still unmistakable is the criticism in the following example:

以下例子中的批评虽然较为温和，但仍然不容忽视：

‘A lady visiting an acquaintance felt very impatient and weary after listening to the other woman’s verbose and long-winded remarks. At last she managed to bring the visit to an end and take her leave, but another torrent of words delayed her as her acquaintance accompanied her into the hall, and even on her way out she had to stand in the doorway and go on listening. At last she interrupted, asking: “Are you at home in the Vorzimmer [the hall]?” Only the other woman’s surprised expression alerted her to her slip of the tongue. Tired of standing in the hall so long, she had intended to conclude the conversation by asking: “Are you at home Vormittag [in the morning]?”, and had inadvertently given away her sense of impatience at being prevented yet again from leaving.’

一位女士拜访一位熟人，听对方喋喋不休、冗长乏味的谈话后，感到十分不耐烦和疲惫。她终于结束了拜访，准备告辞，但熟人又滔滔不绝地讲了起来，直到她走到门厅才肯罢休。即便在离开的路上，她也不得不站在门口继续听。最后，她终于忍不住打断对方，问道：“您在家吗？（Vorzimmer）” 对方惊讶的表情让她意识到自己说漏了嘴。原来，她原本打算以“您早上在家吗？”来结束谈话，却无意中暴露了自己再次被阻拦而产生的不耐烦。

The next example, recorded by Dr Max Graf, is a warning to us to think before we speak:

下一个例子由马克斯·格拉夫博士记录，它警示我们说话前要三思：

‘At the general meeting of the Concordia journalists’ association a young member who was always impecunious delivered a vehement speech of opposition, and in his agitation spoke of Die Herren Vorschussmitglieder (in error for Vorstandsmitglieder or Ausschussmitglieder ) [‘committee members’, ‘members of the board’, whereas Vorschuss means ‘a financial advance’]. The committee was empowered to grant loans, and the young speaker had applied for one.’

在康考迪亚记者协会的全体会议上，一位一向囊中羞涩的年轻会员发表了慷慨激昂的反对演说。他在激动的发言中提到了“Die Herren Vorschussmitglieder”（误写为“Vorstandsmitglieder”或“Ausschussmitglieder”），而“Vorschuss”指的是“预支款项”。该委员会拥有发放贷款的权力，而这位年轻的演讲者已经申请了一笔贷款。

The example of the word Vorschwein for Vorschein showed how easily a slip of the tongue can be made when we have been going to some trouble to suppress indecorous words. We then air our true feelings in this way:

将 Vorschein 误写成 Vorschwein 的例子表明，当我们费尽心思抑制不雅言辞时，很容易就会口误。然后，我们就会这样表达自己的真实感受：

A photographer who had resolved not to call his clumsy assistants any rude names referring to animals told an apprentice who was about to empty a large and very full dish, and of course tipped half the liquid on the floor: ‘Oh, for goodness sake, schöpsen Sie [for schöpfen Sie , ‘take out’, but suggesting Schöps , an Austrian word for ‘sheep’] some of it first!’ And soon afterwards, when a woman assistant had carelessly endangered a dozen valuable plates and he was scolding her at length, he asked, ‘Must you be so hornverbrannt’ [for hirnverbrannt , ‘crack-brained’, but suggesting Hornochse , literally ‘horned ox’ but colloquially ‘fool’]…?’

一位摄影师决心不再用任何与动物有关的粗俗词语称呼他笨手笨脚的助手。当一位学徒正要倒掉一大盘满满的菜肴时，他不小心把一半的汤汁洒在了地上，于是对学徒说：“哦，我的天哪，先倒掉一些吧！”（schöpsen Sie 是 schöpfen Sie 的缩写，但这里暗示的是 Schöps，奥地利语中“羊”的意思）。不久之后，当一位女助手粗心大意地弄脏了十几只珍贵的盘子，他狠狠地训斥了她一番后，又问道：“你非得这么 hornverbrannt 吗？”（hirnverbrannt 是 hirnverbrannt 的缩写，但这里暗示的是 Hornochse，字面意思是“有角的牛”，但口语中是“傻瓜”的意思）……？

The next example illustrates a serious case of a speaker’s giving himself away by a slip of the tongue. Several accompanying circumstances justify its reproduction here in full from the account given by A. A. Brill in the Zentralblatt für Psychoanalyse , year II. 8

下一个例子说明了说话者因口误而暴露自己真实意图的严重案例。鉴于以下几个相关情况，我们在此全文转载A. A. Brill在《精神分析中心杂志》（Zentralblatt für Psychoanalyse）第二年发表的论述。

‘One evening, when Dr Frink and I went out walking, we were discussing several matters raised at the New York Psychoanalytical Society. We encountered a colleague, Dr R., whom I had not seen for years and of whose private life I knew nothing. We were very glad to meet again, and at my suggestion went to a coffee house where we spent two hours in lively conversation. He seemed to know a good deal about me, for after the usual greetings he asked how my small child was, and told me that he heard news of me now and then from a mutual friend, that he had read about my activities in the medical journals and took an interest in them. When I asked whether he was married himself he said no, and added: “Why would someone like me marry?”

“一天晚上，我和弗林克博士外出散步，讨论着纽约精神分析学会提出的一些问题。我们遇到了一位多年未见的同事R博士，我对他的私生活一无所知。我们很高兴再次见面，并在我的提议下去了一家咖啡馆，在那里我们愉快地聊了两个小时。他似乎很了解我，因为在例行问候之后，他问起我的小孩子，并告诉我他偶尔会从一位共同的朋友那里听到我的消息，他在医学期刊上读到过我的活动，并对此很感兴趣。当我问他自己是否已婚时，他说没有，并补充道：‘像我这样的人为什么要结婚呢？’”

‘On leaving the coffee house he suddenly turned to me: “I wonder what you would do in the following situation? I know a nurse who was involved as the other woman in a divorce case. The wife was suing her husband, citing the nurse as co-respondent, and he got the divorce.” 9 Here I interrupted him: “You mean she got the divorce.” He corrected himself at once — “Of course, she got the divorce” — and went on to say that the nurse was so upset by the case and the scandal in general that she took to the bottle, lapsed into a very nervous state, and so forth. He wanted my advice on how he should treat her.

离开咖啡馆时，他突然转向我：“我想知道，如果你遇到以下情况会怎么做？我认识一位护士，她卷入了一场离婚案，成了第三者。妻子起诉丈夫，把这位护士列为共同被告，结果丈夫胜诉了。”我打断他：“你是说她胜诉了？”他立刻纠正自己——“当然，她胜诉了”——然后接着说，那位护士因为这场官司和丑闻而心烦意乱，开始酗酒，精神状态极度紧张等等。他想听听我的建议，该如何对待她。

‘Once I had corrected his mistake, I asked him to explain it, and received the usual rather surprised answers: surely everyone had a right to make a slip of the tongue now and then, it was only a coincidence, there was nothing behind it, etc. I replied that every slip of the tongue was made for some reason, and I would be tempted to believe that he himself had been the protagonist in the story if he hadn’t already told me he was unmarried, since then the slip of the tongue would have been explained by his wish that his wife, not he, had lost the case, with the result that (in line with our laws on marriage) he would not have to pay alimony and could marry again here in New York. He firmly denied that there was anything in my assumption, but at the same time reinforced it by his strong emotional reaction, showing clear signs of agitation followed by laughter. When I asked him to tell me the truth in the interests of scientific research, he replied: “Well, if you don’t want to hear a lie you’ll simply have to take my word for it that I’m a bachelor, so your psychoanalytical explanation is completely wrong.” He added that a man like me, meticulously studying every tiny detail, was positively dangerous, and then he suddenly recollected another appointment and left us.

“我纠正了他的错误后，请他解释一下，得到的回答不出所料，略带惊讶：谁都有可能偶尔说错话，这只是个巧合，没什么特别的，等等。我回答说，每次说错话都有其原因，如果他之前没有告诉我他未婚，我几乎会相信他自己就是故事的主角。因为如果他之前告诉我他未婚，那么他之所以说错话，就是因为他希望败诉的是他的妻子而不是他，这样（根据我们的婚姻法）他就不用支付赡养费，而且可以在纽约再婚。他坚决否认我的猜测，但同时他强烈的情绪反应又印证了我的猜测，先是明显激动，然后又大笑起来。”当我为了科学研究的需要请他告诉我真相时，他回答说：“好吧，如果你不想听谎言，那就只能相信我的话，我是个单身汉，所以你的精神分析解释完全错误。”他还补充说，像我这样一丝不苟地研究每一个细节的人，简直太危险了，然后他突然想起还有另一个约会，就离开了。

‘All the same, Dr Frink and I were both convinced that I had found the explanation for his slip of the tongue, and I decided to prove or disprove it by making inquiries. A few days later I visited a neighbour, an old friend of Dr R.’s, who was able to confirm the whole of my assumption. The case had been heard a few weeks earlier, the nurse being cited as co-respondent. Dr R. is now firmly convinced that the theory behind Freudian mechanisms is correct.’

“尽管如此，弗林克医生和我都确信我已经找到了他口误的原因，所以我决定通过调查来验证我的判断。几天后，我拜访了一位邻居，他是R医生的老朋友，他证实了我的所有假设。几周前，这起案件已经开庭审理，那位护士被列为共同被告。R医生现在坚信弗洛伊德机制背后的理论是正确的。”

In the following case, recounted by O. Rank, another slip of the tongue was an equally obvious self-revelation:

在 O. Rank 叙述的以下案例中，另一次口误同样明显地暴露了个人本性：

‘A father who had no patriotic emotions at all, and intended to bring up his children free of what seemed to him such unnecessary feelings too, blamed his sons for taking part in a patriotic rally, and put their recruitment to the cause down to similar conduct on their uncle’s part, saying: “There’s no call for you to emulate him of all people; he’s an idiot .” The expression of surprise on the children’s faces at the unusual tone their father had adopted made him aware of his slip of the tongue, and he added, apologetically: ‘Of course, I meant to say patriot .’ [In German, as in English, the terms are Idiot and Patriot.]

一位父亲对爱国主义毫无兴趣，也希望自己的孩子不要沾染在他看来毫无必要的情感。他责怪儿子们参加爱国集会，并将他们加入爱国主义事业的原因归咎于叔叔的类似行为，说道：“你们根本没必要效仿他，他就是个白痴。”孩子们对父亲这反常的语气感到惊讶，父亲这才意识到自己说错了话，连忙道歉道：“当然，我本想说的是‘爱国者’（patriot）。”[德语和英语中，这两个词分别是“白痴”（idiot）和“爱国者”（patriot）。]

The woman in a conversation described by J. Stärcke (op. cit.) perpetrated a slip of the tongue that can also be interpreted as self-revelation. Stärcke adds a comment which is very relevant although it goes further than actual interpretation.

J. Stärcke（同上）描述的一段对话中，那位女士说漏了嘴，这也可以解读为自我暴露。Stärcke 补充了一条非常重要的评论，尽管它超越了实际的解读。

‘A woman dentist had agreed to examine her sister’s mouth and see if the contact between two of her molars was correct (that is to say, whether the sides of the molars touched in such a way that bits of food could not get stuck between them). Her sister complained of having to wait so long for the examination, and said, jokingly: “I dare say she’s treating another woman now, some dental colleague of hers, while she keeps her own sister waiting.” The dentist then examined her sister and did in fact find a small hole in one of her molars. “I didn’t know it was as bad as that,” she says. “I just thought you might have no Kontant [ready cash]… I mean Kontakt [contact between the teeth].” “There,” cried her sister, laughing, “now do you agree that it was just your avarice that made you keep me waiting longer than your paying patients?”

一位女牙医答应帮她妹妹检查口腔，看看她两颗臼齿的咬合是否正常（也就是说，臼齿的侧面是否紧密贴合，食物残渣不会卡在牙缝里）。她妹妹抱怨检查等了太久，还开玩笑说：“我敢说她现在肯定在给别的女人看牙，是她的某个牙医同事，却让她自己妹妹等着。” 牙医检查后，果然发现她一颗臼齿上有一个小洞。“我不知道情况这么严重，”她说，“我还以为你牙齿咬合不好呢……我是说，牙齿咬合不好。” “瞧，”她妹妹笑着说，“现在你承认，让你让我等的时间比你的付费病人还长，完全是因为你的贪婪吧？”

‘(I ought not, of course, to add ideas of my own to hers or draw conclusions from them, but on hearing about this slip of the tongue my mind flew straight to the fact that these two delightful and clever young women are unmarried and do not mix in company much with young men, and I wondered whether they would have more contact with young men if they did have more ready money.)’

（当然，我不应该在她的言论基础上添加自己的想法或从中得出结论，但听到她这番口误后，我立刻想到，这两位可爱聪慧的年轻女子都未婚，而且很少与年轻男子交往，我不禁想，如果她们有更多钱，是否会与年轻男子有更多接触。）

The following slip of the tongue, communicated by T. Reik (op. cit.), is another case of self-revelation:

以下这句口误，出自 T. Reik（同上），是又一个自我暴露的例子：

‘A young girl was to be engaged to a young man whom she did not like. Hoping to bring the two young people closer, their parents arranged a party to be attended by the prospective fiancés. The girl had enough self-control not to let her suitor, who was very attentive to her, see that she did not care for him. But when her mother asked if she liked the young man, she replied politely: “Oh yes. He’s very liebenswidrig [‘adverse to love’, in error for liebenswürdig , ‘charming’, literally ‘worthy of love’].”’

一位年轻女孩即将与一位她并不喜欢的年轻男子订婚。为了拉近两人的距离，他们的父母安排了一场宴会，邀请准未婚夫和准新娘参加。女孩很有自制力，没有让对她殷勤的求婚者看出她对他没感觉。但当她母亲问她是否喜欢这位年轻男子时，她礼貌地回答说：“哦，是的。他非常‘liebenswidrig’（误用为‘liebenswürdig’，意为‘迷人’，字面意思是‘值得被爱’）。”

The same may be said of another case, which O. Rank describes as a ‘comical slip of the tongue’.

另一个案例也可以这样说，O. Rank 将其描述为“滑稽的口误”。

‘A young man told the following anecdote to a married woman who liked a good story, and was said to be not unwilling to entertain extra-marital advances if they came with suitable presents attached; he was seeking her favours himself. One of a couple of business acquaintances was trying to win the favour of his colleague’s rather aloof wife, which she finally agreed to grant him in return for a present of a thousand gulden. When her husband was about to go away, his colleague borrowed a thousand gulden from him, promising to return them to his wife next day. He then, of course, gave that sum of money to the wife, allegedly in return for her love, and she thought all was discovered when her husband came home and asked for the thousand gulden, thereby adding insult to injury. When the young man telling this tale had reached the point where the seducer told his companion, “I’ll return the money to your wife tomorrow,” the lady interrupted him with a very significant remark “But haven’t you given it back to me already? Oh, I’m sorry, I meant haven’t you told me that already?” She could hardly have revealed her willingness to give herself to the storyteller more clearly without saying so straight out’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse I, 1914).

一位年轻男子给一位已婚妇女讲了这样一个故事。这位妇女喜欢听故事，据说如果婚外情能附带合适的礼物，她也乐于接受。这位年轻男子自己也在追求她。他的一对生意伙伴中，有一位试图赢得同事那位性格冷淡的妻子的芳心。最终，妻子答应他，条件是他送她一千古尔登。在她丈夫即将出门之际，这位伙伴向他借了一千古尔登，并承诺第二天就还给妻子。然后，他当然把这笔钱给了妻子，说是为了回报她的爱。当她丈夫回家后向她索要那一千古尔登时，她以为一切都败露了，这无疑是雪上加霜。当讲述这个故事的年轻人讲到诱惑者对他的同伴说“我明天会把钱还给你妻子”时，那位女士打断了他，说了一句意味深长的话：“可是你不是已经还给我了吗？哦，对不起，我是说，你不是已经告诉我了吗？”她几乎不可能更清楚地表明她愿意把自己交给讲故事的人，除非她直接说出来。（《国际精神分析杂志》I，1914）

A good case of self-revelation of this kind, but with an innocuous outcome, is recounted by V. Tausk under the title: ‘The Faith of Our Fathers’: ‘Since my fiancée was Christian,’ said Herr A., ‘and did not want to convert to Judaism, I had to convert from Judaism to Christianity myself in order to marry. I changed my religion not without some inner reluctance, but the aim seemed to me to justify my conversion, particularly as I was not an observant Jew, and need not abandon any religious conviction, since I had none. None the less, I always acknowledged my Jewishness later, and few of my acquaintances know that I am baptized. The two sons of my marriage were baptized as Christians. When the boys had grown to a suitable age they were told of their Jewish descent, so that if they came under anti-Semitic influence at school they would not turn against their father for unnecessary reasons. A few years ago I and the children, who were then at primary school, were spending our summer holidays in D. with a teacher and his family. When we were eating a light meal with our very friendly hosts, the lady of the house, knowing nothing of the Jewish descent of her summer guests, made some very cutting remarks about Jews. I ought to have come straight out with the facts, thus setting my sons an example through the courage of my convictions, but I shrank from the unpleasant arguments that usually follow such a revelation. I was also afraid that if our hosts’ attitude to us became less friendly because we were Jewish, we might have to leave the comfortable accommodation we had found, and that would spoil our holiday, which was short enough anyway. However, as I felt it quite likely that my boys would frankly and freely tell the truth, perhaps with serious consequences, if they went on listening to the conversation any longer, I thought I would send them into the garden to get them out of the present company. “Off you run into the garden, Juden [Jews],” I said, quickly correcting myself and saying “ Jungen [boys]”. In this case my slip of the tongue enabled me to express the courage of my convictions after all. Our hosts in fact drew no conclusions from my slip because they did not see it as significant, but I could not help drawing my own, to the effect that the “faith of our fathers” cannot be denied with impunity if one is a father’s son and has sons of one’s own’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse IV, 1916).

V. Tausk 在题为《我们父辈的信仰》的文章中讲述了一个类似的自我揭露的典型案例，其结果并无害处：“A先生说：‘我的未婚妻是基督徒，她不想改信犹太教，所以我为了娶她，不得不从犹太教改信基督教。我改变宗教信仰并非毫无内心的不情愿，但我觉得这样做是合理的，尤其是我并非虔诚的犹太教徒，而且我本来就没有宗教信仰，所以也无需放弃任何宗教信仰。尽管如此，我后来一直承认自己的犹太血统，我的熟人中很少有人知道我受过洗礼。我的两个儿子都受过基督教洗礼。等孩子们长大到合适的年龄，我告诉了他们自己的犹太血统，这样，如果他们在学校受到反犹太主义的影响，就不会因为不必要的原因而与父亲反目。’”几年前，我和孩子们（当时还在上小学）在D地和一位老师一家共度暑假。我们和非常友好的主人一起吃着便餐时，女主人对我们这些暑期客人的犹太血统一无所知，却说了些非常刻薄的关于犹太人的话。我本应该直截了当地说明情况，用我的勇气给儿子们树立榜样，但我却畏惧于揭露真相后通常会引发的不愉快争论。我也担心，如果我们是犹太人，主人对我们的态度会变得冷淡，我们可能不得不离开这间舒适的住处，那样会毁了我们本来就很短暂的假期。然而，我觉得如果孩子们继续听下去，他们很可能会坦率地说出真相，而这可能会带来严重的后果，所以我决定让他们去花园里走走，远离那些人。 “你们这些犹太人，都跑到花园里去吧，”我说，随即赶紧纠正自己，改口说“你们这些男孩”。这次我的口误最终还是让我得以表达自己信念的勇气。事实上，我们的主人并没有从我的口误中得出任何结论，因为他们认为这无关紧要，但我却忍不住得出自己的结论，那就是“如果一个人是父亲的儿子，并且自己也有儿子，那么就不能毫无顾忌地否定‘我们父辈的信仰’”（《国际精神分析杂志》第四卷，1916年）。

The following case of a slip of the tongue was by no means innocuous, and I would not describe it had not the court official during the trial concerned noted it down himself for this collection:

以下这个口误绝非无关紧要，如果不是审判期间的法庭官员亲自记录下来收录于此，我也不会描述它：

A private soldier was accused of breaking and entering, and testified in court that: ‘When it happened I hadn’t yet been released from my military Diebstellung [‘position as thief, in error for Dienststellung , ‘military service’]; I was still in the army at the time.’

一名列兵被指控非法闯入，他在法庭上作证说：“事发时，我还没有从我的军事职务 Diebstellung（误将 Dienststellung 写成了 Dienststellung，即‘兵役’）中退役；当时我还在军队服役。”

A slip of the tongue can be amusing when it emerges in confirmation of something the speaker is denying, and may be very welcome to the doctor practising psychoanalytical methods. I was once interpreting a dream of one of my patients in which the name Jauner occurred. The dreamer did know someone of that name, but it was impossible to discover why that person should feature in the dream, so I ventured to suggest that it could be simply because the name Jauner resembles the pejorative term Gauner [rascal]. My patient instantly and energetically denied it, but his slip of the tongue as he did so confirmed my suggestion when he transposed the same initial letters a second time. He had told me, ‘No, really, that’s too jewagt [for gewagt , ‘far-fetched’].’ When I pointed out the slip, he accepted my interpretation. If a slip of the tongue that turns what the speaker intended to say into its opposite is made by one of the adversaries in a serious argument, it immediately puts him at a disadvantage, and his opponent seldom wastes any time in exploiting the advantage for his own ends.

当口误恰好印证了说话者否认的事情时，可能会让人觉得有趣，而对于运用精神分析方法的医生来说，这或许正是他们乐于见到的。我曾经为一位病人解梦，梦中出现了“Jauner”这个名字。做梦者确实认识一个叫这个名字的人，但却无法解释为什么这个人会出现在梦里。于是我大胆地提出，这或许仅仅是因为“Jauner”这个名字与贬义词“Gauner”（恶棍）相似。我的病人立刻断然否认，但他在否认的同时，又一次口误，将同样的字母顺序颠倒过来，证实了我的推测。他告诉我：“不，真的，这太‘jewagt’（应该是“gewagt”，意为“牵强附会”）了。”当我指出他的口误后，他接受了我的解释。在严肃的辩论中，如果一方说话不慎口误，导致自己想表达的意思与实际意思相反，那么他就会立即处于不利地位，而他的对手很少会浪费时间利用这种优势来达到自己的目的。

It is clear, then, that in general people interpret slips of the tongue, like other slips, just as I do in this book, even if they do not theoretically support my ideas and are not themselves inclined to reject the toleration of slips as a convenient attitude. But the mirth and derision occasioned by such slips of the tongue at important moments militate against what is claimed to be the general consensus of opinion: that a slip of the tongue is merely a lapsus linguae with no psychological significance. It was none other than Prince Bülow, Chancellor of Germany, who tried to save the situation by making that claim when a slip of the tongue in the wording of his speech in defence of his Kaiser in November 1907 turned it into its opposite.

由此可见，人们通常像我在本书中那样，将口误解读为与其他失误一样，即便他们在理论上并不支持我的观点，也不倾向于拒绝容忍口误这种权宜之计。然而，在重要时刻，此类口误所引发的嘲笑和讥讽，却与所谓的普遍共识相悖：即口误仅仅是语言上的失误，不具有任何心理意义。正是德国首相比洛亲王，在1907年11月为德皇辩护的演讲中，因口误而使演讲内容产生了截然相反的效果，他试图通过提出这种说法来挽救局面。

‘Where the present is concerned, the new age of Kaiser Wilhelm II,’ he said, ‘I can only repeat my statement of a year ago: it would be neither right nor just to say that our Emperor was surrounded by a body of responsible advisers … (loud cries of: irresponsible !)…to say that our Emperor was surrounded by a circle of irresponsible advisers. Forgive my lapsus linguae .’ (Laughter.)

“就目前而言，就德皇威廉二世的新时代而言，”他说道，“我只能重申我一年前的说法：说我们的皇帝身边围绕着一群负责任的顾问，既不正确也不公正……（众人高喊：不负责任！）……说我们的皇帝身边围绕着一群不负责任的顾问，既不正确也不公正。请原谅我的口误。”（笑声）

However, the point of Prince Bülow’s remark had to some extent been obscured by its accumulation of negatives, and sympathy for the speaker in his difficult situation prevented anyone from making any further use against him of this slip of the tongue. Another man fared worse in the same situation a year later, when he wanted to encourage his audience to demonstrate unreservedly in favour of the Kaiser, and in the process was reminded that other feelings resided in his loyal breast by a severe slip of the tongue.

然而，比洛亲王那番话的本意在某种程度上被其负面含义所掩盖，人们对他当时困境的同情也阻止了任何人进一步利用他的口误攻击他。一年后，另一个人在同样的情况下遭遇了更糟糕的境遇。他原本想鼓励听众毫无保留地拥护德皇，却因为一次严重的口误而暴露了自己忠诚之心深处的其他情感。

‘Lattmann (German Nationalist): As for the matter of the address, we take our stance on the orders of business of the Reichstag. According to those orders, the Reichstag has every right to offer such an address to the Kaiser. We believe that the united ideas and wishes of the German people are inclined to put forward such a unified demonstration on this point, and if we can do so in a form that pays due respect to our monarch’s feelings then we should do so rückgratlos [without backbone]. (Riotous mirth, lasting several minutes.) Gentlemen, I meant rückhaltlos [without reservations], not rückgratlos (further laughter), and let us hope that such an unreserved expression of popular opinion will be accepted by our Kaiser in these difficult times.’

拉特曼（德国民族主义者）：关于致辞一事，我们的立场取决于国会的议事规则。根据这些规则，国会完全有权向皇帝呈递这样的致辞。我们相信，德国人民的共同思想和愿望倾向于就此问题提出这样的统一示威，如果我们能够以一种既尊重君主感受又不失诚意的方式这样做，那么我们就应该毫无保留地这样做。（一阵哄堂大笑，持续了几分钟。）先生们，我指的是毫无保留地这样做，而不是毫无保留地这样做（又是一阵大笑），让我们希望，在如今这个艰难的时期，皇帝能够接受这种毫无保留的民意表达。

The journal Vorwärts of 12 November 1908 did not hesitate to point out the psychological significance of this slip of the tongue: ‘It is likely that no member of any parliament ever before presented his own attitude towards the monarch, and that of the parliamentary majority, more accurately than the anti-Semitic Lattmann when, on the second day of the interpellation, he involuntarily made the solemn and emotional admission that he and his friends intended to tell the Kaiser what they thought without backbone. General merriment drowned the rest of the unfortunate man’s remarks, and he thought it necessary to stammer out an explicit apology to the effect that he really mean without reservations. ’

1908年11月12日的《先驱报》（Vorwärts）毫不犹豫地指出了这一口误的心理意义：“在质询的第二天，当反犹分子拉特曼不由自主地郑重而激动地承认他和他的朋友们打算毫无保留地向德皇表达他们的想法时，恐怕没有哪个议员比他更准确地表达了自己对君主以及议会多数派的态度。众人的哄笑淹没了这位不幸议员接下来的话，他不得不结结巴巴地做出明确的道歉，大意是他确实毫无保留。”

In another example, a slip of the tongue acquired the almost uncanny character of a prophecy: in the spring of 1923 it was a great sensation in the international world of finance when X., a very young banker, perhaps one of the newest of the nouveaux riches in W. and in any event both the richest and the youngest, acquired the majority shareholding in the ٭٭٭ Bank after a brief contest. Consequently the former directors of that institution, financiers of the old stamp, were not re-elected at a remarkable general meeting, and young X. became chairman of the board of the bank. In the farewell speech made by a member of the board, Dr Y., on behalf of the old chairman who had failed to gain re-election, many of the audience noticed an unfortunate and repeated slip of the tongue on the part of the speaker. He kept speaking not of the ausscheidend [retiring] chairman but of the dahinscheidend [dying] chairman. As a matter of fact the old chairman, after failing to be re-elected, did die a few days after the meeting. However, he was over eighty years old at the time! (Storfer.)

另一个例子是，一次口误竟有了近乎预言般的奇妙效果：1923年春天，一位名叫X的年轻银行家——或许是当时西方世界新贵中最年轻的一位，而且无论如何都是最富有、最年轻的——在短暂的竞争后获得了某银行的多数股权，这在国际金融界引起了巨大轰动。结果，该银行的前任董事们，那些老派的金融家们，在一次非同寻常的股东大会上未能连任，年轻的X成为了该银行的董事长。在一位名叫Y的董事代表未能连任的老董事长发表的告别演说中，许多听众注意到他反复出现了一个不幸的口误。他一直把即将退休的董事长说成即将去世的董事长。事实上，那位老主席在竞选连任失败后，于会议结束后几天就去世了。不过，他当时已经八十多岁了！（斯托弗）

A good example of a slip of the tongue that is as much a case of information for the audience as a revelation of the speaker’s intentions comes in the second part of Wallenstein ( Die Piccolomini , Act I, Scene 5), and shows us that Schiller must have understood the mechanism and purpose of slips of the tongue when he made use of one here. In the previous scene, Max Piccolomini has enthusiastically supported the duke’s cause, and dwells on the blessings of peace revealed to him on his journey when he was escorting Wallenstein’s daughter to the camp. He leaves his father and the court envoy, Questenberg, in a state of great dismay. The fifth scene continues like this [given here in Coleridge’s translation]:

《华伦斯坦》第二部分（《皮科洛米尼》，第一幕第五场）中就有一个口误的绝佳例子，它既向观众传递了信息，又揭示了说话者的意图。这表明席勒运用口误时，必然已经理解了口误的机制和目的。在前一场戏中，马克斯·皮科洛米尼热情地支持公爵的事业，并津津乐道于护送华伦斯坦的女儿前往营地途中感受到的和平之福。他的父亲和宫廷使节奎斯滕贝格对此感到非常失望。第五场戏接下来的台词如下（以下为柯勒律治的译文）：

QUESTENBERG :

奎斯滕贝格：

Alas, alas! and stands it so?

唉，唉！难道就只能这样了吗？

What friend! and do we let him go away

真是个好朋友！我们怎么能让他离开呢？

In this delusion — let him go away?

在这种错觉中——让他离开吧？

Not call him back immediately, not open

不要立即给他回电话，不要开门

His eyes upon the spot?

他的目光是否锁定在那里？

OCTAVIO ( recovering himself out of a deep study ):

奥克塔维奥（从深入的研究中回过神来）：

He has now open’d mine

他现在已经打开了我的矿井。

And I see more than pleases me.

我看到的远超我的预期。

QUESTENBERG :

奎斯滕贝格：

What is it?

那是什么？

OCTAVIO :

奥克塔维奥：

Curse on this journey!

诅咒这段旅程！

QUESTENBERG :

奎斯滕贝格：

But why so? What is it?

但这是为什么呢？究竟是什么原因造成的？

OCTAVIO :

奥克塔维奥：

Come, come along, friend! I must follow up

来吧，朋友！我得跟进一下。

The ominous track immediately. Mine eyes

不祥的预兆立刻浮现。我的眼睛

Are open’d now, and I must use them. Come!

现在都打开了，我必须用它们。来吧！

( Draws Q. on with him )

（和他一起画Q）

QUESTENBERG : What now? Where go you then?

奎斯滕伯格：接下来呢？你要去哪里？

OCTAVIO :

奥克塔维奥：

To her herself.

她对自己而言。

QUESTENBERG :

奎斯滕贝格：

To —

到 -

OCTAVIO ( correcting himself ):

奥克塔维奥（纠正自己）：

To the Duke! Come let us go, (etc.)

去见公爵！放我们走吧！（等等）

This small slip of the tongue (‘to her’ instead of ‘to him’) is designed to tell us that the father understands his son’s present partisanship, while the courtier Questenberg complains that he is speaking in riddles.

这个小小的口误（“对她”而不是“对他”）旨在告诉我们，父亲理解儿子目前的偏袒，而朝臣奎斯滕贝格抱怨说他说话像谜语一样。

Otto Rank found another example of the poetic use of a slip of the tongue in Shakespeare. I quote Rank’s comments from the Zentralblatt für Psychoanalyse I, 3: ‘A poetically very subtle slip of the tongue, exploited with technical brilliance and showing us, like the slip in Wallenstein described by Freud, that dramatists both understand the mechanism and sense of such slips and assume that audiences will also understand them, occurs in Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice (Act III, Scene 2). Portia, forced by her father’s wishes to choose a husband by lot, has hitherto been lucky enough to have escaped all her unwelcome suitors by chance. Now that she has finally found one whom she really likes in the person of Bassanio, she fears that he too will make the wrong choice. She would like to tell him that even so, he can be sure of her love, but her oath prevents her. Shakespeare gives her this speech, delivered to the suitor she favours in a state of inner turmoil [the italics are Freud’s]:

奥托·兰克在莎士比亚的作品中发现了另一个运用口误的诗意例子。我引用兰克在《精神分析中心期刊》第一卷第三期中的评论：“莎士比亚的《威尼斯商人》（第三幕第二场）中出现了一个诗意极其微妙的口误，运用了精湛的技巧，正如弗洛伊德描述的瓦伦斯坦口误一样，向我们展示了剧作家既理解此类口误的机制和意义，又假定观众也能理解。波西亚被迫遵从父亲的意愿，通过抽签选择丈夫，此前她一直幸运地躲过了所有不受欢迎的求婚者。如今，她终于找到了自己真正喜欢的人——巴萨尼奥，却担心他也会做出错误的选择。她想告诉他，即便如此，他也可以确信她对他的爱，但她的誓言阻止了她。”莎士比亚让她在内心充满挣扎的情况下，向她心仪的求婚者发表了这段演说[斜体字为弗洛伊德所加]：

I pray you tarry; pause a day or two,

我恳请你稍作停留；停顿一两天。

Before you hazard: for, in choosing wrong,

在你冒险之前：因为，在做出错误选择时，

I lose your company; therefore, forbear awhile;

我失去了你的陪伴；因此，请稍等片刻；

There’s something tells me ( but it is not love )

我感觉（但那不是爱）

I would not lose you…

我不会失去你……

… I could teach you

我可以教你

How to choose right, but then I am forsworn;

如何做出正确的选择，但我却发誓要放弃；

So will I never be; so may you miss me;

我永远不会成为那样的人；所以，愿你怀念我；

But if you do you’ll make me wish a sin,

但如果你那样做，你会让我渴望犯罪。

That I have been forsworn. Beshrew your eyes,

我已背弃誓言。玷污你的双眼。

They have o’erlooked me, and divided me;

他们忽视了我，并将我分裂了；

One half of me is yours, the other half yours —

我的一半属于你，另一半也属于你——

Mine own, I would say; but if mine, then yours,

我会说，这是我自己的；但如果这是我的，那就是你的。

And so all yours.

所以，这一切都是你的了。

‘With remarkable psychological subtlety, the poet makes Portia’s slip of the tongue reveal the one thing she intended merely to convey in a slight hint, since she should not really have mentioned it at all — that even before Bassanio makes his choice she loves him and is all his. This device allays both her lover’s intolerable uncertainty and the spectator’s equally high suspense about the outcome of Bassanio’s choice.’

“诗人以非凡的心理描写，巧妙地让波西亚的口误揭示了她原本只想略作暗示（因为她本不该提及）的一件事——即便在巴萨尼奥做出选择之前，她也深爱着他，并且只属于他。这一手法既缓解了她爱人难以忍受的不安，也减轻了观众对巴萨尼奥最终选择结果的紧张心情。”

Considering the interest that such support on the part of great writers supplies to my own ideas about slips of the tongue, I think I may be justified in giving a third such example, taken from E. Jones: 10

考虑到伟大作家们对我关于口误的观点所给予的支持，我认为我有理由再举一个例子，这个例子来自 E. Jones： 10

‘In a recently published article Otto Rank drew our attention to a pretty instance of how Shakespeare caused one of his characters, Portia, to make a slip of the tongue that revealed her secret thoughts to an attentive member of the audience. I propose to relate a similar example from the Egoist , the masterpiece of the greatest English novelist, George Meredith. The plot of the novel is, shortly, as follows: Sir Willoughby Patterne, an aristocrat greatly admired by his circle, becomes engaged to a Miss Constantia Durham. She discovers in him an intense egoism, which he skilfully conceals from the world, and to escape the marriage she elopes with a Captain Oxford. Some years later Patterne becomes engaged to a Miss Clara Middleton, and most of the book is taken up with a detailed description of the conflict that arises in her mind on also discovering his egoism. External circumstances, and her conception of honour, hold her to her pledge, while he becomes more and more distasteful in her eyes. She partly confides in his cousin and secretary, Vernon Whitford, the man whom she ultimately marries; but from loyalty to Patterne and other motives he stands aloof.

在最近发表的一篇文章中，奥托·兰克向我们展示了一个莎士比亚笔下人物波西亚的巧妙例子：她无意间说漏了嘴，让一位细心的观众窥见了她内心的秘密。我打算讲述一个类似的例子，出自英国最伟大的小说家乔治·梅瑞狄斯的杰作《利己主义者》。这部小说的情节简述如下：威洛比·帕特恩爵士是一位备受圈内人敬仰的贵族，他与康斯坦蒂娅·达勒姆小姐订婚。达勒姆小姐发现他极度自私，但他却巧妙地将这一点隐藏起来。为了逃避婚约，达勒姆小姐与牛津上尉私奔。几年后，帕特恩与克拉拉·米德尔顿小姐订婚。小说的大部分篇幅都用来详细描述克拉拉在发现帕特恩的自私之后内心的挣扎。外部环境和她对荣誉的执着让她恪守婚约，而帕特恩在她眼中却越来越令人厌恶。她向他的表弟兼秘书弗农·惠特福德（她最终嫁给了他）透露了一些心事；但出于对帕特恩的忠诚和其他原因，他一直保持着距离。

‘In a soliloquy about her sorrow Clara speaks as follows: “‘If some noble gentleman could see me as I am and not disdain to aid me! Oh! to be caught out of this prison of thorns and brambles. I cannot tear my own way out. I am a coward. A beckoning of a finger 11 would change me, I believe. I could fly bleeding and through hootings to a comrade … Constantia met a soldier. Perhaps she prayed and her prayer was answered. She did ill. But, oh, how I love her for it! His name was Harry Oxford … She did not waver, she cut the links, she signed herself over. Oh, brave girl, what do you think of me? But I have no Harry Whitford; I am alone…’ The sudden consciousness that she had put another name for Oxford struck her a buffet, drowning her in crimson.”

在一段关于她悲伤的独白中，克拉拉说道：“如果哪位高贵的绅士能看到我现在的模样，并且不嫌弃地帮助我！哦！多么希望能够从这荆棘丛生的牢笼中脱身。我无法靠自己挣脱。我是个懦夫。我相信，只要有人向我伸出援手，我就会改变。我可以浑身是血，顶着喧闹声，飞奔到战友身边……康斯坦蒂娅遇到了一位士兵。或许她祈祷过，而她的祈祷得到了回应。她做了坏事。但是，哦，我多么爱她！他的名字叫哈里·牛津……她没有动摇，她斩断了束缚，她把自己交给了他。哦，勇敢的姑娘，你觉得我怎么样？但我没有哈里·惠特福德；我孤身一人……”突然意识到自己把另一个名字写在了牛津的头上，这让她如遭雷击，羞愧难当，满脸通红。

‘The fact that both men’s names end in “ford” evidently renders the confounding of them more easy, and would by many be regarded as an adequate cause for this, but the real underlying motive for it is plainly indicated by the author. In another passage the same lapsus occurs, and is followed by the spontaneous hesitation and sudden change of subject that one is familiar with in psychoanalysis and in Jung’s association experiments when a half-conscious complex is touched. Sir Willoughby patronizingly says of Whitford: “‘False alarm. The resolution to do anything unaccustomed is quite beyond poor old Vernon.”’ Clara replies: “‘But if Mr Oxford — Whitford… your swans, coming sailing up the lake, how beautiful they look when they are indignant. I was going to ask you, surely men witnessing a marked admiration for someone else will naturally be discouraged?’ Sir Willoughby stiffened with sudden enlightenment.”

“两人名字都以“ford”结尾，这显然更容易让人把他们混淆，许多人会认为这是造成混淆的充分理由，但作者已经明确指出了其真正的潜在动机。在另一处也出现了同样的口误，随后出现了在精神分析和荣格联想实验中常见的那种自发的犹豫和突然的话题转换，这种现象在触及半意识情结时很常见。威洛比爵士居高临下地评价惠特福德说：‘虚惊一场。可怜的老弗农根本做不出什么不寻常的事。’克拉拉回答说：‘但是，如果牛津先生——惠特福德……你的天鹅，在湖上航行，它们生气的时候看起来多么美丽啊。我本来想问你，人们看到别人明显地欣赏别人，难道不会感到沮丧吗？’威洛比爵士突然顿悟，身体僵硬起来。”

‘In still another passage, Clara by another lapsus betrays her secret wish that she was on a more intimate footing with Vernon Whitford. Speaking to a boyfriend, she says: “‘Tell Mr Vernon — tell Mr Whitford”’.’ 12

在另一段文字中，克拉拉又一次失言，流露出她内心深处的渴望，希望与弗农·惠特福德建立更亲密的关系。她对男友说：“告诉弗农先生——告诉惠特福德先生。”

The theory of slips of the tongue proposed here will stand up to examination even in its minor details. I have often been able to show that the slightest and most apparently obvious cases of such slips make sense, and will admit the same kind of explanation as the more striking examples. A patient who was intent upon making a short excursion to Budapest, although I advised her against it, justified herself by saying she was going only for three days, but made a slip of the tongue and said: only for three weeks , thus revealing that, in defiance of my wishes, she would rather spend three weeks than three days in what I considered unsuitable company. One evening I had to apologize for failing to meet my wife when she came out of the theatre, and told her, ‘But I was there at ten past ten.’ She corrected me: ‘You mean ten to ten.’ Of course I had meant to say ten to ten; I could not have claimed that arriving after ten was any excuse, since I had been told that the posters advertising the play said the performance would be over before ten. When I reached the theatre, I found the foyer darkened and the building empty. The performance had already ended, and my wife had not waited for me to arrive. When I looked at my watch, it was only five to ten. However, I decided to put as good a face as possible on the matter at home, saying I had arrived while there were still ten minutes to go to the hour. Unfortunately, my slip of the tongue foiled my intentions, revealing my deception by making me confess to more than I really needed to admit.

本文提出的口误理论即使在细枝末节上也经得起推敲。我经常能够证明，即使是最轻微、最显而易见的口误也合情合理，并且能够用与那些更引人注目的例子相同的解释来解释。一位病人执意要去布达佩斯短途旅行，尽管我劝阻了她，她还是辩解说自己只去三天，结果却口误说成了“只去三个星期”，这表明她违背了我的意愿，宁愿和我认为不合适的人待三个星期也不愿待三天。一天晚上，我不得不为没能迎接刚从剧院出来的妻子而道歉，我告诉她：“但我十点十分就到了。”她纠正我说：“你是说十点差十点。”我当然想说的是十点差十点；我不能以十点以后到达为借口，因为我听说演出海报上说演出会在十点前结束。当我到达剧院时，发现门厅一片漆黑，整栋楼空无一人。演出已经结束，妻子也没有等我。我看了一眼手表，才差五点十分。但我还是决定回家后尽量掩饰，谎称我是在离整点还有十分钟的时候到的。不幸的是，我的口误破坏了我的计划，让我不得不承认一些我本不必承认的事情，从而暴露了我的谎言。

This brings us to those disturbances of speech that cannot really be called slips of the tongue because they affect not merely a single word but the rhythm and mode of delivery of speech in general, for instance stammering and stuttering in embarrassment. But in both cases disturbed speech reveals an inner conflict. I do not really think that anyone would make a slip of the tongue in an audience with royalty, when seriously paying court to a lover, in a speech made in defence of his name and honour before a sworn jury, in short in all those cases where, as one may say, the mind is really concentrated on the matter in hand. Even when we are assessing an author’s style we must, and habitually do, bear in mind the principle of elucidation so indispensable in tracking down the origin of various slips of the tongue. A clear, unambiguous written style tells us that the author is at ease with himself, but where we find forced, tortuous expressions, which can be rightly said to tend in more than one direction, we recognize the part played in them by a complex train of thought insufficiently worked out, or we hear the suppressed voice of the author’s own criticism of himself. 13

这就引出了那些不能真正称之为口误的言语障碍，因为它们不仅影响单个词语，还影响整体的语速和表达方式，例如因尴尬而结巴。但在这两种情况下，言语障碍都揭示了一种内在的冲突。我并不认为有人会在觐见皇室成员时、在认真地向爱人示爱时、在宣誓就职的陪审团面前为自己的名誉和荣誉辩护时，总之，在所有那些可以说全神贯注于手头事情的情况下，会口误。即使在评价一位作家的文风时，我们也必须（而且通常也确实）牢记阐释原则，这对于追溯各种口误的根源至关重要。清晰明确的写作风格表明作者自在从容；但如果出现生硬晦涩、前后矛盾的表达，我们便能意识到这是作者思路复杂但表达不够清晰的表现，或是作者压抑的自我批评之声。

Since the first publication of this book, foreign friends and colleagues have taken to studying slips of the tongue that can be observed in the languages of their own countries. As one might expect, they have discovered that the laws of such slips are independent of the linguistic material itself, and have interpreted them in the same way as I have explained slips made by native German speakers here. I will cite just one example out of a countless number:

自本书首次出版以来，外国朋友和同事们开始研究他们本国语言中出现的口误。不出所料，他们发现这类口误的规律与语言材料本身无关，并且他们对这些口误的解释方式与我在此解释德语母语者口误的方式相同。我仅举无数个例子中的一个例子：

Dr A. A. Brill (New York) writes of himself: ‘A friend described to me a nervous patient and wished to know whether I could benefit him. I remarked, I believe that in time I could remove all his symptoms by psycho-analysis because it is a durable case wishing to say “ curable ”!’ (‘A Contribution to the Psychopathology of Everyday Life’, Psychotherapy , vol. III, no. 1, 1909).

A. A. Brill 博士（纽约）写道：“一位朋友向我描述了一位神经质的病人，并想知道我是否能帮助他。我评论说，我相信假以时日，我可以通过精神分析消除他所有的症状，因为这是一个持久的病例，我想说的是‘可治愈的’！”（《对日常生活精神病理学的贡献》，《心理治疗》，第 III 卷，第 1 期，1909 年）。

Finally, for those readers who do not shrink from a certain amount of concentration and to whom psychoanalysis is not an entirely alien subject, I will add an example that shows how even the pursuit of a slip of the tongue can lead us into mental profundities.

最后，对于那些不惧一定程度的专注，并且对精神分析并非完全陌生的读者，我将补充一个例子，说明即使是追寻口误也能将我们带入深刻的精神世界。

Dr L. Jekels writes: ‘On the eleventh of December I was addressed in Polish, rather imperiously and challengingly, by a lady whom I know and who demanded: “Now, do tell me why I said I had twelve fingers today!”

L. Jekels 博士写道：“12 月 11 日，一位我认识的女士用波兰语，语气相当专横和挑衅地问我：‘现在，告诉我，我今天为什么说我有十二根手指！’”

‘At my request she gave a fuller account of the circumstances in which she made that remark. She and her daughter were getting ready to go out to pay a social call, and she had asked her daughter, a case of dementia praecox at present in remission, to change her blouse, which the girl did in the next room, When the daughter came back she found her mother busy cleaning her nails, and the following conversation took place:

应我的要求，她更详细地讲述了她发表那番言论时的情形。她和女儿正准备出门拜访，她让患有早发性痴呆症但目前病情缓解的女儿去换件衬衫，女儿在隔壁房间换好了。女儿回来时，发现母亲正在修剪指甲，于是发生了以下对话：

Daughter: Oh, look, I’m ready but you aren’t!

女儿：哦，你看，我已经准备好了，但你还没有！

Mother: Well, you have only one blouse and I have twelve nails.

母亲：嗯，你只有一件衬衫，而我有十二个指甲。

Daughter: What?

女儿：什么？

Mother (impatiently): Well, of course. I have twelve fingers , don’t I?

母亲（不耐烦地）：当然了。我有十二根手指，不是吗？

‘When a colleague who was also listening to this story asked what she associated with the number twelve, her answer was both prompt and decided: “The twelfth of no month means anything very special to me.”

“当一位也在听这个故事的同事问她，她会把数字十二和什么联系起来时，她的回答既迅速又坚定：‘任何月份的十二号对我来说都没有什么特别的意义。’”

‘After a moment’s hesitation, she associated fingers with the following reminiscence: “People in my husband’s family tend to be born with six fingers on their feet.” (There are no separate and distinct words for the digits “fingers” and “toes” in Polish.) “So when our children were born, they were examined at once in case they had six fingers.” But for extraneous reasons we could not continue with the analysis that evening.

她犹豫片刻后，将手指与以下回忆联系起来：“我丈夫家的人似乎天生就有六根脚趾。”（波兰语中没有分别指“手指”和“脚趾”的词。）“所以我们的孩子出生后，都会立即接受检查，看看他们是不是有六根脚趾。”但由于一些其他原因，那天晚上我们无法继续进行分析。

‘Next morning, and it was the twelfth of December, the lady visited me and told me, visibly agitated: “Just think what’s happened! For the last twenty years or so I’ve sent good wishes to my husband’s old uncle on his birthday, which is today, so I always write to him on the eleventh. This year I forgot, and I’ve just had to telegraph him instead.”

“第二天早上，也就是12月12日，那位女士来拜访我，她情绪激动地告诉我：‘想想发生了什么事！过去二十多年来，我都会在今天——我丈夫老叔叔的生日——给他写生日祝福，所以我总是在11号给他写信。今年我忘了，只好给他发了电报。’”

‘I reminded myself and the lady how firmly she had waved aside my colleague’s question about the number twelve, which might have been expected to remind her of the uncle’s birthday, by saying that as a date the twelfth meant nothing special to her.

“我提醒自己和那位女士，她是如何坚决地拒绝了我同事关于数字十二的问题，而这个问题可能会让她想起叔叔的生日，她说十二这个日期对她来说没有任何特殊意义。

‘She now confessed that this uncle of her husband’s was rich, and she had always counted on a legacy from him, a particularly important factor in her present difficult financial situation.

“她现在承认，她丈夫的这位叔叔很有钱，她一直指望着能从他那里继承一笔遗产，这对她目前艰难的经济状况来说是一个特别重要的因素。”

‘So he, or rather his death, had come straight into her mind when a woman friend told her fortune from the cards a few days earlier, and said she would be coming into a great deal of money. It immediately struck her that this uncle was the only person from whom she or her children stood to inherit money, and the scene reminded her instantly that the same uncle’s wife had once promised to remember the narrator’s children in her will. In fact the uncle’s wife died intestate, but she might have given her husband instructions about a legacy.

“所以，几天前一位女性朋友用塔罗牌为她算命，说她会得到一大笔钱时，她立刻想到了他，或者更确切地说，是他的死。她马上意识到，这位叔叔是她和她的孩子唯一可能继承遗产的人，而这一幕也让她立刻想起，这位叔叔的妻子曾经答应过要在遗嘱中给她的孩子们留些遗产。事实上，这位叔叔的妻子去世时没有留下遗嘱，但她可能曾就遗产事宜对丈夫做过安排。”

‘The lady’s wish for her uncle by marriage to be dead must obviously have been very strong, since she had said to the friend who was telling her fortune: “Oh, you could really tempt a person to go out and kill someone!”

“这位女士希望她的姻亲叔叔死去的愿望一定非常强烈，因为她曾对给她算命的朋友说：‘哦，你真的可以诱惑一个人出去杀人！’”

‘In the four or five days between the fortune-telling incident and the uncle’s birthday, she had kept looking at the death announcements in newspapers published in the part of the country where he lived.

在算命事件发生到叔叔生日的四五天里，她一直关注着叔叔居住地所在地区报纸上的讣告。

‘No wonder, then, that as she wished for his death with such intensity, her mind had suppressed the memory and date of his forthcoming birthday so strongly, inducing her not just to forget an occasion she had observed for years, but even to remain unaware of it after my colleague’s question.

“难怪她如此强烈地希望他死去，以至于她的大脑强烈地压制了对他即将到来的生日的记忆和日期，这不仅让她忘记了她多年来一直关注的这个日子，甚至在我同事问起之后，她仍然对此一无所知。”

‘In the lapsus “twelve fingers” the suppressed number twelve had emerged, and played a part in her slip of the tongue.

在“十二根手指”这个口误中，被压抑的数字十二浮现出来，并在她口误中发挥了作用。

‘I say “played a part”, because the striking association she produced for “fingers” allows us to guess at other motivations, showing why the number twelve distorted the usually innocuous phrase about having ten fingers.

“我说‘发挥了作用’，是因为她对‘手指’产生的引人注目的联想，让我们得以猜测其他动机，从而揭示了为什么数字十二会扭曲通常无害的关于有十根手指的说法。

‘The idea in itself ran: “Some children in my husband’s family have been born with six digits on their feet.”

“这个想法本身是这样的：‘我丈夫家族里有些孩子天生脚上有六个脚趾。’”

‘Six digits on hands or feet are signs of a certain abnormality, and thus six fingers mean one abnormal child, and twelve fingers two abnormal children, and that was indeed true in the lady’s own case. She had married very young, and her husband, who had always been regarded as eccentric and abnormal, and who committed suicide after a brief period of married life, left her nothing but two children who had repeatedly been diagnosed by doctors as abnormal and with a severe handicap inherited from their father’s side of the family. The elder daughter had recently come home after a serious catatonic attack, and soon afterwards the younger daughter, who had reached puberty, also fell ill with severe neurosis.

“手脚上的六个手指或脚趾是某种异常的标志，因此六根手指意味着一个畸形儿，十二根手指意味着两个畸形儿，这在这位女士的例子中确实如此。她很年轻就结婚了，她的丈夫一直被认为古怪且不正常，婚后不久便自杀了，给她留下了两个孩子，这两个孩子都曾多次被医生诊断为畸形，并患有从父亲家族遗传的严重残疾。大女儿最近刚从一次严重的紧张性精神症发作中康复回家，不久之后，已经进入青春期的小女儿也患上了严重的神经症。”

‘Since in this case the children’s abnormality was associated with their mother’s death wish against the uncle, and merged with this far more firmly suppressed and psychically stronger element, we can assume that the second factor causing her slip of the tongue was a death wish against her abnormal children.

“由于在这种情况下，孩子的异常与母亲对叔叔的死亡愿望有关，并且与这种被更牢固地压抑和精神上更强大的因素融合在一起，我们可以假设导致她口误的第二个因素是对她异常孩子的死亡愿望。”

‘The dominating significance of the number twelve as expressing a death wish, however, is suggested by the fact that in the narrator’s mind the uncle’s birthday was already very closely associated with ideas of death. For her husband had taken his life on the thirteenth, a day after the birthday of this same uncle, and the uncle’s wife had told the young widow: “Only yesterday he was sending such kind, affectionate birthday wishes — and now this!”

然而，数字十二之所以具有表达死亡愿望的主导意义，是因为在叙述者的脑海中，叔叔的生日早已与死亡紧密相连。因为她的丈夫在十三号——也就是这位叔叔生日的第二天——自杀了，叔叔的妻子曾对这位年轻的寡妇说：“就在昨天，他还送来了那么亲切、充满爱意的生日祝福——而现在却是这样！”

‘I will add that the lady had sufficient real reasons to wish her children dead. They gave her no joy, only sorrow, they severely limited her freedom of action, and she had given up any idea of happiness in love for their sake.

“我还要补充一点，这位女士有充分的现实理由希望她的孩子们死去。他们没有给她带来任何快乐，只有悲伤；他们严重限制了她的行动自由；为了他们，她已经放弃了对爱情幸福的任何幻想。”

‘As usual, she had been extremely anxious not to upset the daughter whom she was taking with her when she went visiting, and it is easy to imagine how much patience and self-denial that involves when someone is suffering from dementia praecox , and how many angry impulses must be suppressed.

“和往常一样，她非常担心在探望女儿时会惹女儿生气，不难想象，当一个人患有早发性痴呆症时，这需要多少耐心和自我克制，以及多少愤怒的冲动必须被压抑。

‘Consequently, the full meaning of the slip would run:

因此，该失误的完整含义是：

‘I wish my husband’s uncle would die, I wish my abnormal children would die (the whole abnormal family, so to speak), and I wish I could get some money out of them.

“我希望我丈夫的叔叔去死，我希望我那些不正常的孩子们去死（可以说，整个不正常的家庭都去死），我希望我能从他们那里得到一些钱。

To my mind, this slip has an unusual structure in several respects:

在我看来，这张纸条在几个方面都具有不寻常的结构：

a) the presence of two determinants compressed into a single element.

a) 两个行列式压缩到一个元素中。

b) the fact that the presence of the two determinants is reflected in the duplication of the slip of the tongue (twelve nails, twelve fingers).

b) 这两个决定因素的存在反映在口误的重复中（十二个指甲，十二个手指）。

c) the striking fact that one meaning of the number twelve, the twelve fingers expressing the children’s abnormality, represents an indirect depiction; here, apsychic abnormality is illustrated by a physical abnormality, and the upper part of the body by the lower part.’ 14

c) 值得注意的是，数字十二的其中一个含义，即十二根手指象征着孩子的异常，是一种间接的描绘；在这里，精神异常通过身体异常来体现，身体的上半部分通过下半部分来体现。

4. 结果证明，她受到了潜意识里关于怀孕和避孕观念的影响。当她说自己“像小刀一样蜷缩起来”时，她故意用这个表达来抱怨，其实是指胎儿在母亲子宫内的位置。我问候语中的“恩斯特”一词让她想起了维也纳一家位于卡恩特纳大街的知名公司（S. Ernst），这家公司过去常常做避孕药具的广告。

5 . One of my patients went on making symptomatic slips of the tongue until we found that they derived from the childhood joke of saying urinieren [to urinate] instead of ruinieren [to ruin]. — Abraham’s observations on slips ‘with a tendency to over-compensate’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse VIII, 1922) can be connected with the temptation to make free use of improper and taboo words by the artificial means of a slip of the tongue. A woman patient with a slight tendency to stammer and thus to duplicate the initial syllable of proper names spoke the name Protagoras as Protragoras. Just before this she had said A-alexandros instead of Alexandros. Inquiry showed that as a child she had been particularly fond of the naughty trick of repeating the initial syllables a and po [echoing nursery terms for ‘faeces’ and ‘behind’], a game often known to induce stammering in children. She now felt there was a danger of leaving the r out of the first syllable of the name ‘Protagoras’ and saying ‘Po-potagoras’, so to avert the danger she clung firmly to the r and added another in the second syllable. Similarly, on other occasions, she distorted the words parterre [ground floor] and Kondolenz [condolence] into partrerre and Kodolenz , to avoid the words associated with them in her mind, pater [father] and Kondom [condom]. Another patient of Abraham’s confessed to a tendency to say angora instead of angina on every occasion, very probably because he feared he might be tempted to replace angina by vagina. These slips of the tongue therefore occur because a tendency to deter prevails against a tendency to distort, and Abraham correctly points out the analogy between this procedure and the development of symptoms in compulsive neuroses.

5. 我的一位病人反复出现症状性的口误，直到我们发现这些口误源于她小时候的一个玩笑：把“ruinieren”（毁坏）说成“urinieren”（小便）。——亚伯拉罕关于“有过度补偿倾向”的口误的观察（《国际精神分析杂志》第八卷，1922年）与通过口误这种人为手段随意使用不恰当和禁忌词语的诱惑有关。一位有轻微口吃倾向的女病人，说话时容易重复专有名词的首音节，她把普罗泰戈拉斯（Protagoras）说成了普罗特拉戈拉斯（Protragoras）。就在这之前，她还把亚历山德罗斯（Alexandros）说成了亚历山德罗斯（A-alexandros）。调查显示，她小时候特别喜欢玩一个恶作剧，就是重复“a”和“po”这两个音节（分别对应童谣中“粪便”和“后面”的意思），这种游戏常常会导致孩子口吃。她现在觉得，如果把“Protagoras”这个名字的第一个音节里的“r”漏掉，说成“Po-potagoras”，可能会出错，所以为了避免这种情况，她就紧紧抓住“r”不放，并在第二个音节里又加了一个“r”。同样地，在其他场合，她也会把“parterre”（底层）和“Kondolenz”（慰问）这两个词念成“partrerre”和“Kodolenz”，以避免联想到她脑海中与它们相关的词“pater”（父亲）和“Kondom”（避孕套）。亚伯拉罕的另一位病人也坦白说，他总是习惯性地把“angina”（心绞痛）说成“angora”（安哥拉），很可能是因为他害怕自己会忍不住把“angina”说成“vagina”（阴道）。因此，这些口误的发生是因为阻止的倾向战胜了歪曲的倾向，亚伯拉罕正确地指出了这一过程与强迫性神经症症状发展之间的相似之处。

6 . Another observation is that aristocrats are particularly apt to distort the names of doctors they have consulted, and we may conclude that in spite of their usual courteous manner towards these doctors they do not privately esteem them much. I will quote here some cogent remarks on the forgetting of names from the English discussion of our subject by Dr E. Jones, who at that time was in Toronto (‘The Psychopathology of Everyday Life’, American Journal of Psychology , October 1911):

6. 另一个观察结果是，贵族们特别容易歪曲他们咨询过的医生的名字，由此我们可以得出结论：尽管他们通常对这些医生彬彬有礼，但私下里他们并不怎么尊重这些医生。我在此引用当时在多伦多的E. Jones博士在英语世界就此主题进行的讨论中的一些精辟论述（《日常生活中的精神病理学》，《美国心理学杂志》，1911年10月）：

‘Few people can avoid feeling a twinge of resentment when they find that their name has been forgotten, particularly if it is by someone with whom they had hoped or expected it would be remembered. They instinctively realize that if they had made a greater impression on the person’s mind he would certainly have remembered them again, for the name is an integral part of the personality. Similarly, few things are more flattering to most people than to find themselves addressed by name by a great personage where they could hardly have anticipated it. Napoleon, like most leaders of men, was a master of this art. In the midst of the disastrous Campaign of France, in 1814, he gave an amazing proof of his memory in this direction. When in a town near Craonne he recollected that he had met the mayor, De Bussy, over twenty years ago in the La Fère regiment; the delighted De Bussy at once threw himself into his service with extraordinary zeal. Conversely there is no surer way of affronting someone than by pretending to forget his name; the insinuation is thus conveyed that the person is so unimportant in our eyes that we cannot be bothered to remember his name. This device is often exploited in literature. In Turgenev’s Smoke the following passage occurs. “‘So you still find Baden entertaining, M’sieu — Litvinov.’ Ratmirov always uttered Litvinov’s surname with hesitation, every time, as though he had forgotten it, and could not at once recall it. In this way, as well as by the lofty flourish of his hat in saluting him, he meant to insult his pride.” The same author in his Fathers and Sons writes: “The Governor invited Kirsanov and Bazarov to his ball, and within a few minutes invited them a second time, regarding them as brothers, and calling them Kisarov.” Here the forgetting that he had spoken to them, the mistake in the names, and the inability to distinguish between the two young men, constitute a culmination of disparagement. Falsification of a name has the same significance as forgetting it; it is only a step towards complete amnesia.’

“当人们发现自己的名字被遗忘时，很少有人能不感到一丝不满，尤其是当遗忘者是自己曾希望或期待记住自己名字的人时。他们本能地意识到，如果自己给对方留下更深刻的印象，对方肯定会再次想起自己，因为名字是人格不可或缺的一部分。同样，对大多数人来说，没有什么比在自己几乎意想不到的情况下被一位伟人叫出名字更令人受宠若惊的了。拿破仑和大多数领袖一样，都是这方面的行家。在1814年灾难性的法国战役中，他在这方面展现了惊人的记忆力。当他在克拉翁附近的一个小镇上想起二十多年前在拉费尔军团见过镇长德·比西时，欣喜若狂的德·比西立刻以非凡的热情投身于他的麾下。反之，没有什么比假装忘记别人的名字更能冒犯别人了；这种暗示表明，在我们眼中，这个人无关紧要，我们甚至懒得记住他的名字。这种手法在文学作品中经常被运用。屠格涅夫的《烟》中有这样一段话：“‘看来您仍然觉得巴登很有趣啊，先生——利特维诺夫。’拉特米罗夫每次念出利特维诺夫的姓氏时都犹豫不决，仿佛他已经忘记了，一时想不起来。他这样做，再加上敬礼时高高举起帽子的动作，都是在羞辱他的自尊心。” 同一位作者在《父与子》中写道：“总督邀请基尔萨诺夫和巴扎罗夫参加舞会，几分钟后又再次邀请他们，把他们当作兄弟，叫他们基萨罗夫。” 在这里，忘记自己曾与他们交谈过、叫错名字以及无法区分这两个年轻人，构成了一种极致的贬低。篡改姓名与遗忘姓名具有相同的意义；这只是迈向彻底失忆的一步。
