IX

第九章

Symptomatic and Fortuitous Actions

症状性及偶然性行为

The actions described up to this point, in which we found an unconscious intention carried out, manifested themselves as disturbances to other, intentional actions, and took cover behind the excuse of clumsiness. The fortuitous actions to be discussed now are distinguished from inadvertent actions only in not requiring any conscious intention to support them, and thus needing no excuse. They stand alone, and are tolerated because we do not assume that there is any purpose or intention behind them. They are performed ‘unthinkingly’, ‘purely by chance’, ‘for something to do with one’s hands’, and we count on such remarks to nip any inquiry into the significance of these actions in the bud Since they no longer claim the excuse of clumsiness, they must fulfil certain conditions in order to enjoy their exceptional position: they must be unobtrusive , and their effects must be minor.

此前所描述的那些行为，都是无意识意图的体现，它们干扰了其他有意识的行为，并以笨拙为借口掩盖其真实性。接下来要讨论的偶然行为与无意行为的区别仅在于，它们无需任何意识意图的支持，因此也无需任何借口。它们独立存在，之所以被容忍，是因为我们不认为它们背后有任何目的或意图。它们被描述为“不假思索的”、“纯属偶然的”、“与手有关的”，我们指望这些说法能扼杀任何对这些行为意义的探究。既然它们不再以笨拙为借口，那么它们必须满足某些条件才能享有这种特殊地位：它们必须不引人注目，并且其影响必须微不足道。

I have collected a large number of such fortuitous actions from my own studies and those of others, and after thorough study of the various examples I think they ought rather to be termed symptomatic actions. They express something that passes unsuspected even by the person executing them, and which he does not as a rule intend to impart, but to keep to himself. They therefore act as symptoms, just like all the other phenomena considered in this work so far.

我从自身及他人的研究中收集了大量此类偶然行为，经过对各种案例的深入研究，我认为它们更应该被称为征兆行为。这些行为表达了一些连行为者本人都未曾察觉的东西，而且行为者通常并不打算将之传达，而是将其保留在心底。因此，它们如同本书迄今为止探讨的所有其他现象一样，起到征兆的作用。

The richest yield of such fortuitous or symptomatic actions, however, is to be found in the psychoanalytic treatment of neurotics, and I cannot resist taking two illustrations from that field to illustrate how wide and subtle is the determination of these little incidents, arising from unconscious ideas. In fact the borderline between symptomatic and inadvertent actions is so blurred that I could quite well have placed these examples in the previous section.

然而，这类偶然或症状性行为最丰富的应用体现在神经症患者的精神分析治疗中。我忍不住要从这个领域举两个例子，来说明这些源于无意识观念的小事件的决定因素是多么广泛而微妙。事实上，症状性行为和无意行为之间的界限如此模糊，以至于我完全可以将这些例子放在上一节中。

1) A young woman told me during our session about something that had occurred to her: as she was cutting her nails the day before, she had ‘cut into the flesh while trying to remove the soft cuticle at the base of the nail’. This seemed so trivial that I wondered, in surprise, why she had remembered and mentioned it at all, and I began to suspect that we were dealing with a symptomatic action. Sure enough, it was her ring finger that suffered this little accident: the finger on which a wedding ring is worn. Furthermore, it had happened on her wedding anniversary, which gave the injury to the cuticle a very distinct and easily divined meaning. She told me at the same time about a dream referring to her husband’s clumsiness and her own lack of sexual feeling in her marriage. But why did she hurt herself on the ring finger of her left hand, since she would usually have worn a wedding ring on the right hand? Her husband is a lawyer, a doctor of law [German: Doktor der Rechte, Recht meaning both ‘law’ and ‘right’] and as a girl she had been secretly attracted to a doctor of medicine (described jocularly as a Doktor der Linke [doctor on the left-hand side]). And marriage on the left hand [a partnership without legal basis] has its own specific meaning.

1）一位年轻女子在咨询过程中告诉我，前一天她剪指甲时，“试图去除指甲根部的软角质层时，不小心割伤了肉”。这件事看似微不足道，我惊讶地发现她竟然记得并提及此事，并开始怀疑这或许是一种征兆行为。果然，受伤的是她的无名指——也就是戴结婚戒指的手指。更巧的是，这件事发生在她的结婚纪念日，这使得指甲根部的伤口具有了非常明确且易于理解的意义。与此同时，她还告诉我她做了一个梦，梦境中提到了她丈夫的笨拙以及她自己在婚姻中缺乏性欲。但她为什么会伤到左手的无名指呢？毕竟，她通常会把结婚戒指戴在右手上。她的丈夫是一名律师，法学博士（德语：Doktor der Rechte，Recht既指“法律”也指“权利”），而她少女时代曾暗恋一位医学博士（被戏称为“左撇子医生”）。而“左撇子婚姻”（指没有法律基础的同居关系）则有其特殊的含义。

2) An unmarried young lady told me: ‘Yesterday, quite unintentionally, I tore a hundred-gulden note in half and gave one of the halves to a lady who was visiting me. Would you call that a symptomatic action too?’ Closer inquiry revealed the following details. Let us take the hundred-gulden note first: the young woman devoted some of her time and her means to charitable works. She and another lady were financing the upbringing of an orphan child. The hundred gulden had been this other lady’s contribution, which she put into an envelope when it arrived and placed temporarily on her desk.

2）一位未婚的年轻女子告诉我：“昨天，我不小心把一张一百荷兰盾的钞票撕成两半，把其中一半给了来访的一位女士。您觉得这也是一种征兆行为吗？” 进一步询问后，我了解到以下细节。先说说这张一百荷兰盾的钞票：这位年轻女子将部分时间和财力投入到慈善事业中。她和另一位女士共同资助一个孤儿的抚养。这张一百荷兰盾是那位女士捐赠的，她收到后把它装进信封，暂时放在了桌子上。

The visitor she had mentioned was a distinguished lady whom she assisted in another charitable project, and who wanted to make a note of the names of people to whom they might apply for support. There was no piece of paper ready to hand, so my patient picked up the envelope on her desk and tore it in half without stopping to think what was in it, keeping one half herself so as to have a copy of the list of names and giving the other to her visitor. Notice the harmless nature of this action, inexpedient as it was, since as everyone knows a hundred-gulden note does not lose its value if it is torn, so long as the torn pieces can be reassembled complete. The importance of the names on the piece of paper guaranteed that my patient’s visitor would not throw it away, and similarly there was no doubt that she would return its valuable contents as soon as she realized what they were.

她提到的那位访客是一位德高望重的女士，她曾协助她参与另一个慈善项目。这位女士想记下一些可能需要帮助的人的姓名。当时手边没有现成的纸，所以我的病人拿起桌上的信封，没多想就把它撕成两半，自己留了一半作为名单的副本，另一半给了那位访客。请注意，尽管这个举动不太方便，但它并无害处。众所周知，一张一百荷兰盾的钞票即使撕破也不会贬值，只要碎片能重新拼凑完整。纸上那些名字的重要性保证了我的病人的访客不会把它扔掉，同样，毫无疑问，一旦她意识到纸上的内容，就会立刻归还。

But what unconscious idea did this chance action, resulting from forgetfulness, actually express? My patient’s visitor approved of the treatment I was giving her, in fact it was she who had recommended me to her in the past, and I believe that my patient felt she owed her gratitude for her advice. Was the half of the hundred-gulden note meant to represent a kind of fee for her good offices? No, that would still be odd.

但这种因遗忘而起的偶然举动，究竟表达了怎样的潜意识想法呢？我的病人的访客认可我的治疗，事实上，正是她之前向病人推荐过我，我相信我的病人觉得应该感谢她的建议。那半张一百荷兰盾钞票，难道是她为病人提供的帮助支付的报酬吗？不，那样还是很奇怪。

But there was more to it than that. A day before, a woman intermediary of quite a different kind had asked a relation of my patient whether she, my patient, would like to make the acquaintance of a certain gentleman, and in the morning, a few hours before the other lady visited her, the suitor’s letter pleading his cause had arrived and had aroused much mirth. When her visitor opened the conversation by asking after her health, my patient may well have thought: ‘Yes, you recommended me the right doctor, but I’d be even more grateful if you could help me to find the right husband’ (‘and a child’, an idea concealed behind that of a husband). This repressed idea made her merge the two intermediaries into one, and she gave her present visitor the fee that, in her imagination, she was prepared to give the other woman. It is an interpretation which carries even more conviction when I add that I had been telling my patient about such fortuitous or symptomatic actions only the evening before — and she took the first opportunity to produce something along the same lines.

但事情远不止如此。前一天，一位身份迥异的女性中间人询问我的病人的一位亲戚，她是否愿意结识一位男士。第二天早上，就在那位女士来访前几个小时，那位求婚者的求婚信寄到了，信中充满了恳求，引得众人哄堂大笑。当来访者上前询问她的健康状况时，我的病人很可能心想：“是的，您推荐的医生很合适，但如果您还能帮我找到合适的丈夫，那就更好了。”（“还有孩子”，这个念头隐藏在丈夫的背后。）正是这种被压抑的想法让她把两位中间人混为一谈，并把原本打算给那位女士的酬劳给了现在的来访者。如果我补充一点，我的解释就更有说服力了：就在前一天晚上，我还跟我的病人讲过这类巧合或征兆性的行为——而她立刻就抓住机会，做出了类似的事情。

One could divide occurrences of fortuitous or symptomatic actions, which are very frequent, into various categories according to whether they are customary, regular in certain circumstances, or occur in isolation. The first kind (like playing with a watch-chain, twirling a moustache, and soon), which may almost look like personal habits, are close to the many kinds of nervous tics and should probably be studied in connection with them. Among the second group I would classify playing with a stick one is holding, doodling with a pencil in one’s hand, chinking coins in the pocket, kneading crumbs and other plastic substances, fiddling with one’s clothes in a number of ways, and many other such actions. Psychic treatment commonly shows that sense and meaning, which have been denied any other expression, are concealed beneath these playful activities. Usually the person concerned has no idea that he is doing anything of the kind or that he has made certain modifications to his usual idle actions, and he fails to notice the effects. He will not, for instance, hear the sound he makes chinking coins, and he will be surprised and incredulous if it is pointed out to him. Similarly, fiddling with one’s clothing, which often passes unnoticed, is significant and worthy of a doctor’s attention. Any change of one’s usual appearance, any small act of negligence — for instance a button left undone — every exposure means something which the person wearing that clothing does not want to say directly, indeed generally does not intend to say at all. The interpretation of these little fortuitous actions and the evidence for its validity will always emerge clearly enough from circumstances mentioned during the session, from the subject under discussion itself, and from the ideas produced when the patient’s attention is directed to something that apparently happened by chance. But the context is such that I shall refrain from supporting my theories here by citing and analysing examples. I mention these things, however, because I believe they do have the same significance in normal people as in my neurotic patients.

我们可以根据偶然或症状性行为的发生频率，将其分为不同的类别，例如是否属于习惯性行为、是否在特定情况下规律性发生，或者是否单独发生。第一类（例如玩弄表链、捻胡须等等）几乎可以被视为个人习惯，与多种神经性抽动症密切相关，或许应该结合神经性抽动症进行研究。第二类包括玩弄手中的棍子、用铅笔涂鸦、在口袋里敲击硬币、揉捏面包屑和其他塑料制品、以各种方式摆弄衣服等等。心理治疗通常表明，这些看似随意的行为背后隐藏着某种意义和情感，而这些意义和情感往往被剥夺了其他表达方式。通常情况下，当事人并不知道自己正在做这类事情，或者没有意识到自己对日常的闲散行为做出了某些改变，因此也察觉不到这些行为的影响。例如，他听不到自己敲硬币发出的叮当声，如果有人指出来，他会感到惊讶和难以置信。同样，摆弄衣服这种常常不被人注意的小动作，其实意义重大，值得医生关注。任何穿着打扮的改变，任何细微的疏忽——比如没扣上纽扣——都意味着穿着者不想直接表达，甚至通常根本不想表达的东西。这些看似偶然的小动作的解读，以及其有效性的证据，总能从诊疗过程中提及的情况、讨论的主题本身，以及当患者的注意力被引导到看似偶然发生的事情上时产生的想法中清晰地显现出来。但鉴于上下文，我在此不赘述具体事例来佐证我的理论。我之所以提及这些，是因为我相信它们对正常人和我的神经症患者都具有同样的意义。

And I cannot refrain from giving at least one example that shows how closely a symptomatic action habitually performed may be linked to the most intimate and important factors in a healthy person’s life: 1

我不得不举一个例子，来说明一个习惯性症状行为与健康人生活中最私密、最重要的因素之间可能存在的密切联系： 1

‘As Professor Freud has taught us, symbolism plays a greater part in the childhood of normal people than was expected from earlier psychoanalytical studies; in this respect the following short analysis may be of some interest, in particular because of its medical insights.

正如弗洛伊德教授教导我们的那样，象征主义在正常人的童年时期所起的作用比早期精神分析研究所预期的要大得多；在这方面，以下简短的分析可能具有一定的意义，特别是因为它的医学见解。

‘A doctor on rearranging his furniture in a new house came upon an old-fashioned, straight, wooden stethoscope, and, after pausing to decide where he should put it, was impelled to place it on the side of his writing-desk in such a position that it stood exactly between his chair and the one reserved for his patients. The act in itself was certainly odd, for in the first place the straight stethoscope served no purpose, as he invariably used a binaural one; and in the second place all his medical apparatus and instruments were always kept in drawers, with the sole exception of this one. However, he gave no thought at all to the matter until one day it was brought to his notice by a patient, who had never seen a wooden stethoscope, asking him what it was. On being told, she asked why he kept it just there; he answered in an off-hand way that that place was as good as any other. This started him thinking, however, and he wondered whether there had been any unconscious motive in his action. Being interested in the psycho-analytic method he asked me to investigate the matter.

一位医生在新家重新布置家具时，偶然发现了一副老式的直式木制听诊器。他停下来思考了一会儿该把它放在哪里，最后却把它放在了书桌旁，正好位于他自己的椅子和病人椅子的中间。这举动本身就很奇怪，因为首先，这副直式听诊器对他来说毫无用处，他通常都用双耳听诊器；其次，他所有的医疗器械和仪器都放在抽屉里，唯独这副听诊器例外。然而，他对此毫不在意，直到有一天，一位从未见过木制听诊器的病人问他这是什么。得知后，病人问他为什么把它放在那里；他漫不经心地回答说，放在那里也没什么问题。但这番话却让他开始思考，他不禁怀疑自己这样做是否有什么无意识的动机。他对精神分析方法很感兴趣，于是请我调查此事。

‘The first memory that occurred to him was the fact that when a student of medicine he had been struck by the habit his hospital interne had of always carrying a wooden stethoscope on his ward visits, although he never used it. He greatly admired this interne, and was much attached to him. Later on, when he himself became an interne, he contracted the same habit, and would feel very uncomfortable if by mistake he left his room without having the instrument to swing in his hand. The aimlessness of the habit was shewn, not only in the fact that the only stethoscope he ever used was a binaural one, which he carried in his pocket, but also in that it was continued when he was a surgical interne and never needed a stethoscope at all.

他首先想起的是，自己还是医学生时，就注意到医院实习医生有个习惯：每次查房都带着一根木制听诊器，尽管从不用。他非常钦佩这位实习医生，也和他关系很好。后来，自己当了实习医生后，也养成了同样的习惯，如果出门时手里没拿着听诊器，就会觉得很不自在。这个习惯的无意义之处不仅在于他唯一用过的听诊器是放在口袋里的双耳听诊器，还在于他当外科实习医生时，根本用不到听诊器，却依然保持着这个习惯。

‘From this it was evident that the idea of the instrument in question had in some way or other become invested with a greater psychical significance than normally belongs to it […] I will forestall the rest of the analysis by saying what this secondary idea was — namely, a phallic one […]

由此可见，所讨论的器物概念在某种程度上被赋予了比其通常意义更为深远的心理内涵。[…] 我将先说明这种次要含义是什么——即，一种阳具象征意义——以此来展开接下来的分析。[…]

‘Then came a number of childhood memories relating to his family doctor. He had been strongly attached to this doctor as a child, and during the analysis long-buried memories were recovered of a double phantasy he had in his fourth year concerning the birth of a younger sister — namely, that she was the child (1) of himself and his mother, the father being relegated to the background, and (2) of the doctor and himself; in this he thus played both a masculine and feminine part […]

“随后，他回忆起一些与家庭医生有关的童年往事。他小时候非常依恋这位医生，在分析过程中，他尘封已久的记忆被唤醒，回忆起他四岁时关于妹妹出生的一个双重幻想——妹妹是（1）他和母亲的孩子，父亲被边缘化；（2）也是他和医生的孩子；在这个幻想中，他同时扮演了男性和女性的角色……”

‘He had had his chest repeatedly examined by the doctor at the age of six, and distinctly recollected the voluptuous sensation of feeling the latter’s head near him pressing the wooden stethoscope into his chest, and of the rhythmic to-and-fro respiratory movement of his breathing. He had been struck by the doctor’s habit of carrying his stethoscope inside his hat; he found it interesting that the doctor should carry his chief instrument concealed about his person, always handy when he went to see patients, and that he only had to take off his hat (i.e., part of his clothing), and “pull it out”. At the age of eight he was impressed by being told by an older boy that it was the doctor’s custom to get into bed with his women patients. It is certain that the doctor, who was young and handsome, was extremely popular among the women of the neighbourhood, including the subject’s own mother. The doctor and his “instrument” were therefore the objects of great interest throughout his boyhood.

六岁时，他曾多次接受医生的胸部检查，并清晰地记得医生将木制听诊器贴近他胸口时那种令人愉悦的感觉，以及呼吸有节奏的起伏。他注意到医生习惯把听诊器藏在帽子里；他觉得医生把最重要的工具藏在身上，随时方便地去看病人，只需要摘下帽子（也就是脱掉一部分衣服），就能“掏出来”，这让他觉得很有意思。八岁时，一个大男孩告诉他，医生有和女病人上床的习惯，这让他印象深刻。可以肯定的是，这位年轻英俊的医生在附近的女性中非常受欢迎，包括他自己的母亲。因此，医生和他的“工具”在他整个童年时期都引起了极大的兴趣。

‘It is probable that, as in many other cases, unconscious identification with the family doctor had been a main motive in determining the subject’s choice of profession. It was here doubly conditioned, (1) by the superiority of the doctor on certain interesting occasions to the father, of whom the subject was very jealous, and (2) by the doctor’s knowledge of forbidden topics and his opportunities for illicit indulgence. The subject admitted that he had on several occasions experienced erotic temptations in regard to his women patients; he had twice fallen in love with one, and finally had married one.

“很可能，如同许多其他案例一样，潜意识里对家庭医生的认同是决定该人选择职业的主要动机之一。在此案例中，这种认同受到双重因素的影响：(1) 医生在某些特定场合的表现优于该人非常嫉妒的父亲；(2) 医生掌握着一些禁忌话题，并有机会进行不正当的放纵。该人承认，他曾多次对女病人产生性欲；他曾两次爱上其中一位，最终与她结婚。”

‘The next memory was of a dream already mentioned in print elsewhere, 2 plainly of a homosexual-masochistic nature; in it a man, who proved to be a replacement-figure of the family doctor, attacked the subject with a “sword” […] The thought of a sword reminded the subject of the passage in the “Nibelung Saga”, where Sigurd sleeps with his naked sword ( Gram ) between himself and Brunhilda, an incident that had always greatly struck his imagination.

“下一个记忆是之前在其他地方印刷品中提到过的一个梦， 2 显然是同性恋受虐性质的；在梦中，一个男人，后来证明是家庭医生的替代者，用一把‘剑’攻击了主人公[…] 想到剑，主人公就想起了《尼伯龙根传奇》中的一段，西格德睡觉时，他的剑（格拉姆）就放在他和布伦希尔德之间，这一幕一直深深地吸引着他。

‘The meaning of the symptomatic act now at last became clear. The subject had placed his wooden stethoscope between himself and his patients, just as Sigurd had placed his sword (an equivalent symbol) between him and the maiden he was not to touch. The act was a compromise-formation; it served both to gratify in his imagination the repressed wish to enter into nearer relations with an attractive patient (interposition of phallus), and at the same time to remind him that this wish was not to become a reality (interposition of sword). It was, so to speak, a charm against yielding to temptation.

“症状行为的意义终于明朗起来。这个人将木制听诊器置于自己和病人之间，正如西格德将剑（一个象征物）置于自己和那位他不能触碰的少女之间一样。这种行为是一种妥协的形成；它既满足了他想象中与一位迷人的病人建立更亲密关系的压抑欲望（阳具的介入），同时也提醒他这种欲望不能成为现实（剑的介入）。可以说，这是一种抵御诱惑的咒语。”

‘I would add that a passage from Lord Lytton’s Richelieu had made a great impression on the boy:

我还要补充一点，利顿勋爵的《黎塞留传》中的一段话给这个男孩留下了深刻的印象：

“‘Beneath the rule of men entirely great

“在完全伟大的人的统治下

The pen is mightier than the sword ” 3 ,

笔比剑更有力” 3 ,

that he had become a prolific writer, and uses an unusually large fountain pen. When I asked him why he needed it, he characteristically replied: “I have so much to say.”

他成了一位多产作家，而且使用一支尺寸异常大的钢笔。当我问他为什么需要这么大的笔时，他一如既往地回答说：“我有很多话要说。”

‘This analysis reminds us once again what far-reaching insights into mental life “innocent” and “pointless” actions afford us, and how early in life a tendency to symbolization is developed.’

“这项分析再次提醒我们，‘无辜的’和‘无意义的’行为能给我们带来多么深远的心理洞察，以及象征化的倾向在生命早期是如何形成的。”

I can add, from my own psychotherapeutic experience, an account of a case in which a hand made an eloquent statement simply by playing with some breadcrumbs. My patient was a boy of not quite thirteen, who had been severely hysterical for almost two years and whom I finally took into psychoanalytical treatment. He had spent a good deal of time in a spa resort, but showed no improvement. I set out by assuming that he must have had sexual experiences and was troubled by sexual matters, which is natural for a lad of his age; however, I was careful not to help him out by offering explanations, since I wanted to put my assumptions to the test. Inevitably, I was curious to see just how the facts I was seeking would emerge in him. One day I noticed him rolling something about in the fingers of his right hand, putting his hand in his pocket, where he went on playing with it, bringing it out again, and so on. I did not ask what he had there, but he showed me when he suddenly opened out his hand. It contained some breadcrumbs kneaded together into a lump. At our next session he brought another such lump with him, and while we were talking formed it into little model figures with extraordinary speed, keeping his eyes closed. The figures attracted my interest. They were undoubtedly little men, each with a head, two arms and two legs, like the most primitive of prehistoric idols, and with a protrusion between the two legs, which he pulled out into a long point. No sooner was the little man finished than he kneaded it together again; later he left one alone but pulled the dough out into similar protrusions on the back and in other places, to hide the significance of the first one. I wanted to show him that I understood, but without giving him the excuse of being able to say he had nothing at all in mind while he was making his little men. With this in view, I suddenly asked if he remembered the story of the Roman king who answered his son’s envoy in mime in his garden. The boy claimed not to remember it, although he must have heard the tale much more recently than I had. He asked if it was the story of the answer written on a slave’s shaven skull. No, I said, that one was out of Greek history, and I told him the Roman story: King Tarquinius Superbus sent his son Sextus to take soundings in secret in an enemy city of Latium. The son, having found adherents there, sent the king a messenger asking what to do next. The king did not answer in words, but went into his garden, got the messenger to repeat the question, and struck off the largest and finest of the poppy heads growing there in silence. The messenger could tell Sextus no more than this. But Sextus understood his father, and realized that he was instructed to have the most prominent citizens assassinated.

根据我自己的心理治疗经验，我可以补充一个案例：一只手仅仅通过摆弄一些面包屑，就表达了一个意味深长的信息。我的病人是一个不到十三岁的男孩，他患有严重的歇斯底里症近两年，最终我决定对他进行精神分析治疗。他曾在温泉疗养院待过很长时间，但病情没有任何好转。我一开始就假设他一定有过性经历，并且对性方面的事情感到困扰，这对于他这个年纪的男孩来说很正常；然而，我小心翼翼地没有给他提供任何解释，因为我想检验我的假设。不可避免地，我很好奇我想要寻找的真相会如何从他身上显现出来。有一天，我注意到他用右手的指尖捻着什么东西，然后把手放进口袋里，继续把玩着，又拿出来，如此反复。我没有问他手里拿的是什么，但他突然张开手，让我看到了。里面装着一些揉成团的面包屑。下次见面时，他又带来了一团这样的面团，在我们交谈的时候，他闭着眼睛，以惊人的速度把它捏成了一个个小人偶。这些小人偶引起了我的兴趣。它们无疑是小人，每个都有头、两条胳膊和两条腿，就像最原始的史前偶像一样，两条腿之间还有一个凸起，他把它拉长成一个尖尖的。小人偶刚捏好，他就又把它揉成团；后来，他留下一个，但在背面和其他地方也拉出类似的凸起，掩盖第一个小人偶的意义。我想让他知道我理解他的意思，但又不想让他有借口说他捏小人偶的时候什么都没想。考虑到这一点，我突然问他是否还记得那个罗马国王在花园里用哑剧回答儿子使者的故事。男孩说他不记得了，尽管他肯定比我更近期才听到这个故事。他问是不是那个把答案写在奴隶剃光头骨上的故事。我说不是，那是希腊历史里的故事，我给他讲了罗马的故事：塔奎尼乌斯·苏佩布斯国王派他的儿子塞克斯图斯秘密前往敌国拉提姆的一个城市打探消息。塞克斯图斯在那里找到了支持者，便派信使去问国王下一步该怎么做。国王没有开口回答，而是走进花园，让信使重复一遍问题，然后默默地砍掉了园中最大最美的罂粟花。信使只能告诉塞克斯图斯这些。但塞克斯图斯明白他父亲的意思，知道他奉命要刺杀那些最显赫的公民。

As I was talking the boy stopped kneading his figure, and when I was telling him about the king’s mimed answer in the garden he tore the head off his little man with a lightning movement as soon as I reached the words ‘struck off … in silence’. He had understood what I meant, and he knew that I understood him. Now I could ask him direct questions, give him the information he needed, and we very soon put an end to his neurosis.

我说话的时候，那男孩停止了揉捏他的小人偶。当我讲到国王在花园里用肢体语言回答问题时，我刚说到“默默地……被击落”，他就以迅雷不及掩耳之势扯掉了小人偶的头。他明白了我的意思，也知道我理解他。现在我可以直接问他问题，给他需要的信息，我们很快就结束了他的神经质。

Those symptomatic actions that can be observed in almost inexhaustible profusion in both the healthy and the sick deserve our interest for several reasons. They often give the doctor valuable help in finding his way in new or unfamiliar circumstances, and they are extremely revealing to the observer of human nature, sometimes uncovering even more than he wanted to know. Anyone with a good understanding of them must sometimes feel like King Solomon, said in oriental legend to know the language of animals. One day I was to give a medical examination to a young man previously unknown to me in his mother’s house. When he came to meet me I noticed a large stain of egg white on his trousers, identifiable by its characteristically clear-cut rim. After a moment’s embarrassment, the young man apologized by saying he had been eating a raw egg to ease his hoarse voice, and some of the slippery egg white must have been spilt on his clothing. By way of confirmation, he pointed to the eggshell still lying on a little plate in the room. This was an innocuous enough explanation of the suspect stain, but when his mother had left us alone together I thanked him for making my diagnosis so much easier, and I immediately took his admission that he suffered from the ills attendant on masturbation as the starting-point of our conversation. On another occasion I was visiting a lady as rich as she was avaricious and foolish, who used to make her doctor work his way through a host of complaints before he could get to the simple reason for her condition. When I arrived she was sitting at a small table building silver gulden into little piles, and as she rose she knocked some of the coins on the floor. Helping her to pick them up, I soon interrupted her description of her wretched state of health, and asked: ‘Dear me, has your distinguished son-in-law wormed so much money out of you?’ She denied the very idea bitterly, only to launch soon afterwards into the pathetic tale of the anxiety her son-in-law’s extravagance gave her. She did not call me in again; it cannot be said that those who are told the meaning of their symptomatic actions always like one for it.

无论在健康人还是病人身上，几乎都能观察到大量类似的症状行为，这些行为值得我们关注，原因有几点。它们常常能为医生在新的或不熟悉的环境中提供宝贵的帮助，而且对于观察人性的人来说，它们也极具启发性，有时甚至揭示出一些意想不到的信息。任何对这些症状行为有深刻理解的人，有时都会觉得自己像东方传说中的所罗门王一样，能听懂动物的语言。有一天，我要去一位我之前并不认识的年轻人的家中做体检。他来见我时，我注意到他裤子上有一大块蛋清污渍，边缘清晰可见。年轻人尴尬地道歉说，他为了缓解嗓子沙哑，吃了个生鸡蛋，一些滑溜溜的蛋清可能洒在了衣服上。为了证明这一点，他指了指房间里小碟子上还放着的蛋壳。这原本只是对可疑污渍的一个无关紧要的解释，但当他母亲离开后，我感谢他让我的诊断变得容易得多，并立刻将他承认自己患有手淫相关疾病作为我们谈话的切入点。还有一次，我拜访了一位既富有又贪婪愚蠢的女士，她总是让她的医生费尽周折地找出她病症的根本原因。我到的时候，她正坐在小桌旁，把银币堆成小堆，起身时不小心碰掉了一些硬币。我帮她捡起硬币，打断了她对自身糟糕健康状况的描述，问道：“哎呀，难道你那位显赫的女婿从你身上榨取了这么多钱吗？”她断然否认，但随即又开始可怜兮兮地讲述她女婿的挥霍无度给她带来的焦虑。之后她再也没有叫我进去。不能说那些被告知其症状行为含义的人总是会喜欢它。

Another ‘confession’ conveyed by a slip is reported by Dr J. E. G. van Emden of The Hague: ‘When I was paying the bill in a small Berlin restaurant the waiter claimed that the price of a certain dish had risen by ten pfennigs because of the war; when I wondered why the menu did not show this price rise he said it must have been left off by mistake, but he could assure me that he was right! As he was taking my payment he fumbled with the coins and let a ten-pfennig coin fall on the table, as if for me!

海牙的J. E. G. van Emden博士报告了另一则通过纸条传达的“坦白”： “我在柏林一家小餐馆结账时，服务员声称某道菜的价格因为战争上涨了10芬尼；我问为什么菜单上没有显示涨价，他说一定是漏掉了，但他向我保证他说的没错！他收钱的时候，笨手笨脚地摆弄硬币，让一枚10芬尼的硬币掉在了桌子上，好像是故意给我的！”

“‘Well,” I said, “now I know for certain that you’ve overcharged me. Do you want me to inquire at the cash desk?”

“好吧，”我说，“现在我确定你多收了我的钱。你想让我去收银台问问吗？”

“‘If you’d be good enough to wait a moment…” and off he went.

“‘如果您能稍等片刻……’”说完，他就走了。

‘Naturally I allowed him his face-saving retreat, and a couple of minutes later, when he apologized and said that for some mysterious reason he must have mixed up one dish with another, I gave him the ten pfennigs to reward him for his contribution to the psychopathology of everyday life.’

“我当然让他体面地退场了，几分钟后，他道歉说，由于某种神秘的原因，他一定是把一道菜和另一道菜搞混了，于是我给了他十芬尼，作为他对日常生活心理病理学的贡献的奖励。”

Anyone watching his fellow men eating will notice some very interesting and instructive symptomatic actions.

任何观察他人进食的人都会注意到一些非常有趣且有启发性的症状行为。

Dr Hanns Sachs gives us the following account:

汉斯·萨克斯博士向我们讲述了如下情况：

‘I happened to be present when two of my family, an elderly married couple, were eating their evening meal. The lady had a delicate stomach and was obliged to stick to a very strict diet. A helping of roast meat had just been put in front of the husband, and he asked his wife, who was not allowed to share this dish, to pass the mustard. His wife opened the sideboard, reached into it, and put her little bottle of digestive drops on the table in front of her husband. Of course the barrel-shaped mustard jar was not in the least like the bottle of digestive drops, so there was no similarity to explain the mistake, but the wife noticed what she had done only when her husband pointed it out to her with a smile. The meaning of that particular symptomatic action needs no explanation.’

“我碰巧在场，看到我的两位家人——一对年长的夫妇——正在吃晚饭。夫人肠胃不好，必须严格控制饮食。烤肉刚端到丈夫面前，他便让妻子递芥末酱，因为妻子不能和他一起吃。妻子打开餐具柜，伸手进去，把她的小瓶助消化药放在了丈夫面前的桌子上。当然，桶状的芥末酱罐和助消化药瓶完全不一样，所以根本无法解释这个错误，但妻子直到丈夫笑着指给她看才意识到自己做错了。这个举动背后的含义无需赘述。”

I owe an excellent example of this kind, very ingeniously explained by the observer himself, to Dr Bernhard Dattner of Vienna:

我要感谢维也纳的伯恩哈德·达特纳博士，他以非常巧妙的方式解释了这类现象：

‘I was sitting in a restaurant having lunch with my colleague from the department of philosophy, Dr H. He was talking about the trials and tribulations of academics with only probationary status, and mentioned in passing that before the end of his studies he had been secretary to the Chilean ambassador, or rather the Chilean plenipotentiary minister extraordinary. “But then the minister was moved elsewhere, and I did not introduce myself to his successor.” As he said this last sentence he carried a piece of tart to his mouth, but let it drop off the fork as if out of clumsiness. I immediately saw the hidden meaning of this symptomatic action, and said as if casually to my colleague, who was not familiar with psychoanalysis: “Well, you let a choice morsel go there.” Failing to notice that my remark could equally well apply to his symptomatic action he repeated, in a curiously attractive and surprising lively tone, as if I had literally taken the words out of his mouth, exactly what I had just said: “Yes, that was indeed a choice morsel I allowed to go.” He then relieved his feelings by giving me an exhaustive account of the awkwardness that had lost him his well-paid post.

“我当时正和哲学系的同事H博士在餐厅吃午饭。他正谈论着那些只有试用期身份的学者所面临的种种磨难，顺便提到，在他毕业之前，他曾担任过智利大使的秘书，或者更确切地说，是智利特命全权公使的秘书。“但后来公使调任他处，我也没有向他的继任者自我介绍。”说完这句话，他用叉子叉起一块馅饼送到嘴边，却不小心让它从叉子上掉了下来，仿佛是出于笨拙。我立刻明白了这个动作背后的含义，便漫不经心地对这位不了解精神分析的同事说：“哎呀，你竟然把这么美味的一块馅饼给弄丢了。”他没有意识到我的话同样适用于他当时的举动，于是用一种出奇地迷人且充满活力的语气，仿佛我亲口说出了他的话，重复了我刚才说的话：“是啊，我放走的那块美味佳肴确实可惜。” 随后，他为了排解心中的郁闷，向我详尽地讲述了导致他丢掉高薪工作的种种尴尬经历。

‘Further light is cast on his symptomatic action by the fact that my colleague felt some scruples in telling me about his straitened finances, since I am not a close friend, and that the thought coming to the forefront of his mind thus emerged in the form of a symptomatic action symbolically expressing what ought to have been hidden, helping the speaker’s unconscious to relieve his feelings.’

“我的同事因为和我并非挚友，所以不好意思告诉我他捉襟见肘的财务状况，这进一步揭示了他的症状性行为。他脑海中浮现的想法因此以一种症状性行为的形式出现，象征性地表达了本应隐藏的事情，帮助说话者的潜意识缓解了他的感受。”

Dr B. Dattner tells us that: ‘A colleague of mine was visiting a girl he had known and been very fond of in his youth for the first time since her marriage. He told me about this visit, saying that while he had meant to stay with her for only a short time he had not stuck to this intention, which surprised him. Then he told me about a curious slip he had made while he was there. His friend’s husband, who took part in the conversation, looked round for a box of matches, which had certainly been on the table when my colleague arrived. He too searched his clothing to see if he might have “picked it up” by mistake, but in vain. [In German the pronoun for ‘it’ here is sie , agreeing with the gender of die Zündhölzchenschachtel , ‘matchbox’, and thus could by inference mean ‘her’.] Some time later he actually did find the box in his pocket, and noticed that there was only a single match left in it. A few days later a dream in which the matchbox symbol figured prominently, together with the friend of my colleague’s youth, confirmed my explanation that his symptomatic action found him trying to reclaim his right of priority and demonstrate that he had sole possession of the lady (there was only one match in the box).’

B·达特纳博士告诉我们：“我的一位同事去拜访一位他年轻时就认识并非常喜欢的女孩，这是她结婚后他第一次见到她。他跟我讲了这次拜访，说他原本只打算待一会儿，但后来却没能坚持下去，这让他自己也感到惊讶。然后他又告诉我，他在拜访期间犯了一个奇怪的错误。他朋友的丈夫也参与了谈话，他四处寻找一盒火柴，这盒火柴在我同事到达时肯定放在桌子上。他也翻遍了自己的衣服，看看是不是自己不小心‘拿’到了，但一无所获。[德语中，这里的“它”的代词是sie，与die Zündhölzchenschachtel（火柴盒）的性一致，因此可以推断为“她”。] 过了一会儿，他竟然在口袋里找到了那盒火柴，并注意到里面只剩下一根火柴了。”几天后，一个梦境证实了我的解释：火柴盒的符号在梦中占据了显著位置，梦中还有我同事年轻时的朋友。他的这种症状性行为表明他试图重新获得优先权，并证明他独自拥有这位女士（盒子里只有一根火柴）。

Dr Hanns Sachs describes the following incident: ‘Our maidservant is particularly fond of eating a certain tart — a fact that admits of no doubt, for it is the only dish which she always, without exception, makes well. One Sunday she was going to serve us this tart, put it on the sideboard, took the used plates and cutlery from the previous course and stacked them on the tray on which she had carried in the tart. She then put the tart back on the tray too on top of the pile of plates, instead of placing it on the table in front of us, and bore it off back into the kitchen. At first we thought she had seen something about the tart that needed to be put right, but when she failed to reappear my wife rang the bell and asked, “Betty, what happened to the tart?” “What do you mean?” asked the maid, at a loss. We had to point out that she had taken the tart away with her; she had loaded it on the tray, taken it out and put it down in the kitchen again “without noticing”. Next day, when we were about to eat what remained of the tart, my wife remarked that all we had left of it the day before was still there, so the maid had refrained from eating the slice of her favourite dish which was properly hers. When asked why she said, in some embarrassment, that she didn’t feel like it. There are clear signs of an infantile attitude on both occasions; first the child-like greed that does not want to share the object of its desires with anyone else, then the equally childlike and defiant reaction: if you won’t let me have it then you can just keep it, I don’t want any now.’

汉斯·萨克斯博士描述了以下事件：“我们的女佣特别喜欢吃一种馅饼——这一点毋庸置疑，因为这是她唯一一道每次都能做得完美的菜。一天星期天，她准备给我们上这道馅饼，便把它放在餐具柜上，然后把上一道菜用过的盘子和刀叉叠放在她用来盛馅饼的托盘上。接着，她没有把馅饼放在我们面前的桌子上，而是又把它放回托盘上，放在盘子堆上，然后端回了厨房。起初我们以为她发现馅饼有什么不对劲的地方需要纠正，但她迟迟没有出现，我妻子便按响了门铃，问道：‘贝蒂，馅饼怎么了？’‘什么意思？’女佣一脸茫然地问道。我们只好解释说，她把馅饼带走了；她把馅饼放在托盘上，拿出来又放回厨房，“浑然不觉”。第二天，当我们准备吃剩下的馅饼时，我妻子说，前一天剩下的馅饼还在，看来女佣没吃她最爱吃的那块本来就属于她的馅饼。我问她为什么，她有些尴尬地说，她不想吃。这两件事都明显体现了她幼稚的态度：先是孩子般的贪婪，不愿与任何人分享自己想要的东西；然后是同样幼稚又叛逆的反应：“如果你不让我吃，那就留着吧，我现在不想吃。”

Those fortuitous or symptomatic actions that occur in a marriage are often of very considerable significance, and could persuade people who know nothing about the psychology of the unconscious mind to believe in omens. It is not a good start for a young wife to lose her wedding ring on her honeymoon, although in most such cases it has just been mislaid and is soon found again. I know a lady now divorced from her husband who would often sign documents relating to the management of her property with her maiden name, for some years before she did in fact revert to it. I was once visiting a young married couple and heard the young wife, laughing, tell the tale of a recent experience of hers: the day after she came home from a journey, she had visited her unmarried sister, as she habitually did, to go shopping while her husband went out to work. She had suddenly seen a gentleman on the other side of the street, nudged her sister, and said: ‘Oh, look, there’s Herr L.’ She had forgotten that Herr L. had actually been her husband for some weeks. A shiver ran down my spine at this tale, but I did not venture to draw conclusions. I remembered the little incident only years later, when the marriage had come to an unhappy end.

婚姻中发生的那些偶然或征兆性的行为往往意义重大，甚至能让对潜意识心理学一无所知的人相信预兆的存在。对于一位年轻的妻子来说，蜜月旅行中丢失结婚戒指并非吉兆，尽管大多数情况下，戒指只是不小心落下了，很快就会找回来。我认识一位已经离婚的女士，她经常用娘家姓签署与财产管理相关的文件，直到几年后才恢复使用娘家姓。我曾拜访一对年轻夫妇，听到年轻的妻子笑着讲述她最近的一次经历：她旅行回来后的第二天，像往常一样去拜访她未婚的姐姐，趁着丈夫外出工作时一起购物。她突然看到街对面有个男人，便碰了碰妹妹，说：“哦，看，那是L先生。”她忘了L先生其实已经是她几周前的丈夫了。听到这个故事，我不禁脊背发凉，但我不敢妄下结论。直到多年以后，这段婚姻以不幸告终，我才想起这件小事。

I take the following observation, which could equally well have been included in the chapter on ‘Forgetfulness’, from the interesting works of A. Maeder, 4 published in French in Zurich.

我从 A. Maeder 的有趣著作中摘录了以下观察结果，该观察结果同样可以包含在关于“遗忘”的章节中， 4 该著作在苏黎世以法语出版。

‘Une dame nous racontait récemment qu’elle avait oublié d’essayer sa robe de noce et s’en souvint la veille du mariage à huit heures du soir, la couturière désespérait de voir sa cliente. Ce détail suffit à montrer que la fiancée ne se sentait pas très heureuse de porter une robe d’épouse, elle cherchait à oublier cette représentation pénible. Elle est aujourd’hui … divorcée [A lady recently told us that she had forgotten to try on her wedding dress, and remembered only at eight in the evening on the day before her marriage, by which time the dressmaker despaired of seeing her client. This detail was quite enough to show that the fiancée was not very happy about wearing a wedding dress, and was trying to forget this painful idea. Today…she is divorced].’

一位女士最近告诉我们，她忘记试穿婚纱，直到婚礼前一天晚上八点才想起来。裁缝当时都绝望了，觉得可能再也见不到她了。仅凭这一点就足以说明，这位新娘对穿婚纱这件事并不满意，她试图忘记这件让她痛苦的事。她现在已经离婚了。

A friend who had learnt to pay attention to meaningful signs told me that the great Eleonora Duse introduced a symptomatic action into one of her roles, clearly illustrating what a consummate actress she was. The play was a drama of adultery; Duse’s character had just quarrelled with her husband, and was now standing to one side in thought before her would-be seducer approached. In this brief pause she played with the wedding ring on her finger, taking it off, putting it on again, then taking it off once more. She was now ready for the other man.

一位善于观察细微信号的朋友告诉我，伟大的埃莉奥诺拉·杜丝在她出演的一个角色中加入了象征性的动作，这充分展现了她精湛的演技。那部戏讲述的是婚外情；杜丝饰演的角色刚刚和丈夫吵了一架，正站在一旁沉思，等待着那个想要勾引她的男人走近。在这短暂的停顿中，她把玩着手指上的结婚戒指，一会儿摘下来，一会儿戴上，一会儿又摘下来。她已经准备好迎接那个男人了。

Here I will add some remarks by T. Reik about other symptomatic actions involving rings.

在这里，我将补充 T. Reik 关于其他涉及环的症状行为的一些评论。

‘We know about the symptomatic actions performed by married people when they take off a wedding ring and put it on again. My colleague M. described a whole series of similar symptomatic actions. He had been given a ring as a present by a girl whom he loved, and who told him that if he lost it she would know he had stopped loving her. After that he felt increasingly anxious about losing the ring. When he took it off now and then, for instance to wash his hands, he regularly mislaid it and often had to search for a long time before finding it again. When he put an envelope into the letterbox he could not help fearing that his ring might be pulled off by the edges of the slot, and once he did in fact post a letter so clumsily that his ring fell into the box. The letter concerned on this occasion was a farewell to a former lover, he felt guilty about her — and at the same time his desire for her was reawakened, conflicting with his feelings for the present object of his affections’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychologie III, 1915).

“我们都知道已婚人士在摘下婚戒再戴上时会出现一些症状性行为。我的同事M先生就描述了一系列类似的症状性行为。他心爱的女孩送给他一枚戒指，并告诉他，如果他弄丢了戒指，她就知道他不再爱她了。从那以后，他越来越担心会弄丢戒指。比如，他偶尔会摘下戒指，比如洗手的时候，但经常会弄丢，而且往往要找很久才能找到。他把信封投进信箱时，总是担心戒指会被信箱边缘夹掉，有一次他真的笨手笨脚地投了一封信，结果戒指掉进了信箱里。”这次所涉信件是写给前情人的告别信，他对她感到愧疚——与此同时，他对她的渴望又重新燃起，这与他对现在爱慕对象的感情相冲突’（《国际心理学杂志》第三卷，1915年）。

Yet again, the theme of a ring shows how difficult it is for a psychoanalyst to discover any new insight that has not already been clear to a creative writer before him. In Fontane’s novel Vor der Sturm [ Before the Storm ] there is a game of forfeits in which Councillor of Justice Turgany says: ‘Believe it or not, ladies, forfeits are a clue to the deepest secrets of human nature.’ One of the examples he gives to prove his claim is of special interest: ‘I remember a professor’s wife who showed some middle-aged spread, and who kept pulling her wedding ring off her finger. You must allow me to refrain from describing the marital happiness of that household.’ He then continues: ‘There was a gentleman in the same company who never tired of dropping his English pocket-knife into the ladies’ laps — it had ten blades, a corkscrew and a flint and steel. At last, after tearing rents in several silk gowns and in the face of general and horrified outcry, that monstrosity of a knife disappeared.’

戒指这一主题再次表明，对于精神分析学家而言，要发现任何此前未被其他作家清晰阐述的新见解是多么困难。在冯塔纳的小说《暴风雨前夕》中，有一场惩罚游戏，法官图尔加尼说道：“信不信由你，女士们，惩罚游戏是揭示人性最深层秘密的线索。”他举的一个例子尤其引人注目：“我记得一位教授的妻子，她身材有些发福，总是把结婚戒指从手指上摘下来。恕我直言，我还是不要描述这个家庭的婚姻幸福了。”他接着说：“同属一个圈子的男士，总是乐此不疲地把他的英国折叠刀扔到女士们的腿上——这把刀有十个刀片、一个开瓶器和一个打火石。”最后，在撕破了几件丝绸长袍，并引发了众人惊恐的抗议之后，那把可怕的刀消失了。

It is not surprising that an object of such great symbolic significance as a ring can also feature in slips that mean something but do not denote an erotic link, as with a wedding or engagement ring. Dr M. Kardos has given me the following example of such an incident:

戒指作为一种具有重大象征意义的物品，出现在一些不带有情色意味的便条中并不奇怪，例如结婚戒指或订婚戒指。M. Kardos 博士曾给我举过这样一个例子：

‘Several years ago a much younger man attached himself to me; he shared my intellectual interests, and in some ways he stood in the same relation to me as a pupil to his teacher. On a certain occasion I had given him a ring, which had caused him to make certain slips or perform a symptomatic action several times already, whenever something in our relationship displeased him. He recently told me the following particularly neat case, which is easily interpreted: he had made some excuse for missing a weekly meeting where he regularly used to see and talk to me, because he had an appointment with a young lady which was a more attractive prospect. Next morning he noticed, but only long after leaving home, that the ring was not on his finger. He thought no more of it, assuming that he had left the ring behind on the bedside table where he placed it every evening, and would find it there when he got home again. And as soon as he returned he did look for it, but in vain, so now, equally unsuccessfully, he began searching the whole room. At last it struck him that the ring had been lying on the bedside table, just where he had left it at night for over a year, beside a small knife, which he used to put in his waistcoat pocket, and he began to think that he might “absent-mindedly” have put away the ring with the knife. He felt inside the pocket, and sure enough found the ring he was looking for. Proverbially, a man puts his wedding ring in his waistcoat pocket when he is planning to be unfaithful to the woman who gave it to him. His guilty conscience first made my friend punish himself (“You don’t deserve to wear this ring any more”), and second to confess his unfaithfulness, although merely in the form of a slip to which there were no witnesses. Only in the circuitous process of giving an account of the outcome — which could easily be foreseen — did he admit to the little act of “unfaithfulness” that he had committed.’

“几年前，一个比我年轻很多的男人开始对我特别亲近；他和我志趣相投，某种程度上，我们之间的关系就像学生和老师一样。有一次，我送了他一枚戒指，这枚戒指让他每次遇到不顺心的事，都会做出一些失态或反应。最近，他跟我讲了一个特别巧合的例子，很容易理解：他找了个借口，没去参加每周一次的例行见面，因为他约了一位更有吸引力的年轻女士。第二天早上，他出门很久之后才发现戒指不见了。他也没多想，以为戒指像往常一样落在了床头柜上，回家就能找到。他一回家就去找，但一无所获，于是又开始在房间里到处翻找，同样一无所获。”他终于恍然大悟，戒指一直放在床头柜上，就在他一年多来每晚睡觉时放的地方，旁边还有一把小刀，他以前习惯把小刀放在马甲口袋里。他开始反思，自己是不是“心不在焉”地把戒指和刀放在一起了。他摸了摸口袋，果然找到了他要找的戒指。俗话说，男人把结婚戒指放进马甲口袋，就是打算背叛送给他戒指的女人。我的朋友先是良心不安，惩罚自己（“你不配再戴这枚戒指了”），然后才承认了自己的不忠，尽管只是一张没有证人的纸条。只有在解释事情的来龙去脉时——而结果其实很容易预料——他才承认了自己犯下的“不忠”小错。

I also know of a gentleman getting on in years who married a very young girl, and was going to spend the wedding night in a city hotel before going away on honeymoon. No sooner did the couple arrive at the hotel than he realized with alarm that his wallet was missing. It contained the entire sum of money intended for the honeymoon trip, and he had either mislaid or lost it. He managed to get in touch with his manservant by telephone; the manservant found the missing wallet in the coat the bridegroom had been wearing for the wedding and brought it round to the hotel, where the husband who had thus embarked on marriage penniless, with nothing to offer his bride, was waiting. He was therefore able to set out on his honeymoon with his young wife next morning, but on the wedding night itself, just as his fears had predicted, he had ‘nothing to offer her’.

我还认识一位上了年纪的绅士，他娶了一位非常年轻的姑娘，打算在蜜月旅行前先在城里的一家酒店度过新婚之夜。然而，这对新人刚到酒店，他就惊慌地发现自己的钱包不见了。钱包里装着他准备用于蜜月旅行的全部钱，他一定是弄丢了。他设法打电话联系上了男仆；男仆在新郎婚礼当天穿的外套里找到了丢失的钱包，并把它带回了酒店。这位就这样身无分文、一无所有地踏上婚姻之路的丈夫，正在酒店里等着他。因此，第二天早上他得以和年轻的妻子一起出发去度蜜月，但到了新婚之夜，正如他所担心的那样，他“一无所有”。

It is comforting to think that our human way of ‘losing’ things is more of a symptomatic action than we divine, and is therefore not unwelcome to the loser’s secret intentions. Often it conveys no more than a low opinion or secret dislike of the lost object or the person from whom it came. Alternatively, the inclination to lose something has been transferred to the object concerned from other and more important items, through a symbolic train of thought. Losing something valuable often serves to express all kinds of emotional impulses; the loss may symbolically represent a suppressed idea, and thus repeats a warning that we would rather not hear, but above all it may be a sacrifice to those dark powers of fate which we still feel we should propitiate.

令人欣慰的是，我们人类“丢失”物品的方式与其说是预知未来，不如说是一种症状性的行为，因此，它并非与丢失者内心深处的意图背道而驰。通常，它仅仅表达了对丢失物品或物品来源者的轻视或隐秘的厌恶。或者，这种丢失的倾向可能通过某种象征性的思维模式，从其他更重要的物品转移到了丢失的物品上。丢失贵重物品往往能表达各种各样的情感冲动；这种丢失可能象征性地代表着某种被压抑的想法，从而重复着我们宁愿不去听的警告；但最重要的是，它可能是对我们仍然觉得应该安抚的命运黑暗力量的一种献祭。

Here are just a few examples to illustrate my remarks above about losing things:

以下仅举几个例子来说明我上面关于丢失物品的说法：

From Dr B. Dattner: ‘A colleague told me that he had unexpectedly lost his Penkala pencil, which he had had for over two years. He thought a lot of it because it was such a good one. Analysis showed that the previous day my colleague had received a distinctly unpleasant letter from his brother-in-law, which concluded: “I do not have the time or inclination just now to support your light-minded and idle conduct.” The emotion stirred up by this letter was so strong that next day my colleague promptly sacrificed his Penkala pencil, a present from his brother-in-law , to avoid having to feel too grateful to him.’

B·达特纳博士写道：“一位同事告诉我，他意外丢失了一支用了两年多的彭卡拉铅笔。他为此非常难过，因为这支铅笔非常好用。分析显示，就在前一天，我的同事收到了一封来自他姐夫的语气非常不友好的信，信的结尾写道：‘我现在既没时间也没心情支持你这种轻浮懒散的行为。’这封信激起了他强烈的情绪，以至于第二天，我的同事为了避免对姐夫心存感激，竟然毫不犹豫地把姐夫送的彭卡拉铅笔捐了出去。”

A lady I knew refrained, for understandable reasons, from going to the theatre while she was in mourning for her old mother. There were only a few days left before the formal year’s mourning came to an end, and she let some friends persuade her to accept a ticket for a particularly interesting theatrical performance. When she reached the theatre she discovered that she had lost the ticket, and thought later that she must have thrown it away with her tram ticket as she got out of the vehicle. But this same lady boasts of never carelessly losing anything.

我认识的一位女士，因为可以理解的原因，在她老母亲去世的哀悼期内没有去看戏。当时距离正式的一年哀悼期结束只剩几天了，她还是被几个朋友劝说，接受了一张特别精彩的戏剧演出的票。到了剧院，她才发现票丢了，后来她想，一定是下车的时候把票和电车票一起扔掉了。可是这位女士却一直吹嘘自己从不粗心大意地丢东西。

One must assume, therefore, that another occasion on which she lost something was also well motivated.

因此，我们必须假设，她另一次丢失东西也是有充分理由的。

On arriving at a spa resort, she decided to visit a boarding house where she had stayed on an earlier occasion. She was welcomed as an old friend, well entertained, and when she wanted to pay for her meal she was told that she must consider herself a guest, although she did not feel very happy about that. She was allowed, however, to leave a tip for the waitress, so she opened her purse to put a one-mark note on the table. That evening the manservant from the boarding house came round with a five-mark note that had been found under the table, and that the owner of the boarding house thought must belong to her. It had fallen out of her purse when she took out the waitress’s tip — she was probably trying to pay her bill after all.

抵达温泉度假村后，她决定去之前住过的一家旅馆看看。旅馆老板像对待老朋友一样热情地招待了她，当她想付账时，却告诉她必须把自己当成客人，这让她很不高兴。不过，她被允许给服务员小费，于是她打开钱包，拿出一张一马克的纸币放在桌上。那天晚上，旅馆的男仆拿着一张五马克的纸币过来，说是在桌子底下找到的，旅馆老板认为这张纸币一定是她的。原来是她拿出给服务员的小费时，不小心从钱包里掉了出来——她大概是想用这张纸币付账吧。

Otto Rank has written a paper of some length 5 casting light on the sacrificial attitude behind such actions, and their more profound motivation, with the aid of the analysis of dreams. 6 Interestingly, he adds that on occasion not only losing but also finding something seems to be predetermined. His own observations, which I quote here, show how we are to understand this. Obviously, when something is lost its nature is already known, whereas when something is found, its nature has to be identified first.

奥托·兰克曾撰写一篇篇幅较长的论文 5 ，借助梦境分析，阐明了此类行为背后的牺牲精神及其更深层次的动机。 6 有趣的是，他补充道，有时不仅丢失，就连找到某物似乎也是命中注定的。我在此引用他自己的观察，以阐明我们应该如何理解这一点。显然，当某物丢失时，它的本质是已知的；而当某物被找到时，它的本质必须先被识别。

‘A young girl who was financially dependent on her parents saw and wanted to buy an inexpensive piece of jewellery. She asked the price of the item in the shop, and was sorry to learn that it cost more than her savings. Yet the sum of only two crowns prevented her from enjoying this small pleasure. She was walking home in downcast mood through the hurry and bustle of the city streets during the evening. In one of the busiest squares, and although according to her own account of it she was deep in thought, she suddenly realized there was a little piece of paper lying on the ground; she had just passed it by without noticing it. She turned back, picked it up, and saw to her surprise that it was a folded two-crown note. Fate has put this in my way so that I can buy the piece of jewellery I saw, she told herself, happily turning back to put the idea into practice. At the same moment, however, she told herself not to, since the money she had found was “lucky money”, which one is not supposed to spend.

一个经济上依赖父母的年轻女孩看中了一件价格不贵的首饰，很想买。她在店里问了价格，得知价格超过了她的积蓄，不禁感到沮丧。然而，仅仅两克朗的钱却让她无法享受这份小小的快乐。傍晚时分，她心情低落地走在熙熙攘攘的城市街道上。在一个最热闹的广场上，虽然据她自己说，当时她正沉浸在自己的思绪中，却突然发现地上有一张小纸片；她刚才路过的时候并没有注意到。她转过身，捡起纸片，惊讶地发现那是一张折叠起来的两克朗纸币。“命运安排我买下那件首饰，”她心想，高兴地转身准备付诸行动。然而，就在这时，她又告诫自己不要这样做，因为她捡到的钱是“压岁钱”，是不应该花的。

‘The small amount of analysis required to understand this “fortuitous action” could probably be gleaned from the situation, even without information provided by the girl herself. Among the thoughts occupying her on her way home, her poverty and her material restrictions were probably to the forefront of her mind, and we may suspect that they took the form of wish-fulfilment as she imagined being liberated from her difficult circumstances. How she could most easily come by the sum of money she needed is an idea that will not have been very far from her mind, interested as it was in satisfying her modest wish, and that idea will have suggested the simple solution of finding it. In this way her unconscious (or pre-conscious) mind was already open to the idea of “finding” the money, even if she was not to become fully conscious of it because of other claims on her attention (she was “deep in thought”). On the basis of the analysis of similar cases, we may even say that an unconscious “readiness to search” can more easily lead to success than a conscious and attentive decision to do so. It would be difficult to find any other explanation of the way in which this one person, out of all the many hundreds of people in the street, could make the find that surprised her so much, particularly as the dim street-lighting in the evening and the dense crowds did not favour her chances. The strong extent to which this unconscious or pre-conscious readiness actually existed is evident from the curious fact that even after making her find, that is, after her readiness to find something had already become superfluous, and was certainly no longer in her conscious mind, the girl also found a handkerchief in a dark and isolated place in a suburban street as she continued on her way home.’ 7

即使没有女孩本人提供的信息，我们或许也能从情境中略窥一二，从而理解这一“偶然之举”。在她回家的路上，贫困和物质匮乏很可能占据了她的思绪，我们可以推测，她当时可能正幻想摆脱困境，并以此实现愿望。如何才能最轻松地获得所需的钱财，这个想法在她脑海中挥之不去，因为她一心想要满足自己微不足道的愿望，而这个想法自然而然地指向了最简单的解决办法——找到钱。这样一来，即使她因为其他事情的牵绊（她当时“沉思”）而没有完全意识到这一点，她的潜意识（或前意识）中也已经萌生了“找到”这笔钱的想法。基于对类似案例的分析，我们甚至可以说，潜意识中的“寻找意愿”比有意识地、专注地做出寻找的决定更容易带来成功。很难找到其他解释，为何在街上数百人中，只有她一个人能找到令她如此惊讶的东西，尤其是在昏暗的夜色和拥挤的人群中，这显然不利于她找到。这种无意识或前意识的准备状态确实存在，这一点可以从一个奇特的现象中看出：即使在她找到东西之后——也就是说，在她寻找东西的准备状态已经变得多余，并且肯定不再存在于她的意识中之后——这位女孩在回家的路上，又在郊区街道一个黑暗偏僻的地方找到了一条手帕。

It must be said that it is such symptomatic actions that often provide the best access to an understanding of the intimate mental life of human beings.

必须指出的是，正是这些症状性行为往往能为理解人类的内心世界提供最佳途径。

Of the kinds of fortuitous actions that occur in isolation, I will choose an example which allowed deeper interpretation even without analysis, is a cogent illustration of the conditions in which such symptoms can be very inconspicuously produced, and to which I may add a note of practical significance. While I was away on a summer holiday I happened to have to wait some days in a certain place for my travelling companion to arrive. During this time I made the acquaintance of a young man who also seemed to be feeling lonely and was very ready to keep me company. As we were staying in the same hotel, we easily fell into the habit of eating all our meals together and going for walks with each other. On the afternoon of the third day, my new friend suddenly told me that he was expecting his wife to arrive by express train that evening. This aroused my psychological interest, for that morning I had already noticed that my companion had declined my suggestion of a longer walk, and while we were out on our little stroll he had been disinclined to take a certain path, saying that it was too steep and dangerous. On our walk that afternoon he suddenly told me I must be hungry, and said I wasn’t to postpone my evening meal on his account; he would take his own with his wife after her arrival. I understood the hint and sat down at the supper table while he went to the station. Next morning we met in the hotel lobby. He introduced his wife to me, and added: ‘I hope you’ll join us for breakfast?’ I had a small purchase to make in the next street, and told them I would be back soon. When I entered the breakfast room I saw the couple both sitting on the same side of a little table in the window. There was only one chair on the opposite side of the table, but the man’s large, heavy loden coat was draped over the back of it, covering the seat. I had a very good idea of the reason for this arrangement of his coat, which was certainly not intentional but was all the more eloquent for that; it said: there’s no room here, you’re superfluous to requirements now. The man did not notice me standing by the table, unable to sit down, but the lady did, and she immediately nudged her husband and whispered: ‘Look, you’ve taken the gentleman’s seat.’

在众多偶然发生的事件中，我将选择一个例子，即使不加分析也能进行更深入的解读，它有力地说明了此类症状可能在何种情况下悄然产生，而且我还想补充一点实际意义。暑假期间，我碰巧需要在某个地方等我的旅伴几天。在此期间，我结识了一位年轻人，他似乎也感到孤独，并且很乐意陪伴我。由于我们住在同一家酒店，我们很快就养成了一起吃饭、一起散步的习惯。第三天下午，我的新朋友突然告诉我，他妻子当晚会乘特快列车抵达。这引起了我的心理兴趣，因为那天早上我已经注意到，我的旅伴拒绝了我提出的散步远行的提议，而且在我们散步时，他也不愿意走某条路，说那条路太陡峭、太危险。那天下午散步时，他突然说我肯定饿了，还说我不用因为他而推迟晚饭；他妻子到了之后，他会和她一起吃。我心领神会，便在他去车站的时候坐到了餐桌旁。第二天早上，我们在酒店大堂碰面。他向我介绍了他的妻子，然后问道：“希望你能和我们一起吃早餐？”我还要去隔壁街买点东西，就告诉他们我很快就回来。我走进餐厅，看到这对夫妇坐在靠窗一张小桌子的同一侧。桌子对面只有一把椅子，但那男人的厚重粗呢大衣搭在椅背上，盖住了椅面。我大概明白他这样摆放大衣的用意，这当然不是他有意为之，但也正因如此，才更显意味深长：这里没地方坐了，你现在对我们来说是多余的。那男人没有注意到我站在桌旁，无法坐下，但那位女士注意到了，她立即碰了碰她的丈夫，低声说：“你看，你占了男士的座位。”

In this and similar incidents, I have concluded that actions unintentionally performed are bound to be a source of misunderstanding in human intercourse. The perpetrator, who has no idea that there is any intention linked to them, does not credit himself with one, nor does he consider himself responsible for them. The second person concerned, however, since he regularly draws conclusions about the intentions and attitudes of the first from such actions, knows more about that first person’s psychic processes than he is ready to admit himself or thinks he has imparted. He will be indignant if faced with any such conclusions made on the basis of his symptomatic actions, declaring them groundless, since he was unaware of having any intention to carry them out, and he will complain that the second person misunderstands him. Such misunderstandings, strictly speaking, actually arise from too great and too subtle a process of understanding. The more ‘edgy’ two people are, the more likely they are to give each other occasion for disagreements, each denying his own responsibility for them while taking it as proven for the other party. This may well be the penalty we pay for our inner dishonesty in allowing ourselves to express certain ideas only through the devices of forgetfulness, inadvertent and unintentional actions, ideas that, even if we cannot control them, we would do better to admit to ourselves and to others. In general, it may be said that everyone is always psychoanalysing his fellow men, and as a consequence learns to know them better than they know themselves. The way to carrying out the famous injunction to know thyself is through studying our own apparently fortuitous actions and omissions.

在此类事件中，我得出结论：无意之举必然会成为人际交往中误解的根源。行为者本人并不知晓其行为背后有任何意图，因此既不认为自己有此意图，也不认为自己对此负有责任。然而，另一方却常常根据此类行为推断行为者的意图和态度，从而对行为者的心理活动了解得比行为者本人愿意承认的或自认为透露的要多得多。如果有人根据行为的表象做出推断，行为者会感到愤慨，声称这些推断毫无根据，因为他根本没有意识到自己有任何实施这些行为的意图，并抱怨另一方误解了他。严格来说，这类误解实际上源于理解过程过于复杂和微妙。两个人越是“敏感”，就越容易彼此制造矛盾，各自否认自己对此负有责任，却认定是对方的错。这或许就是我们内心不诚实所要付出的代价：我们允许自己只通过遗忘、无意或无意识的行为来表达某些想法，而这些想法即便我们无法控制，也最好坦诚地承认，并告知他人。总的来说，可以说每个人都在不断地分析他人，结果往往比他人更了解他们。践行“认识你自己”这句名言的方法，正是通过审视我们那些看似偶然的行为和疏忽。

Of all the creative writers who have sometimes expressed their opinions of such small symptomatic actions and slips, or have used them in some way in their work, none has recognized their secret nature so clearly or described them with such uncanny faithfulness as Strindberg — whose brilliant perception, however, rested on his own profound psychic abnormality. Dr Karl Weiss of Vienna has drawn our attention to the following passage in one of his works ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse I, 1913, p. 268):

在所有曾表达过对这类细微症状性行为和失误的看法，或以某种方式在作品中运用过它们的作家中，没有谁能像斯特林堡那样清晰地认识到它们的隐秘本质，或以如此惊人的忠实度来描述它们——然而，他敏锐的洞察力却建立在他自身深刻的精神异常之上。维也纳的卡尔·魏斯博士曾提请我们注意他著作中的一段话（《国际精神分析杂志》第一卷，1913年，第268页）：

‘After a while the count did arrive, and went calmly up to Esther as if he had arranged a rendezvous with her.

过了一会儿，伯爵来了，他平静地走到埃丝特面前，好像早就和她约好见面一样。

“‘Have you been waiting long?” he asked, in a quiet voice.

“你等了很久了吗？”他轻声问道。

“‘Six months, as you know,” replied Esther. “But didn’t you see me yesterday?”

“你知道，已经六个月了，”埃丝特回答说。“可是你昨天没见到我吗？”

“‘Why, yes, in the tram, and I looked into your eyes and felt as if I were speaking to you.”

“是的，在电车上，我看着你的眼睛，感觉就像在和你说话一样。”

“‘A great deal has ‘happened’ since last time.”

“自上次以来，发生了很多事情。”

“‘Yes, I thought it was all over between us.”

“是的，我以为我们之间已经结束了。”

“‘Why?”

“'为什么？”

“‘All the little presents you had given me broke in a most mysterious way. But noticing such things is nothing new.”

“你送我的那些小礼物都以一种非常神秘的方式碎掉了。不过，注意到这种事对我来说并不新鲜。”

“‘Why, goodness me! Now that you say so, I remember a whole series of incidents which I took for chance. While we were on good terms my grandmother once gave me a pair of pince-nez. They were made of polished rock crystal and very useful when I was carrying out post-mortems — in fact they were wonderful, and I looked after them carefully. One day I quarrelled with the old lady, and she was cross with me. Next time I was performing a post-mortem the lenses fell right out. I thought the pince-nez were simply broken and sent them off to be repaired, but it was no use, they would not work for me, so I put them away in a drawer and lost track of them.”

“哎呀，我的天哪！你这么一说，我才想起来之前发生过一系列事，当时我以为都是偶然。我们关系还不错的时候，我奶奶送了我一副夹鼻眼镜。眼镜是用抛光水晶做的，我做尸检的时候特别好用——实际上，它们简直太棒了，我一直很爱惜它们。有一天，我和奶奶吵了一架，她很生气。下次我做尸检的时候，眼镜的镜片竟然掉了出来。我以为眼镜只是坏了，就拿去修，结果修不好了，根本没法用，我就把它们收进抽屉里，从此就忘了它们的存在了。”

“‘Well, think of that! How strange that anything to do with the eyes is so particularly sensitive! I had been given a pair of opera glasses by a friend; they suited my eyes so well that it was a pleasure to use them. Then my friend and I fell out. You know how these things happen, for no obvious reason; it seems as if one just can’t agree. Next time I was going to use the opera glasses I couldn’t see clearly through them: the shank was too short and I saw two images instead of one. I hardly need to tell you that the shaft was no shorter than before, nor had the distance of the lenses from my eyes increased! Peculiar things like this happen all the time, although the unobservant don’t notice them. So what is the explanation? Why, the psychic force of hatred must be greater than we think. Oh, and that ring you gave me lost its stone and absolutely refuses to be repaired. So — do you want to break with me now?”’ The Gothic Rooms ).

“‘哎呀，想想看！多么奇怪，凡是跟眼睛有关的东西，竟然都这么敏感！我朋友送了我一副歌剧镜；它非常适合我的眼睛，用起来简直是一种享受。后来我和朋友闹翻了。你知道这种事是怎么发生的，没什么明显的原因；好像就是无法达成共识。下次我想用歌剧镜的时候，却看不清楚了：镜柄太短，我看到了两个影像而不是一个。不用我说你也知道，镜柄的长度和以前一样，镜片离眼睛的距离也没有增加！这种怪事时有发生，只是不细心的人察觉不到。那么，这究竟是怎么回事呢？唉，看来仇恨的心理力量比我们想象的要强大得多。哦，对了，你送我的那枚戒指上的宝石掉了，怎么也修不好。所以——你现在想跟我断绝关系吗？’（《哥特房间》）

Psychoanalysts must also give precedence to literary writers in the field of symptomatic actions. We can only repeat what they said long ago. Herr Wilhelm Stross has pointed out to me the following passage in the famous humorous novel Tristram Shandy (part VI, chapter V ):

精神分析学家也必须优先考虑文学作家在症状行为领域的作用。我们只能重复他们很久以前说过的话。威廉·斯特罗斯先生曾向我指出著名幽默小说《项狄传》（第六部第五章）中的以下段落：

‘… and I am not at all surprised that Gregory of Nazianzum, upon observing the hasty and untoward gestures of Julian, should foretell he would one day become an apostate; or that St Ambrose should turn his amnuensis out of doors, because of an indecent motion of his head, which went backwards and forwards like a flail; — or that Democritus should conceive Protagoras to be a scholar, from seeing him bind up a faggot, and thrusting, as he did it, the small twigs inwards. — There are a thousand unnoticed openings, continued my father, which let a penetrating eye at once into a man’s soul; and I maintain it, added he, that a man of sense does not lay down his hat in coming into a room, — or take it up in going out of it, but something escapes, which discovers him.’

“……我一点也不惊讶纳齐安的格列高利看到尤利安鲁莽轻佻的举动，便预言他有朝一日会背弃信仰；圣安布罗斯因为尤利安头部不雅地前后摆动，如同挥舞连枷一般，便将他的圣餐杯扔到门外；德谟克利特看到普罗泰戈拉捆柴时，一边将细枝塞入柴堆，一边认为他是个学者。——我父亲继续说道，世间有无数不易察觉的缝隙，能让洞察人心的目光瞬间看透一个人的灵魂；我坚持认为，一个有识之士进屋时不会放下帽子，——出屋时也不会摘下帽子，总有一些东西会从中流露出来，从而暴露他的内心。”

Here is a small collection from the many kinds of symptomatic actions observed in both healthy people and neurotics:

以下是健康人和神经质患者身上观察到的多种症状行为中的一小部分：

An older colleague, who does not like losing at cards, one evening lost quite a large sum of money, and paid it without a murmur but in a noticeably muted frame of mind. When he had gone home he turned out to have left behind almost everything he had with him: his glasses, his cigar case and his handkerchief. Translated into words, his action meant: well, you thieves, you’ve well and truly fleeced me.

一位年纪较大的同事，不喜欢打牌输钱，一天晚上输了一大笔钱，他默默地把钱付了回去，但情绪明显低落。回家后，他发现自己几乎把所有东西都落下了：眼镜、雪茄盒和手帕。他的行为用一句话来表达：哼，你们这些小偷，真是把我坑惨了。

A man who suffered from occasional sexual impotence because his childhood relationship with his mother had been so close said he used to mark his writings and drawings with an S, the initial of her name. He could not bear letters from home to be in contact with other and less sacrosanct correspondence on his desk, and was obliged to keep them somewhere else.

一位因童年时期与母亲关系过于亲密而偶尔出现性功能障碍的男子说，他过去常常在自己的文字和绘画作品上标记“S”，那是母亲名字的首字母。他无法忍受家里的信件与桌上其他不那么神圣的信件接触，因此不得不把它们藏在别处。

A young lady suddenly opened the door of the consulting room where the previous patient was still sitting. She apologized, excusing herself on the grounds of ‘thoughtlessness’, but it soon turned out that she was showing the same kind of curiosity which had led her to burst into her parents’ bedroom in the past.

一位年轻女子突然推开了诊室的门，之前的病人还坐在里面。她连忙道歉，以“考虑不周”为由推开了门，但很快人们就发现，她表现出的好奇心和过去闯入父母卧室的好奇心如出一辙。

Girls who are proud of their beautiful hair arrange their combs and hairpins so skilfully that their hair is bound to come down in the middle of a conversation.

有些女孩对自己美丽的秀发引以为傲，她们会非常巧妙地整理梳子和发夹，以至于在谈话过程中，头发很容易掉下来。

Many men will scatter small change out of their trouser pockets while they are lying down during their treatment, thus symbolically paying the fee for the session according to their own estimate of its value.

许多男性在接受治疗时，躺下后会从裤兜里掏出零钱，象征性地支付治疗费用，金额根据他们自己对治疗价值的估计而定。

Patients who forget something they have brought with them when visiting a doctor — pince-nez, gloves, a wallet — are suggesting that it is hard to tear themselves away and that they want to come back soon. E. Jones has said: ‘One can almost measure the success with which a physician is practising psychotherapy, for instance by the size of the collection of umbrellas, handkerchiefs, purses, and so on, that he could make in a month.’

患者去看医生时如果忘记带东西——比如夹鼻眼镜、手套、钱包——这表明他们很难离开，并且希望很快能再次就诊。E·琼斯曾说过：“例如，我们几乎可以通过医生一个月内收集到的雨伞、手帕、钱包等等的数量来衡量他进行心理治疗的成功程度。”

The smallest actions habitually and inconspicuously performed, for instance winding up one’s watch before going to sleep, putting out the light before leaving the room, and so forth, are sometimes prone to disruptions that unmistakably illustrate the influence of unconscious complexes on what appear to be the most firmly established of habits. Maeder writes in the journal Coenobium of a hospital doctor who had important business one evening in town, and decided to go out although he was on call and ought not really to have left the hospital. On coming back he was surprised to see his room lit up. He had forgotten to put the light out when he left, something that had never happened before. But he soon pinpointed the motive for his forgetfulness: the director of the hospital, who lived in the same building, would conclude from seeing his houseman’s light on that he too was in the building.

一些习惯性且不易察觉的小动作，例如睡前给手表上弦、离开房间前关灯等等，有时也容易被打乱，这无疑表明了无意识情结对看似最根深蒂固的习惯的影响。梅德尔在《共生》（Coenobium）杂志上写道，一位医院医生某天晚上有要事在城里，尽管他当时值班，本不该离开医院，但他还是决定出门。回来后，他惊讶地发现自己的房间亮着灯。他出门时忘记关灯了，这种情况以前从未发生过。但他很快就找到了自己忘记的原因：住在同一栋楼里的医院院长，看到他房间的灯亮着，就会推断院长也在楼里。

A man with many anxieties who was sometimes subject to fits of depression told me that he regularly found his watch had run down in the morning if life had seemed to him too harsh and forbidding the evening before. Failing to wind his watch was a symbolic expression of his disinclination to face the coming day. Another man, not personally known to me, writes: ‘When a hard blow of fate fell on me, life seemed so hostile that I felt I could not summon up the strength to live another day, and then I noticed that almost daily I forgot to wind my watch, something I had never been in the habit of forgetting before, when I regularly and unconsciously or almost mechanically did so before going to bed. Now I very seldom remembered to wind it, in fact only when I had some important project next day, or something was to happen in which I took a particular interest. Could that be a symptomatic action as well? I couldn’t explain it to myself at all.’

一位焦虑不安、时常陷入抑郁的男士告诉我，如果前一天晚上生活对他来说过于艰难困苦，他第二天早上就会发现自己的手表没电了。忘记给手表上弦，象征着他不愿面对新的一天。另一位我并不认识的男士写道：“当命运重重打击我时，生活似乎如此充满敌意，我感觉自己再也提不起劲活下去。这时我注意到，我几乎每天都会忘记给手表上弦，这在以前是从来没有过的。以前，我总会在睡前不自觉地、几乎是机械地给手表上弦。现在，我很少记得给它上弦，事实上，只有第二天有重要的事情要做，或者有什么我特别关心的事情发生时，我才会想起。这会不会也是一种症状呢？我完全无法解释。”

Anyone who, like Jung ( Über die Psychologie der Dementia praecox , 1907, p. 62) and Maeder (‘Une voie nouvelle en psychologie — Freud et son école’, Coenobium , Lugano 1909), takes the trouble to listen to the tunes people involuntarily hum to themselves, often without noticing, will regularly find some connection between the words to the tune being hummed and a subject preoccupying the person who hums it.

任何像荣格（《论早发性痴呆的心理学》，1907 年，第 62 页）和梅德尔（《心理学新路径——弗洛伊德及其学派》，《共和报》，卢加诺，1909 年）那样，费心倾听人们不由自主哼唱的曲调的人，都会经常发现哼唱的曲调的歌词与哼唱者所关注的主题之间存在某种联系。

Subtler determination of the way in which we express our ideas in speaking or writing deserves close study. We generally believe that we can choose the words in which we clothe our ideas, or the image in which we cloak them. But closer observation shows that this choice is made for other reasons, and that a deeper and often unintentional sense shows faintly through in the form taken by the idea. The images and style that people use for preference seldom prove irrelevant to assessment of their characters, while other phrases often turn out to refer to a background subject which has taken strong hold on the speaker. There was a time when I often heard a man using the expression, in theoretical discussion: ‘When something suddenly shoots through your mind [German: Kopf , ‘head’],’ when in fact I knew he had recently heard that a Russian bullet had passed right through the army cap his son was wearing on his head.

我们用言语或文字表达思想的方式，其微妙之处值得我们深入研究。我们通常认为，我们可以选择用来包装思想的词语，或者用来呈现思想的意象。但仔细观察就会发现，这种选择并非出于本意，思想的形式中往往隐隐透露着更深层次、常常是无意的意义。人们偏爱的意象和风格，很少能与对其性格的评价无关；而其他一些短语，则常常指向某个深深影响说话者的背景事件。我曾经常听到一个人在理论讨论中使用这样的表达：“当某件事突然闪过你的脑海（德语：Kopf，意为“脑袋”）”，而实际上我知道，他不久前听说一颗俄罗斯子弹穿过了他儿子头上戴着的军帽。

第七届国际精神分析杂志 III，1915 年。
