X

X

Making Mistakes

犯错

Making mistakes in remembering facts is to be distinguished from forgetfulness attended by a faulty memory in only one feature: we do not realize that we have made a mistake, but think we are right. The use of the term ‘mistake’, however, seems to depend on a different aspect of the phenomenon. We speak of ‘making mistakes’ instead of faulty memory when we want to emphasize the objective reality of the mental material we are reproducing, that is, when we want to remember something outside our own psychic lives, something which is capable of confirmation or refutation by other people’s memories. In this sense, ignorance is the opposite of a mistaken memory.

记忆事实出错与记忆力衰退导致的遗忘之间的区别仅在于一点：我们意识不到自己犯了错误，反而认为自己是对的。然而，“错误”一词的使用似乎取决于这一现象的另一个方面。当我们想要强调我们所复述的心理材料的客观真实性时，我们便会说“犯错”而不是“记忆力衰退”，也就是说，当我们想要记住一些存在于我们自身精神世界之外的事物，一些可以被他人记忆所证实或证伪的事物时。从这个意义上讲，无知与记忆错误截然相反。

In my book The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), 1 I was guilty of a series of falsifications of historical facts and indeed factual material in general, and became aware of them, to my own surprise, only after the publication of the book. On closer examination I found that they did not derive from my ignorance, but could be traced back to mistakes of memory which I could clear up by analysis.

在我的著作《梦的解析》（1900年）中，我犯了一系列篡改历史事实乃至一般事实材料的错误，令我惊讶的是，直到该书出版后我才意识到这些错误。仔细检查后，我发现这些错误并非源于我的无知，而是可以追溯到记忆失误，而这些失误可以通过分析加以澄清。

1) On p. 266 [VI.G] of the first edition, I had said that Schiller’s birthplace was the Hessian city of Marburg , a place name also found in Styria. This mistake comes in the analysis of a dream I had while travelling by night, from which I was woken when the guard called out the name of Marburg station. The content of the dream refers to a book by Schiller. In fact Schiller was born not in the university town of Marburg, but in Marbach in Swabia, as I am sure I have always known.

1）在第一版第266页[VI.G]中，我曾说过席勒的出生地是黑森州的马尔堡，这个地名在施蒂利亚州也有出现。这个错误源于我对夜间旅行时做的一个梦的分析，当时我被站长喊出的马尔堡车站的名字惊醒。梦的内容与席勒的一本书有关。事实上，席勒并非出生于大学城马尔堡，而是出生于施瓦本的马尔巴赫，这一点我一直都确信无疑。

2) On p. 135 [V.B] I gave the name of Hannibal’s father as Hasdrubal. I found this a particularly annoying mistake to have made, but it did much to confirm my ideas of the way in which such mistakes occur. Few of the readers of the book will have known more about the history of the Barca family than the author himself, yet I put the wrong name down and let it pass through three sets of proofs. Hannibal’s father was Hamilcar Barca — Hasdrubal was the name of Hannibal’s brother, and also of his brother-in-law who preceded him as commander of the Carthaginian army.

2）在第135页[V.B]，我把汉尼拔的父亲的名字写成了哈斯德鲁巴。我发现这是一个特别令人懊恼的错误，但它也印证了我之前对这类错误发生方式的看法。这本书的读者中，恐怕很少有人比我更了解巴卡家族的历史，但我却写错了名字，而且还让它通过了三轮校对。汉尼拔的父亲是哈米尔卡·巴卡——哈斯德鲁巴是汉尼拔的兄弟的名字，也是他姐夫的名字，这位姐夫曾是迦太基军队的统帅。

3) On pp. 177 [V.D] and 370 [VII.F] I said that Zeus castrated his father Kronos and usurped his throne. By mistake I had shifted this grisly act one generation forward; in Greek mythology, it was Kronos who castrated his father Uranus. 2

3）我在第177页[V.D]和370页[VII.F]中提到宙斯阉割了他的父亲克洛诺斯并篡夺了他的王位。由于疏忽，我将这件骇人听闻的事情提前了一代；在希腊神话中，是克洛诺斯阉割了他的父亲乌拉诺斯。

How can I explain the way in which my memory provided false information on these points, while as readers of the book can see for themselves it placed other material of a most obscure and unusual nature at my disposal? What is more, how could I have missed seeing the mistakes, as if afflicted by sudden blindness while I was carefully correcting three sets of proofs?

我该如何解释我的记忆为何在这些方面提供了错误信息？而读者们却能从书中看到，我的记忆中却包含了一些极其晦涩难懂、不同寻常的素材。更何况，我在仔细校对三套校样时，怎么可能像突然失明一样，对这些错误视而不见呢？

Goethe said of Lichtenberg: ‘When he makes a joke, there is a problem behind it.’ Something similar could be said of the passages from my book cited here: where I had made a mistake, some repression lay behind it. Or, more accurately, some insincerity or distortion, ultimately based on a repression. In the analysis of the dreams that I gave there, the nature of the subjects to which the dream ideas related meant that at some times I had to break off the analysis before it was complete, and at others I was forced to distort an indiscreet detail slightly in order to blur its point. I had no other choice, and indeed there was no alternative if I were to cite any examples and produce any evidence at all; the situation in which I found myself derived inevitably from the very nature of dreams, their ability to bring out what has been repressed and is incapable of conscious expression. Even so, there seems to have been enough left to give offence to certain more sensitive souls. The modification or elimination of ideas when I myself knew how they would continue could not, however, be carried out without leaving any trace. What I wanted to suppress often made its way, against my will, into what I did say, emerging as a mistake that passed unnoticed. In addition, the same subject lies at the heart of all three of the examples I mentioned above; my mistakes arose from repressed ideas connected with my late father.

歌德曾评价利希滕贝格说：“他讲笑话的时候，背后总藏着问题。”我书中引用的段落也类似：我犯的错误背后，往往隐藏着某种压抑。或者更准确地说，是某种虚伪或扭曲，而这些最终都源于压抑。在我分析梦境的过程中，梦境所涉主题的性质决定了我有时不得不中断分析，有时则不得不略微歪曲一些不妥的细节，以模糊其意义。我别无选择，事实上，如果我要举例子、提供证据，就别无他法；我所处的境地，必然源于梦境本身的性质，梦境能够揭示那些被压抑且无法用意识表达的东西。即便如此，似乎仍有一些内容足以冒犯某些较为敏感的人。即使我自己也清楚某些想法会如何发展，试图修改或消除它们也并非万无一失。我想要压制的东西，常常违背我的意愿，悄然渗入我的言语之中，最终以不为人知的错误形式出现。此外，我上面提到的三个例子都指向同一个核心问题：我的错误源于与已故父亲相关的、被压抑的想法。

1) It will be partially obvious to readers of the dream analysed on p. 266 [VI.G], and they will be able to draw further conclusions from some hints, that I stopped short there of expressing adverse criticism of my father. Part of the train of thoughts and memories as it would have continued depends on a painful story involving books and a business friend of my father’s, a man whose name was Marburg, the same name that woke me from sleep when I heard it called out at Marburg station on the Southern Railway. In the course of analysing the dream I wanted to leave this Herr Marburg out, concealing his existence from both myself and my readers, but he avenged himself by intruding where he did not belong and changing the name of Schiller’s birthplace from Marbach to Marburg.

1）对于阅读过第266页[VI.G]梦境分析的读者来说，部分显而易见，他们也能从一些暗示中得出进一步的结论：我当时并未对父亲提出任何负面批评。原本应该继续下去的思绪和记忆，部分取决于一个痛苦的故事，这个故事与书籍以及我父亲的一位生意伙伴有关，此人名叫马尔堡（Marburg），正是这个名字在南方铁路的马尔堡车站响起，将我从睡梦中惊醒。在分析梦境的过程中，我本想忽略这位马尔堡先生，对他本人和读者都隐瞒他的存在，但他却以不属于他的地方——马尔巴赫（Marbach）——来报复我，并将席勒的出生地改名为马尔堡（Marburg）。

2) The mistake Hasdrubal instead of Hamilcar , where I gave the name of Hannibal’s brother instead of his father, was made in a context concerning my Hannibal fantasies when I was at secondary school and my dislike of my father’s attitude to the ‘enemies of our people’, I could have gone on to mention that my relationship with my father was altered after a visit to England, where I met my half-brother from my father’s first marriage, who lived in that country. His eldest son is my own age, so there was no age difference in the way of my fantasies when I thought how different it would have been if I had come into the world as my brother’s son and not my father’s. These suppressed fantasies falsified the text of my book just where I interrupted the analysis by making me put the name of Hannibal’s brother instead of his father.

2）我把汉尼拔的兄弟哈斯德鲁巴尔（Hasdrubal）误写成哈米尔卡（Hamilcar），也就是把汉尼拔的父亲的名字写成了他的兄弟，这源于我中学时期对汉尼拔的幻想，以及我对父亲对待“我们民族的敌人”态度的反感。我本可以继续提到，我和父亲的关系在我去英国旅行后发生了改变。在那里，我遇到了父亲第一次婚姻所生的同父异母的哥哥，他当时就住在英国。他的长子和我同龄，所以当我幻想如果我是哥哥的儿子而不是父亲的儿子，人生会是多么不同时，年龄差异并不会阻碍我的幻想。正是这些被压抑的幻想，导致我把汉尼拔的兄弟的名字写成了他的父亲，从而打断了分析的思路。

3) I ascribe my shifting the mythological horrors enacted by the gods of ancient Greece one generation forward to the influence of the same brother’s memory. One of the pieces of advice he gave me remained in my mind for a long time: ‘As your life goes on,’ he told me, ‘don’t forget that you are really in the third rather than the second generation of our father’s family.’ In fact he — our father — was getting on in years by the time he remarried, so that he was a great deal older than the children of that second marriage. I made the mistake mentioned above in the book at the very place where I was discussing the dutiful relationship between parents and children.

3）我将古希腊诸神所演绎的神话恐怖故事向前推进一代，归因于我同一位兄弟的记忆。他给我的一条建议我铭记于心：“随着你的人生继续，”他告诉我，“不要忘记，你实际上是我们父亲家族的第三代，而不是第二代。”事实上，我们的父亲再婚时已年迈，比他第二次婚姻所生的孩子年长许多。我在书中讨论父母与子女之间应尽的责任关系时，犯了上面提到的那个错误。

Friends and patients whose dreams I have described or referred to in dream analysis have sometimes told me that my account of the details we shared with each other was inaccurate. Again, these mistakes could be called historical in nature, for I checked the various passages concerned after being set right, and realized that my memory of facts was at fault only where I had intentionally distorted or concealed some part of the analysis. Once again, a mistake passed unnoticed as the substitute for an intentional omission or repression.

我曾描述过一些朋友和病人的梦境，或者在梦境分析中提及过他们的梦境，他们有时会告诉我，我对彼此分享的梦境细节的描述并不准确。这些错误也可以归结为历史遗留问题，因为在得到纠正后，我查阅了相关的段落，发现只有当我故意歪曲或隐瞒了分析中的某些部分时，我的记忆才会出现偏差。再一次，一个错误被误认为是故意遗漏或压抑的替代品，而未被察觉。

Mistakes deriving from repression can be clearly distinguished from mistakes that are the result of real ignorance. It was plain ignorance, for instance, when I thought that I had seen Emmersdorf, where the revolutionary Fischhof lived, while I was on an expedition to the Wachau area. In fact there are two places of that name, and the Emmersdorf where Fischhof lived is in Carinthia, but I knew no better.

因压制而导致的错误与因真正无知而导致的错误截然不同。例如，我在瓦豪地区考察时，误以为自己看到了革命家菲施霍夫居住的埃默斯多夫，这完全是出于无知。事实上，有两个同名的地方，菲施霍夫居住的埃默斯多夫位于克恩顿州，但我当时对此一无所知。

4) Another humiliating but instructive mistake was what I might describe as a case of temporary ignorance. A patient reminded me one day that I had promised to lend him two books on Venice to read in preparation for his Easter holiday. I told him that I had got them out ready for him, and went to my library to fetch them. In fact I had forgotten to look them out, for I was not too pleased about my patient’s journey; I regarded it as an unnecessary interruption to his treatment, and also financially disadvantageous to me as his doctor. I quickly glanced around the library looking for the two books I had thought of. One was a book on The Art of Venice , and I was sure I also had another historical work in a similar series. Sure enough, there it was: The Medici. I took it off the shelf and gave it to my waiting patient, only to confess my mistake with some embarrassment, since I really knew quite well that the Medici have nothing to do with Venice. For a brief moment, however, it had seemed to me not at all unlikely. Now in all fairness — since I had so often pointed out the patient’s own symptomatic actions to him — I could retrieve my authority in his eyes only by being honest and telling him the reasons, which I had not mentioned to him, for my reservations about his journey.

4）另一个令人尴尬却又颇有启发意义的错误，我称之为一时疏忽。一天，一位病人提醒我，我曾答应借给他两本关于威尼斯的书，让他为复活节假期做准备。我告诉他我已经准备好了，然后去书房取书。事实上，我忘了去找，因为我不太乐意病人出行；我认为这会不必要地打断他的治疗，而且作为他的医生，我的经济利益也会受到影响。我匆匆环顾书房，寻找我印象中的那两本书。其中一本是关于威尼斯艺术的，我确信我还有另一本同系列的古籍。果然，找到了：《美第奇家族》。我把它从书架上取下来，递给等候的病人，然后才有些尴尬地承认自己弄错了，因为我其实很清楚美第奇家族和威尼斯毫无关系。然而，在那短暂的一瞬间，我竟然觉得这并非完全不可能。公平地说——因为我曾多次向病人指出他自己的症状行为——我只有诚实地告诉他我对他治疗方案有所保留的原因（而这些原因我之前并没有向他提及），才能重新获得他在我眼中的权威。

In general, it is surprising to find that our compulsion to tell the truth is so much stronger than is usually thought. It may be a result of my study of psychoanalysis, but I now find it very difficult to lie. Whenever I try to be evasive, I make a mistake or some other slip that gives away my devious intentions, as in this and the previous examples.

总的来说，我们想要说真话的冲动远比人们通常认为的要强烈得多，这着实令人惊讶。或许是因为我学习了精神分析，我现在发现自己很难说谎。每当我试图回避问题时，我都会犯错或露出其他不轨之举，从而暴露我的险恶用心，就像这个例子和之前的例子一样。

The mechanism whereby mistakes are made seems to be more flexible than in other kinds of slips; that is to say, making a mistake in general shows that the mental activity involved was in conflict with some disruptive influence, but the nature of the mistake is not determined by the quality of the disruptive idea, which remains obscure. I should add at this point, however, that the same may be assumed in many simple cases of slips of the tongue or pen. Whenever we make such a slip we must suppose that mental processes outside our intention have disrupted it, but one has to admit that slips of the tongue and pen often operate through similarity of sound, laziness or a tendency to be hasty, and the disruptive factor does not succeed in making its own character felt in the resultant mistake. Co-operation on the part of the verbal material alone both facilitates and limits determination of the mistake.

与其他类型的失误相比，这种错误发生的机制似乎更为灵活；也就是说，一般来说，犯错表明相关的心理活动受到了某种干扰因素的影响，但错误的性质并非由这种干扰因素的性质决定，因为这种干扰因素本身仍然难以捉摸。然而，我在此补充一点，在许多简单的口误或笔误中，也可以这样假设。每当我们犯这种错误时，我们都必须假定是我们意图之外的心理过程干扰了它，但必须承认，口误和笔误通常是由于发音相似、懒惰或急躁等原因造成的，而干扰因素本身并不能在最终的错误中体现出来。语言材料本身的配合既促进又限制了对错误的判断。

To avoid citing nothing but mistakes of my own, I will add a few examples which could, however, equally well have been classified as slips of the tongue or actions that missed their mark, but that makes little difference in view of the similarity between all these kinds of slips.

为了避免只引用我自己的错误，我将补充一些例子，这些例子也可以被归类为口误或失策的行为，但考虑到所有这些类型的失误之间的相似性，这并没有什么区别。

5) I had a patient who wanted to end a relationship, and I strongly advised him not to talk to his lover on the telephone, since every conversation made it harder for him to break with her. I said he should write instead, although there was some difficulty in getting letters delivered to her. He visited me at one o’clock to tell me he had found a way round that problem, and asked, among other things, whether he could cite my medical authority. At two o’clock, when he was busy writing the farewell letter, he suddenly interrupted himself and said to his mother, who was in the room: ‘Oh, I forgot to ask the professor if I could mention him by name in the letter.’ He hurried to the telephone, was connected, and put his question: ‘Could I speak to the professor if he’s finished lunch, please?’ His answer was a startled: ‘Are you out of your mind, Adolf?’ in the very voice that, had he followed my advice, he would not have heard again. He had simply ‘made a mistake’, and called his lover’s number instead of his doctor’s, mine.

5）我有个病人想结束一段感情，我强烈建议他不要和情人打电话，因为每次通话都会让他更难下定决心。我说他应该写信，虽然把信寄给她有点困难。下午一点，他来看我，告诉我他找到了解决办法，还问我是否可以引用我的医学权威。两点钟，他正忙着写告别信，突然停了下来，对房间里的母亲说：“哦，我忘了问教授能不能在信里提到他的名字。”他赶紧跑到电话旁，接通后问道：“请问教授午饭后可以接电话吗？”教授惊讶地回答：“你疯了吗，阿道夫？”如果他听了我的建议，就不会再听到这种语气了。他只是“犯了个错误”，把电话打给了他的情人而不是他的医生，也就是我的医生。

6) A young lady was going to call on a recently married friend in Habsburgergasse. She was talking about her visit around the family table, but said by mistake that she had to go to Babenbergergasse. Laughing, her companions at table pointed out the mistake — or slip of the tongue, if you prefer. Two days previously, the Austrian republic had been declared in Vienna, the black and yellow colours of the former empire had gone, to be superseded by the red, white and red of the old Ostmark, home of the House of Babenberg, and the Habsburgs were stripped of power; the speaker had made the same substitution in her friend’s address. There is, as it happens, a very well-known street in Vienna called Babenberger strasse , but no Viennese would speak of it as a Gasse or alley-way.

6) 一位年轻女士要去拜访一位住在哈布斯堡街（Habsburgergasse）的新婚朋友。她和家人围坐在餐桌旁，谈论着这次拜访，却不小心说错了，说她要去的是巴本堡街（Babenbergergasse）。同桌的朋友们笑着指出了她的错误——或者说，如果你愿意，也可以称之为口误。两天前，奥地利共和国在维也纳宣告成立，昔日帝国的黑黄相间旗帜被弃用，取而代之的是巴本堡家族故乡——旧东区（Ostmark）的红白红三色旗，哈布斯堡家族也被剥夺了权力；这位女士在介绍朋友时，也犯了同样的错误。事实上，维也纳确实有一条非常著名的街道叫做巴本堡街（Babenbergerstrasse），但维也纳人绝不会把它称为“街”（Gasse）或“巷子”。

7) The local schoolteacher at a holiday resort, a poor but handsome young man, had been courting the daughter of a man from the city who owned a villa there until the girl fell passionately in love with him. In spite of the differences of race and social standing between them, she persuaded her family to agree to the marriage. One day the schoolmaster wrote his brother a letter, commenting: ‘The girl is not beautiful, but very sweet-natured, so everything would be all right there. But I can’t say whether I shall be able to bring myself to marry a Jewess in the end.’ When he sent this letter to his fiancée the engagement was broken off, while his brother was surprised to receive a missive full of loving vows. The source of this story assured me that it really was a mistake, not a clever ruse. However, I have heard of another case in which a lady was dissatisfied with her doctor, but did not want to say so and leave him openly, instead achieving her end by mixing up two letters, and there at least I can guarantee that this familiar comic device was a real mistake and not a device consciously employed.

7）一位在度假胜地任教的当地教师，虽然家境贫寒但相貌英俊。他一直追求一位城里男子的女儿，这位男子在那里拥有一栋别墅。女孩对他一见钟情。尽管两人种族和社会地位悬殊，女孩还是说服了家人同意这门婚事。一天，这位教师写信给他的兄弟，信中写道：“这姑娘长得并不漂亮，但心地善良，所以一切都会好起来的。只是我不知道自己最终能否接受娶一个犹太女子。”当他把这封信寄给未婚妻时，婚约解除了。而他的兄弟却意外地收到了一封充满爱意的信。故事的来源向我保证，这确实是一个误会，而不是什么精心策划的骗局。然而，我还听说过另一个例子，一位女士对她的医生不满意，但又不想直接说出来离开他，而是通过混淆两个字母达到了目的。至少我可以保证，这种常见的喜剧手法是一个真正的错误，而不是有意为之。

8) Brill gives an account of a lady who asked after another woman whom they both knew, and erroneously called her by her maiden name. When he drew her attention to the mistake, she admitted that she did not like their friend’s husband and was not at all happy about her marriage.

8）布里尔讲述了这样一个故事：一位女士打听另一位他们都认识的女士，却误叫了她的娘家姓。当他指出错误时，她承认自己不喜欢这位朋友的丈夫，对她的婚姻也并不满意。

9) This is a mistake that could also be called a slip of the tongue: a young father went to the registrar’s office to report his second daughter’s birth. When asked the child’s name he replied: ‘Hanna.’ ‘But you already have a child called Hanna,’ the registrar told him. We may infer that this second daughter was not quite such a welcome addition to the family as the first.

9）这算是一个口误：一位年轻的父亲去户籍登记处登记第二个女儿的出生。当被问及孩子的名字时，他回答说：“汉娜。”户籍员告诉他：“但您已经有一个孩子叫汉娜了。”由此我们可以推断，这个第二个女儿对这个家庭来说，并不像第一个女儿那样受欢迎。

10) Here are some further observations of names being confused. Again, they could just as well have been included in other sections of this book.

10）以下是一些关于人名混淆的进一步观察。同样，这些内容也完全可以放在本书的其他章节中。

A lady had three daughters, two of whom had been married for some time, while the youngest had not yet become engaged. Another lady, who was a friend of the family, had given the identical present of a valuable silver tea set at the two weddings. Whenever anyone mentioned this tea set, the mother made the mistake of naming her third daughter as its owner. Obviously the mother’s mistake expressed her wish to see her third and last daughter married too; she was assuming that she would get the same wedding present.

一位女士有三个女儿，其中两个已经结婚一段时间了，最小的女儿还没有订婚。另一位与她家交好的女士在两个女儿的婚礼上都送了同样的礼物——一套珍贵的银茶具。每当有人提起这套茶具，这位母亲都会误以为是三女儿的。显然，母亲的这个错误反映了她希望三女儿也能出嫁的愿望；她以为三女儿也会收到同样的结婚礼物。

It is equally easy to interpret the frequent cases in which a mother mixes up the names of her daughters, sons or sons-in-law.

母亲经常把女儿、儿子或女婿的名字搞混，这种情况也很容易解释。

11) A good and easily explained example of the persistent confusion of names is provided by the self-observation of one Herr J. G. while he was in a sanatorium: ‘At dinner in the sanatorium one day I used a particularly attentive phrase to my neighbour at table during a conversation which did not much interest me, and was very conventional in tenor. This neighbour of mine, a spinster getting on in years, could not help observing that I was not usually so attentive and gallant to her — an observation that conveyed a certain regret, but even more clearly was a derogatory reference to a lady we both knew and to whom I was accustomed to pay more attention. Of course I knew what she meant at once. During the rest of our conversation — and I found this very embarrassing — my neighbour pointed out several times that I had just addressed her by the name of the lady whom she saw, not without justification, as her more successful rival for my affections.’

11）J. G. 先生在疗养院期间的亲身经历，很好地说明了名字混淆的普遍性：“一天在疗养院吃晚饭时，我和邻桌聊着一些无关紧要、很普通的话题，我特意用了一句特别殷勤的话。我的邻桌是一位上了年纪的未婚女士，她忍不住指出我平时对她并不这么殷勤——这句话里带着一丝遗憾，但更明显的是，她是在贬低一位我们都认识的女士，而我平时对那位女士更加关注。我当然立刻明白了她的意思。在接下来的谈话中——这让我非常尴尬——我的邻桌好几次指出，我刚才叫的正是她认为（并非毫无道理）更胜一筹的那位女士的名字。”

12) An instance with a serious background, told to me by a witness who was closely concerned, can also be described as a ‘mistake’. A lady had been spending the evening out of doors with her husband, in the company of two other men. One of them was in fact a very intimate friend of hers, but the others did not know that, nor must they. The married couple’s friends accompanied them to their door, and said goodbye as they waited for it to be opened. The lady bowed to one of the other men, gave him her hand, and said a few cordial words. Then she took her unacknowledged lover’s arm, turned to her husband, and was about to say goodbye to him in the same way. The husband understood, took off his hat, and said with the utmost courtesy: ‘Well, goodbye to you too then, ma’am!’ The wife, in alarm, let go of her lover’s arm, and before the caretaker appeared had just time to sigh: ‘Good gracious, what a silly thing to do!’ Her husband was one of those married men who like to think it absolutely impossible for their wives to be unfaithful, and he had often said that if he had reason to suspect such a thing, more than one life would be in danger. He therefore had the strongest unconscious motives not to notice the challenge inherent in his wife’s mistake.

12）一位与此事关系密切的目击者向我讲述了一个背景严重的案例，这个案例也可以被描述为“错误”。一位女士当晚与丈夫在户外与另外两位男士共度时光。其中一位男士实际上是她的一位非常亲密的朋友，但其他两位男士并不知情，他们也不应该知道。这对夫妇的朋友陪同他们走到门口，在等待开门时道别。女士向其中一位男士鞠躬，伸出手，说了几句客套话。然后，她挽起那位她并不认识的情人的手臂，转身面向丈夫，正要以同样的方式向他道别。丈夫明白了，脱下帽子，彬彬有礼地说：“那么，夫人，您也再见了！”妻子惊慌地松开了情人的手臂，在看门人出现之前，她只来得及叹了口气：“哎呀，真是太傻了！”她的丈夫是那种喜欢认为妻子绝对不可能不忠的已婚男人，他常说，如果他有理由怀疑妻子不忠，那可就不是人命了。因此，他潜意识里极力想要忽略妻子犯下的错误所带来的挑战。

13) A mistake by one of my patients was repeated with the opposite significance, and is thus particularly instructive: an over-apprehensive young man, after a long internal struggle with himself, had brought himself to promise marriage to a girl who had long loved him, as indeed he loved her. He took his fiancée home, said goodbye, boarded a tram in a state of high delight, and asked the conductor for two tickets. Six months later he was married, but he had not yet really adjusted to the benefits of married life. He wondered whether he had done right, he missed his old friends, and he had all kinds of objections to his parents-in-law. One evening he fetched his young wife from her parents’ home, got into the tram with her, and on this occasion asked the conductor for a single ticket only.

13）我的一位病人犯过一个错误，结果却截然相反，因此特别具有启发意义：一个过度焦虑的年轻人，经过一番内心的挣扎，终于鼓起勇气向一位深爱着他、他也深爱着她的女孩许下婚约。他把未婚妻送回家，道别后，兴高采烈地上了电车，向售票员要了两张票。六个月后，他结婚了，但还没有真正适应婚姻生活。他开始怀疑自己当初的决定是否正确，想念以前的朋友，而且对岳父母也颇有微词。一天晚上，他去岳父母家接妻子，和她一起上了电车，这次他只向售票员要了一张票。

14) Maeder gives a good example of the way in which a ‘mistake’ can grant a reluctantly suppressed wish. A colleague wanted to enjoy a day off work undisturbed; however, he had to pay a call in Lucerne, and he was not looking forward to it. After much thought, he decided that he would pay the call after all. To occupy his mind he read the daily papers on his journey from Zurich to Arth and Goldau, he changed trains at the last-named station, and he continued reading. As the journey went on, the ticket inspector told him that he was in the wrong train: he had bought a ticket to Lucerne, but he was now on his way back from Goldau to Zurich (‘Nouvelles contributions’, etc., Archives de Psychoanalyse VI, 1908).

14）梅德尔举了一个很好的例子，说明“错误”如何能实现一个被压抑已久的愿望。一位同事想不受打扰地享受一天假期；然而，他必须去卢塞恩拜访一位客人，他对此并不期待。经过一番思索，他最终决定还是去拜访。为了打发时间，他在从苏黎世到阿尔特和戈尔道的旅途中阅读报纸。他在戈尔道换乘了火车，然后继续阅读。随着旅程的进行，检票员告诉他，他坐错了车：他买的是去卢塞恩的车票，但现在他正从戈尔道返回苏黎世（《新贡献》等，《精神分析档案》第六卷，1908年）。

15) An analogous if not entirely successful attempt to help a suppressed wish to express itself through the same mechanism is described by Dr V. Tausk under the heading ‘Going the Wrong Way’.

15) V. Tausk 博士在“走错路”一文中描述了一种类似的尝试，尽管这种尝试并不完全成功，但它旨在帮助被压抑的愿望通过相同的机制表达出来。

‘I had come on leave to Vienna from the front. A former patient had heard that I was there and sent a message asking if I would visit him, since he was sick in bed. I agreed to his request, and spent two hours with him. When I left him, my patient asked what he owed me. “I’m here on leave, not as a consultant,” I replied. “Please think of this visit as an act of friendship.” The sick man demurred, probably feeling that he had no right to claim professional services purely out of friendship. However, he finally agreed, saying, in a respectful tone dictated by his pleasure at saving the money, that as a psychoanalyst I must surely know the right thing to do. A little later I myself began doubting whether my high-minded approach had been right, and full of these doubts — which scarcely admitted any ambiguity — I got into the electric tramline X. After a short ride I had to change to tram Y. As I was waiting at the stop, I forgot about the fee and thought of my patient’s symptoms. Meanwhile, the tram I was waiting for came along and I got in. But I had to get out again at the next stop. Without noticing, I had boarded an X instead of a Y tram by mistake, and I was going back the way I had just come, as if to visit the patient from whom I had refused to take a fee. But my unconscious mind did want to take that fee ’ ( Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse IV, 1916/17).

“我从前线休假回维也纳。一位以前的病人听说我在这里，便捎信问我是否可以去看看他，因为他卧病在床。我答应了他的请求，陪了他两个小时。离开时，病人问我该付我多少钱。“我是休假来的，不是以顾问的身份，”我回答说，“请把这次探望当作一次友谊之举。”病人有些犹豫，大概觉得自己无权仅仅出于友谊就要求我提供专业服务。然而，他最终还是同意了，语气中带着一丝恭敬，显然是为省钱而高兴，他说，作为一名精神分析师，我肯定知道该怎么做。不久之后，我自己也开始怀疑自己这种高尚的做法是否正确，带着这些几乎不容置疑的疑虑，我坐上了X线有轨电车。没开多远，我就得换乘Y线。在车站等车的时候，我把车费的事忘得一干二净，满脑子都是病人的症状。”与此同时，我等候的电车来了，我上了车。但到了下一站，我又得下车。不知不觉中，我错上了一辆X线电车，而不是Y线电车，我正沿着来时的路往回走，仿佛要去探望那位我拒绝收取费用的病人。但我潜意识里却想收取那笔费用。（《国际精神分析杂志》第四卷，1916/17年）

16) I once played a trick on myself very similar to the one described in example 14. I had agreed with my eldest brother, a man of rather strict ideas, to pay him a long-overdue visit at an English seaside resort that summer, and as I was short of time I had decided to go by the shortest route without stopping on the way. I did ask him for an extra day’s delay which I could spend in Holland, but he said I could leave that until I was travelling home. So I was going by way of Munich and Cologne to Rotterdam and the Hook of Holland, where I was to catch the boat for the crossing to Harwich at midnight. I had to change in Cologne, and left the train from Munich in order to board the Rotterdam express, but it was nowhere to be seen. I asked various railway officials, was sent from platform to platform, found myself getting very agitated, and soon worked out that during this unsuccessful search I must have missed my connection. On getting confirmation that I had indeed missed it, I wondered whether to spend the night in Cologne. Family feeling among other factors suggested that idea, since according to an old family tradition my forebears had fled Cologne during a pogrom. However, I decided against it and caught a later train to Rotterdam, where I arrived quite late at night, so that now I was in fact obliged to spend a day in Holland. I used the time to fulfil my long-cherished wish of seeing the wonderful Rembrandts in The Hague and the Rijksmuseum. Only next morning, when I was able to gather my impressions together during the railway journey through England, did a perfectly clear memory emerge in my mind of seeing a large notice-board at Cologne station saying ‘Rotterdam-Hook of Holland’, only a few paces from where I had got out of the Munich train, in fact on the very same platform. The train in which I should have continued my journey was waiting there all the time. I would have had to account for my overlooking this obvious notice and hurrying off to look for my train elsewhere as an incomprehensible instance of ‘blindness’, had I not assumed that my real intention was to defy my brother’s wishes and see the Rembrandts on my outward journey. Everything else, the good show of agitation I put on, the emergence of a pious inclination to spend the night in Cologne, was merely a way of concealing my intention from myself until I had carried it out.

16）我曾经跟例14里描述的非常相似地捉弄过自己。那年夏天，我跟我那思想比较严谨的大哥约好去英国海滨度假胜地拜访他，这次去他家已经很久没见了。因为时间紧迫，我决定走最短路线，中途不停。我跟他说可以多耽搁一天，去荷兰玩玩，但他让我等回程的时候再去。于是我途经慕尼黑和科隆，前往鹿特丹和荷兰角，准备在那里搭船，午夜时分渡海去哈里奇。我在科隆换乘，从慕尼黑下了火车，准备去鹿特丹，结果却找不到那趟车。我问了好几个铁路工作人员，被他们从一个站台送到另一个站台，越来越焦躁不安，最后才意识到，我一定是在这徒劳的寻找过程中错过了换乘。确认自己确实错过了火车后，我犹豫着是否要在科隆过夜。出于家庭情感以及其他一些因素，我萌生了这个想法，因为根据家族的古老传说，我的祖先曾在科隆遭遇迫害时逃离那里。然而，我最终还是放弃了这个想法，搭乘晚些的火车前往鹿特丹。抵达鹿特丹时已是深夜，这意味着我不得不在荷兰待上一天。我利用这段时间实现了长久以来的愿望——参观海牙的伦勃朗名画和国立博物馆。直到第二天早上，当我回想起在穿越英国的火车旅途中所见所闻时，我才清晰地记得在科隆火车站看到一块巨大的告示牌，上面写着“鹿特丹——荷兰之角”，距离我下慕尼黑火车的地方只有几步之遥，实际上就在同一个站台上。我本应乘坐的火车一直停在那里。如果不是因为我认定自己真正的目的是违背哥哥的意愿，在去程途中欣赏伦勃朗的画作，我或许会把忽略这显而易见的告示，匆匆忙忙地去别处寻找火车，归咎于自己“一时糊涂”。其他的一切，包括我装出的焦躁不安，以及突然冒出的在科隆过夜的虔诚念头，都不过是掩饰自己真实意图的一种方式，直到我付诸行动为止。

17) J. Stärcke (op. cit.) describes a similar incident from his own experience, on the face of it caused by ‘forgetfulness’, but really intended to grant a wish that he had apparently abandoned:

17) J. Stärcke（同上）描述了他自己经历的类似事件，表面上是由于“健忘”造成的，但实际上是为了实现他显然已经放弃的一个愿望：

‘I was once to give a lecture illustrated by slides in a certain village, but then it was put forward a week. I had answered the letter notifying me of the postponement, and had written down the change of date. I would have liked to visit the same village one afternoon to see a writer of my acquaintance who lived there. To my regret, however, I could find no afternoon free around then, and with reluctance I gave up the idea of visiting my friend.

我原定在某个村庄做一场幻灯片讲座，但后来讲座提前了一周。我回复了通知我延期的信，并记下了新的日期。我原本想找个下午去那个村庄拜访一位住在那里的作家朋友。可惜的是，我当时找不到空闲的下午，只好遗憾地放弃了拜访朋友的计划。

‘When the evening of the lecture arrived, I set off in great haste to the station with a bag full of lantern slides. I had to take a taxi to catch the train (I quite often do leave my departure so late that I have to take a taxi to get to my train on time!). Once I reached my destination I was rather surprised to find no one at the station to meet me (as is usual when one is giving a lecture in a small town or village). Suddenly I remembered that the lecture had been postponed for a week, and I had now made a fruitless journey on the original date. When I had heartily cursed my forgetfulness, I contemplated catching the next train home again. On further deliberation, however, it struck me that I now had an excellent opportunity of making the call I had been wanting to pay, and so I did. Only on the way there did it occur to me that my unfulfilled wish to have time for this visit had hatched an ingenious plot against me. Lugging my heavy bag of slides and hurrying to catch the train were very good ways of concealing my unconscious intention all the better.’

讲座当晚，我匆匆忙忙地带着满满一袋幻灯片赶往车站。我不得不打车去赶火车（我经常出发太晚，以至于不得不打车才能赶上火车！）。到达目的地后，我惊讶地发现车站竟然没有人来接我（在小镇或乡村演讲时，这种情况很常见）。我突然想起讲座推迟了一周，而我却白跑了一趟。我狠狠地咒骂了自己的健忘，并考虑要不要搭下一班火车回家。然而，经过一番思量，我意识到现在我正好有机会打个电话，完成我一直想做的那件事，于是我就打了。直到路上，我才意识到，我一直想抽出时间拜访的愿望，竟然在我心中酝酿了一个巧妙的阴谋。拖着沉重的幻灯片包，匆匆赶火车，这样能更好地掩盖我无意识的意图。

One may not be inclined to think that the kinds of mistakes I have elucidated here are very numerous or particularly significant. However, I think we may wonder whether we should extend the same ideas to assessing those much more important errors of judgement made by people in their daily lives and in scientific studies. Only the most unusual and well-balanced minds seem able to preserve the perceived image of outward reality from the distortion it usually suffers by being filtered through the psychic individuality of the subject perceiving it.

人们或许不会认为我在此阐述的这些错误种类繁多或意义重大。然而，我们或许应该思考，是否应该将同样的思路延伸到评估人们在日常生活和科学研究中犯下的那些更为重要的判断失误。似乎只有那些思维极为独特且平衡的人，才能避免感知到的外部现实图像因感知主体自身的心理特质而产生的扭曲。

# ↩

XI

十一

Combined Slips

联合滑道

Two of the examples mentioned above — my error in connecting the Medici with Venice, and the young man’s slip in speaking to his lover on the telephone despite my advising him against it — were not described with perfect accuracy, for on careful examination they represent a combination of slips: of forgetfulness with a mistake. The same combination of slips can be demonstrated even more clearly from some other examples.

上面提到的两个例子——我误将美第奇家族与威尼斯联系起来，以及那位年轻人不顾我的劝阻，还是给情人打了电话——描述得并不完全准确，因为仔细分析就会发现，它们实际上是两种失误的结合：既有遗忘，也有错误。其他一些例子更能清晰地证明这种失误的组合。

1) A friend told me about the following incident: ‘A few years ago I accepted election to the committee of a certain literary society because I thought it might help me to get the play I had written staged some day, and I attended the meetings, which took place every Friday, regularly if without much interest. A few months ago I was assured that my drama would be produced at the theatre in F., and after that I regularly forgot to attend the meetings of the society. When I read what you had written about such subjects I felt ashamed of my forgetfulness, blaming myself for my mean-minded conduct in staying away once I no longer needed these people. I decided that I would be sure not to forget to go on the next Friday. I kept reminding myself of this resolution, until the time came to put it into practice and I was at the committee room door. To my surprise it was closed, and the meeting was already over. I had mistaken the day — it was now Saturday!’

1）一位朋友跟我讲了这样一件事：“几年前，我接受了某个文学社团委员会的选举，因为我觉得这或许能帮我把写的剧本搬上舞台。虽然没什么兴趣，但我还是坚持参加每周五的例会。几个月前，有人向我保证我的剧本会在F区的剧院上演，之后我就经常忘记去参加社团的会议。读了你写的关于这类事情的文章后，我为自己的健忘感到羞愧，也责怪自己因为不再需要这些人就疏远他们，真是太没良心了。我下定决心，下周五一定不会再忘记去。我一直提醒自己这个决心，直到真正要付诸行动的时候，我走到了委员会会议室门口。令我惊讶的是，门关着，会议已经结束了。我搞错了日子——今天是星期六！”

2) The next example combines a symptomatic action with a case in which something was mislaid: it came to me from a good if more remote source.

2) 下一个例子将症状行为与丢失物品的情况结合起来：它来自一个虽然比较远但却可靠的来源。

A lady was travelling to Rome with her brother-in-law, a famous artist. The German expatriates living in Rome welcomed him with great respect, and among other presents given to him was a gold medal of antique classical origin. The lady felt some vexation, believing that her brother-in-law did not value this fine piece properly. When her sister had come to take her place, and she herself was home again, she found on unpacking that she had brought the medal with her. Just how it had happened she could not imagine. She wrote at once to her brother-in-law to tell him about the misappropriated item, and said she would send it back to Rome next day. Next day, however, it had been so skilfully mislaid that it was impossible to find it and send it on, and then the true meaning of her ‘absence of mind’ dawned on the lady: she really wanted to keep the medal for herself.

一位女士陪同她的姐夫——一位著名艺术家——前往罗马旅行。居住在罗马的德国侨民热情接待了姐夫，并赠送给他许多礼物，其中就包括一枚古董古典时期的金质奖章。这位女士感到有些恼火，认为姐夫没有真正珍惜这件珍贵的物品。当她的妹妹代替她前往罗马，而她自己回到家后，打开行李时才发现自己竟然把奖章带了回来。她百思不得其解，究竟是怎么回事。她立即写信告诉姐夫这件事，并表示第二天就会把奖章寄回罗马。然而，第二天，奖章却被巧妙地遗失了，根本无法找到并寄回。这时，这位女士才恍然大悟，原来她所谓的“疏忽”其实是她想把奖章留给自己。

3) In some cases a slip is persistently repeated, changing its method of operation in the process:

3）在某些情况下，滑移现象会反复发生，并在过程中改变其运行方式：

Jones (op. cit, p. 483) tell us that, for reasons unknown to him, he once left a letter lying on his desk for several days before sending it off He finally brought himself to do so, but it was returned by the ‘dead letter office’ because he had forgotten to write the address on it. When he had addressed it he took it back to the post office, but this time he had forgotten to stamp it. He could no longer ignore the fact that he did not want to send the letter at all.

琼斯（同上，第483页）告诉我们，出于他自己也不清楚的原因，他曾把一封信放在桌上好几天才寄出去。最终他还是决定寄出去，但因为忘记写地址，信被“死信办公室”退回了。写好地址后，他又把信拿到邮局，但这次他又忘了贴邮票。他再也无法忽视自己根本不想寄这封信的事实。

4) A short account by Dr Karl Weiss of Vienna cogently describes unsuccessful attempts to carry out an action to which there is internal opposition:

4）维也纳的卡尔·魏斯博士的一篇简短记述精辟地描述了在内部遭到反对的情况下，开展某项行动的失败尝试：

‘The consistency with which the unconscious can make itself felt when it has a reason not to let a project be carried out, and the difficulty of guarding against this tendency, are obvious from the following incident. An acquaintance asked me to lend him a book and bring it round to him next day. I immediately agreed, but with a distinct sense of reluctance which I could not at first explain to myself. Later, I realized why: the man concerned had owed me a sum of money for years, and seemed to have no intention of paying it back. I thought no more of the matter, but I did remember it next morning, with the same sense of reluctance, and told myself at once: “Your unconscious will try to make you forget the book. But you don’t want to be churlish, so you will do your best to remember it.” I went home, wrapped the book up in a piece of paper and put it beside me on my desk while I wrote some letters. After a while I went out; having gone a few steps, I remembered that I had left the letters I was going to take to the post on my desk. (In one of those letters, incidentally, I had been forced to express displeasure to someone who was supposed to be supporting me in a certain matter.) I turned back, fetched the letters, and went out again. In the electric tram I remembered that I had promised my wife I would buy her something, and I was pleased to think that it would be only a small packet. Here I suddenly made the association between packet and book, and now I realized that I still did not have the book with me. Not only had I forgotten it the first time I went out, I had also continued to overlook it when I went back to pick up the letters from where it was lying.’

“当潜意识有理由阻止某个计划实施时，它会以多么强烈的方式表现出来，以及抵御这种倾向的难度，从以下事件中便可看出。一位熟人请我借一本书，第二天带过去。我立刻答应了，但心中却隐隐感到不情愿，起初我自己也说不清原因。后来我才明白原因：这个人欠了我一笔钱好几年，而且似乎没有还钱的打算。我当时没再多想这件事，但第二天早上我又想起了这件事，同样感到不情愿，于是我立刻告诉自己：‘你的潜意识会试图让你忘记这本书。但你不想显得无礼，所以你一定要尽力记住。’我回到家，用一张纸把书包好，放在书桌旁，然后开始写信。过了一会儿，我出门了；走了几步，我才想起要寄出去的信还放在桌子上。（顺便一提，其中一封信里，我不得不向一位本应在某件事上支持我的人表达不满。）我转身回去，拿了信，又出门了。在电车上，我想起答应过妻子要给她买点东西，想到只是个小包裹，我很高兴。这时，我突然把“包裹”和“书”联系起来，这才意识到我还没带书。不仅第一次出门时忘了带，回去拿信的时候，我又一次把它忘在了脑后。

5) A similar illustration is provided by an observation that Otto Rank has analysed in detail:

5）奥托·兰克详细分析的一个观察结果也提供了类似的例子：

‘A man of meticulously tidy and painfully precise habits told me about the following experience, an extremely unusual one for him. One afternoon, when he was out in the street and wanted to know the time, he realized that he had left his watch at home, which as far as he could remember he had never done before. Since he had an appointment to be kept punctually that evening, and he did not have time to go back for his watch now, he took the opportunity of visiting a lady who was a friend of his to borrow her watch for the evening; this was particularly convenient because he had to visit her again next morning to keep an appointment they had already made, and he promised to return the watch then. However, when he was about to give the borrowed watch back to its owner next day, he realized to his surprise that he had left it at home, putting his own watch in his pocket instead. He made a firm resolution to return the lady’s watch in the afternoon, and so he did. But when he was going to look at the time as he left, he found to his great annoyance and amazement that yet again he had forgotten his own watch. The repetition of the slip seemed to this normally well-organized man so pathological that he thought he would like to discover its psychological motivation, which promptly emerged from the psychoanalytical question of whether he had suffered any distressing experience on the crucial day when he first forgot the watch, and if so in what context. He immediately said that after lunch, just before he went out and forgot his watch, he had been talking to his mother, and she told him that a family member with an irresponsible disposition, who had already caused him a great deal of annoyance and expense, had pawned his own watch but needed it at home, so he had left a message asking our well-organized friend to let him have the money to redeem it. This way of borrowing money, almost amounting to blackmail, had affected our subject very unpleasantly, reminding him of all the vexation this family member had caused him over many years. His own symptomatic action thus proved to have been determined in several ways. First, it expressed a train of thought to the effect that he was not going to let anyone extort money from him like this, and if a watch was necessary he would simply leave his own at home; however, as he needed it in order to keep his evening appointment he could carry out that intention only unconsciously and in the form of a symptomatic action. Second, his forgetfulness meant something like: squandering money on that useless creature all the time will ruin me, and I shall have to give up everything. Although he said himself that he felt only momentary annoyance on hearing about the message, the duplication of his symptomatic action showed that it was still at work in his unconscious, rather as if his conscious mind were saying: I can’t get this business out of my head. 1 The fact that the same fate then befell the lady’s watch that he had borrowed is not surprising, given this attitude adopted by the unconscious mind. But perhaps there were other and more particular motives favouring this transference to the “innocent” lady’s watch. The most obvious is that he would probably have liked to keep it to replace his own watch, which he had sacrificed, and so forgot to give it back next day. In addition, perhaps he would have liked to keep the watch as a memento of the lady herself. Furthermore, forgetting the watch belonging to this lady — whom he admired — gave him an opportunity for a second visit to her; after all, he already had an appointment to visit her in the morning on other business, and he seems to have been indicating, by forgetting the watch, that it was a waste to hand her back her own watch casually during a visit that had been planned well in advance. Forgetting his own watch twice, which enabled him to pay another visit in order to return hers, suggests that our man was trying unconsciously to avoid carrying both watches at the same time. He clearly did not want to give such an impression of excess, which stood in stark contrast to his relation’s indigence; on the other hand, he also wanted to keep a cautious check on his apparent intention of marrying the lady by reminding himself that he had irremovable obligations to his own family (in the person of his mother). Finally, another reason for failing to return the watch may have been that on the previous evening he had been embarrassed, as a bachelor, to let his friends see him consulting the lady’s watch and had done so only on the sly, and to avoid any repetition of this awkward eventuality he did not want to have it in his pocket again. On the other hand, as he had to return it, the result was the unconscious performance of a symptomatic action which took the form of a compromise between his conflicting feelings and the hard-won victory of his unconscious’ ( Zentralblatt für Psychoanalyse II, 5).

一位生活习惯极其整洁、一丝不苟的男士向我讲述了这样一段对他来说极为罕见的经历。一天下午，他走在街上，想看看时间，却突然发现自己把手表落在家里了——据他回忆，这种情况以前从未发生过。由于当晚他有个约会必须准时赴约，现在又没时间回去取表，于是他便趁此机会去拜访一位女友，借了她的手表戴一晚上。这非常方便，因为他第二天早上还要再去拜访她，赴约之前已经约好的事，而且他答应第二天早上就归还手表。然而，第二天他准备把借来的手表还给女士时，却惊讶地发现自己竟然把手表落在家里了，而把自己的手表放进了口袋。他下定决心下午一定要把手表还给那位女士，而且他也确实做到了。但当他准备出门看时间时，却懊恼地发现自己又一次忘记带手表了。对于这位平时做事井井有条的人来说，这种反复的疏忽显得十分反常，他想探究一下背后的心理原因。于是，他立刻想到了一个心理分析问题：在他第一次忘记带手表的那天，是否经历过什么痛苦的事情？如果有，又是在什么情况下发生的？他马上说，午饭后，就在他出门忘记带手表之前，他和母亲聊过天。母亲告诉他，一个不负责任的亲戚——之前已经给他添了不少麻烦和损失——把自己的手表当掉了，但家里又需要，所以他留言请这位做事井井有条的朋友借钱去赎手表。这种近乎敲诈勒索的借钱方式令主人公非常不快，让他想起多年来这位家人给他带来的种种烦恼。他自身的这种表现性行为，其背后有多重原因。首先，它表达了一种想法：他绝不允许任何人这样敲诈他的钱财，如果需要手表，他干脆把自己的留在家里；然而，由于他需要手表才能赴约，他只能无意识地、以一种表现性行为的方式来实现这一想法。其次，他的健忘意味着：一直把钱浪费在那个没用的人身上会让我破产，我将不得不放弃一切。虽然他自己说听到消息时只感到一时的恼怒，但他重复同样的行为表明，这件事仍然在他的潜意识中起作用，仿佛他的意识在说：这件事一直萦绕在我心头。考虑到潜意识的这种态度，他借来的那位女士的手表也遭遇了同样的命运也就不足为奇了。但或许还有其他更具体的动机促使他将这种情绪转移到那位“无辜”女士的手表上。最显而易见的动机是，他可能想把手表留下来代替自己被他牺牲的手表，所以第二天忘记归还。此外，或许他还想把手表作为那位女士的纪念品。而且，忘记这位他仰慕的女士的手表，也给了他再次拜访她的机会；毕竟，他第二天上午已经约好因其他事务拜访她，而他忘记带手表似乎是在暗示，既然这次拜访是事先安排好的，那么随意地把自己的手表还给她就太浪费了。他两次忘记带自己的手表，从而得以再次拜访归还她的手表，这表明这位男士下意识地试图避免同时携带两块手表。他显然不想给人留下铺张浪费的印象，这与他亲戚的贫困形成了鲜明的对比；另一方面，他也想谨慎地控制自己与这位女士的婚事，时刻提醒自己对家庭（他的母亲）负有不可推卸的责任。最后，他未能归还手表的另一个原因可能是，前一天晚上，作为单身汉的他不好意思让朋友们看到自己偷偷查看女士的手表，为了避免再次发生这种尴尬的情况，他不想再把手表放在口袋里。另一方面，由于他不得不归还手表，结果就变成了一种无意识的症状行为，这种行为体现了他内心矛盾的情感与他无意识艰难取得的胜利之间的一种妥协（《精神分析中心学报》第二卷，第5页）。

The three following observations were made by J. Stärcke (op. cit):

以下三点观察结果由 J. Stärcke（同上）提出：

6) Mislaying, breaking and forgetting things — as the expression of the suppressed ability of the negative counter-will : ‘One day I was going to lend my brother several items from a collection of illustrations I had made for a scientific work, which he wanted to use as slides in a lecture. Although it did briefly cross my mind that as I had gone to a good deal of trouble to collect these reproductions, I would prefer them not to be publicly shown or published in any way before I could do it myself, I promised him to look out the negatives of the pictures he wanted and make slides of them. However, I could not find the negatives. I looked through the whole stack of boxes of negatives on the subject, I picked up a good two hundred negatives one by one, but those I was looking for were not there. I suspected that I was in fact reluctant to let my brother have the pictures. When I had become aware of these grudging ideas and had done my best to overcome them, I realized that I had set aside the box on top of the pile without looking through it, and it was the box containing the negatives I was looking for. It had a brief note of its contents on the lid, at which I had probably cast a fleeting glance before setting that particular box aside. In fact I did not quite seem to have got over my reluctance, because all kinds of other mishaps occurred before the slides were ready to be sent off. I broke one of them while I was holding it and cleaning the glass over the picture (and I never usually break slides). When I had made another slide from the plate I dropped it, and saved it from being broken only by putting out my foot to catch it. While I was mounting the slides the whole stack fell to the floor once again, but luckily none of them broke. Finally, however, it was several more days before I actually packed them up and dispatched them. Every day I had planned to do so, and every time I forgot.’

6）遗失、损坏和遗忘物品——这是被压抑的负面反意志能力的表现：“有一天，我打算把之前为一部科学著作绘制的几幅插图借给弟弟，他想在讲座中用作幻灯片。虽然我曾短暂地想过，既然我费了那么多功夫才收集到这些复制品，我宁愿它们在我自己使用之前不要以任何方式公开展示或出版，但我还是答应他要帮他找到他想要的那些图片的底片，并制作成幻灯片。然而，我却找不到那些底片。我翻遍了所有关于这个主题的底片盒，一张一张地拿出了足足两百张，但我想要的那些却不在那里。我怀疑，我其实是不愿意把这些图片借给弟弟的。”当我意识到这些不情愿的想法并尽力克服它们之后，我才发现我把放在最上面的那个盒子放在一边，却没打开看过，而那个盒子里装的正是我要找的底片。盒盖上贴着一张简短的纸条，上面写着里面的东西，我可能在把那个盒子放到一边之前只是匆匆瞥了一眼。事实上，我似乎并没有完全克服我的不情愿，因为在幻灯片准备好寄出之前，还发生了各种各样的意外。我拿着一张幻灯片擦拭照片上的玻璃时，不小心弄碎了一张（我通常不会弄碎幻灯片）。当我用底片制作另一张幻灯片时，我不小心把它掉在了地上，幸亏我伸出脚接住了才没摔碎。当我装裱幻灯片时，整叠幻灯片又一次掉到了地上，但幸运的是，没有一张摔碎。然而，最终，我又过了好几天才真正把它们打包寄出去。我每天都计划着要寄，但每次都忘记了。

7) Repeated forgetfulness — actions that miss their mark when they are finally carried out : ‘I once had to send an acquaintance a postcard, but I kept putting it off for days on end, and I had a strong suspicion why: he had written to tell me that someone whom I did not particularly want to see was planning to visit me that week When the week was over, and the prospect of the visit to which I was not looking forward had become very slight, I finally wrote the postcard and told my acquaintance when I would be available. When I wrote the card I originally meant to say that I had been prevented from writing before because of druk werk (the pressure of work), but in the end I left that out: no reasonable person believes in that hackneyed excuse any more. Whether this small untruth still insisted on being expressed in some way I do not know, but when I took the postcard to the letterbox I posted it, by mistake, in the lower slot for Drukwerk (printed matter).’

7）反复遗忘——最终执行时却未能达到预期效果的行为：“我曾经不得不给一位熟人寄明信片，但我总是拖延好几天，而且我强烈怀疑原因：他写信告诉我，一个我不太想见到的人计划这周来拜访我。一周过去了，我并不期待的拜访也变得微乎其微，我终于写了明信片，并告诉熟人我什么时候有空。写明信片时，我原本想说之前因为工作压力太大而没能写信，但最后还是省略了：现在谁还会相信这种老掉牙的借口呢？我不知道这个小小的谎言是否仍然执意要以某种方式表达出来，但当我把明信片拿到信箱时，我不小心把它投进了投递印刷品的下层投递口。”

8) Forgetfulness and mistakes : ‘A girl went out one fine morning to draw the plaster casts in the Rijksmuseum. Although she would rather have gone for a walk on such a nice day, she decided to work hard at her drawing. But first she had to buy some drawing paper. She went to the shop (which was about ten minutes’ walk away from the museum), bought pencils and other drawing instruments, but forgot the paper. Then she went to the museum, and was sitting on her little stool ready to start work when she realized that she still had no paper, so she had to go back to the shop again. Once she had her paper she really did begin drawing, and was getting on well with her work when, some time later, she heard several chimes from the clocktower of the museum. It must be twelve noon, she thought, but she went on working until the bell struck the quarter hour. Oh, she thought, that must be twelve-fifteen, and at this point she put away her drawing instruments and decided to walk through the Vondelpark and go to her sister’s house for coffee (as the Dutch call lunch). But on reaching the Suasso Museum she saw, to her surprise, that instead of being twelve-thirty it was only twelve noon! The enticingly fine weather had outwitted her industrious intentions, and when the bell struck at eleven-thirty she had forgotten that a bell in a clocktower strikes the half hours too.’

8）健忘和失误：一个阳光明媚的早晨，一个女孩去国立博物馆画石膏像。虽然她更想在这么好的日子里散步，但她还是决定认真画画。不过，她首先得买些画纸。她去了商店（离博物馆大约十分钟步行路程），买了铅笔和其他绘画工具，却忘了买纸。然后她去了博物馆，坐在小凳子上准备开始画画，这时她才意识到自己还没有纸，只好又回到商店。拿到纸后，她真的开始画了，而且画得非常顺利。过了一会儿，她听到博物馆钟楼传来几声钟响。她心想，一定是中午十二点了，但她还是继续画，直到钟声敲响一刻钟。 “哦，”她心想，“那一定是十二点十五分了。”于是她收起画具，决定穿过冯德尔公园去姐姐家喝咖啡（荷兰人把午餐叫做“咖啡”）。可是，当她走到苏阿索博物馆时，却惊讶地发现，时间不是十二点半，而是十二点！这诱人的好天气让她原本的计划落空了，当十一点半的钟声响起时，她才想起钟楼上的钟也会敲响半点。

9) As several of the observations above show, an unconsciously disruptive tendency can also achieve its purpose by persistently repeating the same kind of slip. I take an amusing example of this from a little book called Frank Wedekind und das Theater [ Frank Wedekind and the Theatre ], published by the firm of Drei-Masken-Verlag in Munich, but I must leave responsibility for the little story itself, which is told in Mark Twain’s style, to the author of the book.

9）正如以上几点观察所示，无意识的破坏性倾向也可以通过不断重复同一种错误来达到目的。我举一个有趣的例子，出自慕尼黑Drei-Masken出版社出版的一本名为《弗兰克·韦德金德与剧院》（Frank Wedekind und das Theater）的小册子，但这个小故事本身（以马克·吐温的风格讲述）的责任，必须交给本书作者。

‘In Wedekind’s one-act play Die Zensur [ Censorship ], one of the characters says, at the climax of the play: “Die Furcht vor dem Tode ist ein Denkfehler [‘The fear of death is a fallacy’].” In rehearsal the author, feeling pleased with this phrase, asked the actor to pause briefly before the word Denkfehler. That evening the actor entered fully into the spirit of the thing, inserted the pause precisely where it was required, but then solemnly announced: “Die Furcht vor dem Tode is ein Druckfehler [misprint].” The author assured the artist, on being asked about it after the performance, that he had not the slightest objection to the effect of the pause, except that at that particular point his play did not say that fear of death was a misprint , and the word was fallacy. At the following evening’s performance the actor said, at the crucial point, and yet again in the most solemn of tones: “The fear of death is a — Denkzettel [memorandum].” Once again Wedekind heaped praise on the actor, merely commenting in passing that he had not said the fear of death was a memorandum but a fallacy. On the following evening Die Zensur was performed again, and when the crucial moment came the actor, with whom the author was on very friendly terms and exchanging views on art by this time, said with the most solemn feeling imaginable: “The fear of death is a — Druckzettel [printed pamphlet].” The actor received the author’s unstinting approbation, and the one-act play had many more performances, but by now the author had given up his “fallacy” as a lost cause.’

在韦德金德的独幕剧《审查制度》（Die Zensur）中，一个角色在剧终时说道：“‘对死亡的恐惧是一种谬误’（Die Furcht vor dem Tode ist ein Denkfehler）。”排练时，作者对这句话很满意，便要求演员在“Denkfehler”这个词前稍作停顿。当晚，演员完全领会了其中的意境，准确地在需要的地方加了停顿，然后郑重其事地宣布：“‘对死亡的恐惧是印刷错误’（Die Furcht vor dem Tode is ein Druckfehler）。”演出结束后，当被问及此事时，作者向演员保证，他对停顿的效果没有任何异议，只是在那个特定的时刻，他的剧本并没有说“对死亡的恐惧是印刷错误”，而是说“谬误”（fallacy）。在第二天晚上的演出中，演员在关键时刻，再次以极其严肃的语气说道：“对死亡的恐惧是一份——备忘录。”韦德金德再次对这位演员赞不绝口，只是顺带提了一句，说他之前说的不是对死亡的恐惧是备忘录，而是一种谬论。第二天晚上，《禅宗》再次上演，当关键时刻到来时，这位演员——此时他与作者已十分友好，并就艺术问题交换意见——以你能想象到的最严肃的语气说道：“对死亡的恐惧是一份——印刷小册子。”这位演员得到了作者毫不吝啬的赞赏，这部独幕剧也上演了更多场次，但此时作者已经放弃了他所谓的“谬论”，认为它毫无希望。

Rank has also studied the very interesting connections between ‘slips and dreaming’ ( Zentralblatt für Psychoanalyse II, p. 266, and Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse III, p. 158), but they cannot be traced without close analysis of the dreams to which the slips related. I once had a rather complicated dream in which I had lost my wallet. In the morning, sure enough, I could not find it when I was getting dressed; I had forgotten to take it out of my trouser pocket and put it in its usual place the night before my dream. I was not unaware, therefore, of this act of forgetfulness, which was probably intended to express an unconscious idea ready to surface in the context of a dream. 2

兰克也研究过“口误与梦境”之间非常有趣的联系（《精神分析中心学报》第二卷，第266页；《国际精神分析杂志》第三卷，第158页），但如果不仔细分析与口误相关的梦境，就无法追溯这些联系。我曾经做过一个相当复杂的梦，梦里我丢了钱包。第二天早上，果然，我穿衣服的时候找不到它；原来，在做梦的前一天晚上，我忘了把它从裤兜里拿出来放回原位。因此，我并非没有意识到自己犯了这个错误，这很可能是为了表达一个潜意识里的想法，而这个想法正准备在梦境中浮现出来。

I do not claim that such cases of combined slips can tell us anything we could not learn from cases of slips in isolation, but this change of the form of the slip, while the result is the same, does give the distinct impression that the will is trying to achieve some definite purpose, and strongly contradicts the idea that slips simply happen by chance and need no interpretation. It is also striking that in these examples a conscious intention entirely fails to prevent the slip from occurring. My friend did not manage to attend his committee meeting; the lady was unable to part with the Roman medal. The unconscious motive opposing their intentions found another way to express itself when foiled on the first occasion. Something more than a conscious intention is necessary to overcome an unconscious motive; it takes psychic investigation to bring something unknown to the attention of the conscious mind.

我并不认为这种组合式失误能告诉我们任何单独失误案例无法提供的信息，但失误形式的改变，尽管结果相同，却确实给人一种明显的印象，即意志试图达成某种明确的目的，这有力地反驳了失误仅仅是偶然发生且无需解释的观点。同样引人注目的是，在这些例子中，有意识的意图完全未能阻止失误的发生。我的朋友未能出席他的委员会会议；那位女士无法割舍那枚罗马奖章。当他们的意图第一次受挫时，潜意识中与之对抗的动机找到了另一种表达方式。要克服潜意识的动机，需要的不仅仅是有意识的意图；它需要心灵的探索才能将未知的事物带入意识层面。

Notes

笔记

1 . This continued working in the unconscious mind can also be expressed in the form of a dream following the slip, or sometimes in the repetition of the slip, or in omitting to correct it.

1. 这种在潜意识中持续运作的方式也可以表现为在失误之后做梦，或者有时表现为重复失误，或者表现为不去纠正失误。

2 . It is not unusual for a slip such as losing or mislaying something to be corrected by a dream in which the dreamer discovers where to find the missing item, but there is nothing occult about it so long as the dreamer is the same as the person who suffered the loss. A young lady wrote: ‘About four months ago, in the bank, I found that I had lost a very pretty ring. I searched every corner of my room, but could not find it. A week ago I dreamed it was near the cupboard beside the radiator. Of course the dream would not let me rest, and sure enough, I found it there next morning.’ She was surprised by the incident, but said it often happened that her ideas and wishes were fulfilled in this way, although she did not ask herself what change had occurred in her life between her loss of the ring and its recovery.

2. 梦见丢失或遗落物品等小失误得到纠正并不罕见，梦中做梦者会发现丢失物品的下落，但这并非什么神秘现象，只要做梦者与丢失物品的人是同一人即可。一位年轻女士写道：“大约四个月前，我在银行发现自己丢失了一枚非常漂亮的戒指。我把房间的每个角落都找遍了，但还是找不到。一周前，我梦见戒指在暖气片旁边的橱柜附近。当然，这个梦让我寝食难安，第二天早上果然在那里找到了它。”她对这件事感到惊讶，但她说自己的想法和愿望经常以这种方式实现，尽管她并没有探究在丢失戒指到找回戒指之间，她的生活中究竟发生了什么变化。

# ↩

XII

十二

Determinism — Belief in Chance and
Superstition — Some Points of View

决定论——相信偶然性和迷信——一些观点

The following statement may be made as the general conclusion to be drawn from the various discussions above: certain inadequacies in our psychic performance — the character they all share will be more closely defined below — and certain actions performed apparently unintentionally prove, when methods of psychoanalytical investigation are applied to them, to he well motivated and determined by factors of which the conscious mind is unaware.

从以上各种讨论中可以得出以下总体结论：我们的心理表现存在某些不足——这些不足的共同特征将在下文中更详细地定义——并且某些看似无意的行为，当运用精神分析调查方法进行研究时，会被证明是有充分动机的，并且是由意识层面没有意识到的因素决定的。

To be classified with phenomena capable of explanation in this way, a psychic slip must fulfil the following conditions.

要被归类为可以用这种方式解释的现象，心理失误必须满足以下条件。

a) It must not go beyond a certain point, a point that is established by our judgement and complies with our ideas of what is ‘within the range of normality’.

a) 它不能超过某个点，这个点是由我们的判断确定的，并且符合我们对“正常范围”的理解。

b) It must have the character of a brief and temporary disturbance. We must have carried out the same action correctly before, or believe ourselves capable of carrying it out more correctly at any time. If someone else corrects our slip, we must immediately acknowledge the justice of the correction and the malfunctioning of our own psychic process.

b) 它必须具有短暂且暂时性干扰的性质。我们必须之前正确地执行过同样的行动，或者相信自己随时都有能力更正确地执行它。如果他人纠正了我们的错误，我们必须立即承认这种纠正的合理性以及我们自身心理过程的失误。

c) If we notice the slip at all, we must not recognize any motivation for it in ourselves; instead, we must be tempted to put it down to ‘carelessness’ or ‘chance’.

c) 如果我们注意到这种失误，我们绝不能从自身角度考虑这种失误的任何动机；相反，我们应该倾向于将其归因于“粗心”或“偶然”。

The category of psychic slip, therefore, comprises cases of forgetfulness, mistakes that we make although we know better, slips of the tongue, slips in reading, slips of the pen, inadvertent actions and so-called fortuitous actions.

因此，精神失误这一类别包括遗忘、明知故犯的错误、口误、阅读错误、笔误、无意行为以及所谓的偶然行为。

The same word formation, with the prefix ver - [in German, all the nouns Freud uses but one derive from verbs beginning ver -: vergessen, versprechen, verlesen, verschreiben and vergreifen ; the odd one out is Zufallshandlungen , fortuitous actions] gives a linguistic indication of the internal similarity of most of these phenomena. However, a series of comments which may be of further interest can be connected with the explanation of the psychic processes thus defined.

同样的构词法，加上前缀ver-（在德语中，弗洛伊德使用的所有名词，除了一个之外，都源自以ver-开头的动词：vergessen、versprechen、verlesen、verschreiben和vergreifen；例外的是Zufallshandlungen，意为偶然行为），从语言学角度表明了这些现象内部的相似性。然而，一系列可能更有价值的评论可以与对上述心理过程的解释联系起来。

A) By saying that some of our psychic actions cannot be explained as the work of intention, we fail to recognize the extent of determination present in our mental life. It goes further, both here and in other areas, than we suspect. In 1900 I explained in an essay on the literary historian R. M. Meyer in Die Zeit , illustrated by examples, that it is impossible to compose something entirely nonsensical intentionally and voluntarily. For quite a long time I have known that one cannot contrive to think of either a number or a name completely at random. If we study a number apparently plucked from thin air jokingly or in high spirits, a number which may perhaps run to several digits, it will become evident that it is really strictly determined, unlikely as that might have seemed. I will begin with a brief account of a first name arbitrarily chosen, and then analyse a similar example of a number ‘unthinkingly thrown out’.

A）如果我们说某些心理活动无法用意图来解释，那就忽略了我们精神生活中存在的决定性程度。这种决定性，无论在此领域还是其他领域，都比我们想象的要广泛得多。1900年，我在《时代周报》（Die Zeit）上发表了一篇关于文学史家R. M. Meyer的文章，并举例说明，我们不可能有意地、自愿地创作出完全无意义的东西。我早就知道，我们不可能完全随机地想到一个数字或一个名字。如果我们研究一个看似随意或一时兴起凭空想出的数字，一个可能是几位数的数字，就会发现它实际上是经过严格决定的，尽管这看起来似乎不太可能。我将首先简要描述一个随意选择的名字，然后分析一个类似的“不假思索”的数字的例子。

1) When I was writing up the case history of a woman patient of mine for publication, I wondered what first name to give her. I seemed to have a very wide choice; of course certain names excluded themselves from the start, first and foremost her real name, then the names of my own family, something to which I would object, and in addition any really unusual women’s names; but that surely left a wide range available. One would expect, and I myself did expect, that a whole host of women’s names would suggest themselves to me. Instead, only a single name came into my mind: the name Dora. I wondered what had determined it. Who else was called Dora? I felt like rejecting the next idea to occur to me as incredible, for it told me that the nanny who looked after my sister’s children was called Dora, but I had enough self-discipline, or enough experience of analysis, to follow that idea and take it further. I immediately thought of a small incident the previous evening, which brought me the association determining the name I was seeking. I saw a letter addressed to ‘Fräulein Rosa W.’ lying on the table in my sister’s dining room. In surprise, I asked who that was, and learned that the nanny Dora was really called Rosa, but had been obliged to change her name on entering the household because my sister is a Rosa too and could have taken the name to mean herself. I said, sympathetically: Poor servants, they can’t even keep their own names! And now that I came to think of it, I said no more for a moment, but began meditating on various serious subjects. My thoughts trailed vaguely away, but I could now easily recall them to my conscious mind. So when next day I was looking for a name for someone who could not be allowed to keep her own , only Dora sprang to mind. In this instance the fact that it was the sole name to occur to me was based on a strong similarity of content, for in my patient’s case history the crucial influence on her course of treatment had also been exerted by someone working in the capacity of a servant in a strange house, this time as a governess.

1）当我为一位女病人撰写病例报告准备发表时，我一直在思考该给她取什么名字。我似乎有很多选择；当然，有些名字一开始就被排除在外，首先是她的真名，其次是我家人的名字（我不太喜欢用这些名字），此外还有一些非常罕见的女性名字；但这确实留下了很大的选择余地。人们会认为，我自己也确实认为，我会想到很多女性名字。然而，我脑海中却只浮现出一个名字：朵拉。我很好奇是什么让我想到这个名字。除了朵拉，还有谁叫朵拉？接下来我想到一个想法，觉得不可思议，因为它告诉我，照顾我姐姐孩子的保姆也叫朵拉，但我还是足够自律，或者说足够有分析经验，让我继续思考并深入探究这个想法。我立刻想起了前一天晚上发生的一件小事，正是这件事让我联想到了我一直在寻找的名字。我在姐姐餐厅的桌子上看到一封写着“罗莎·W小姐”的信。我惊讶地问她是谁，才知道原来保姆朵拉真名叫罗莎，但因为我姐姐也叫罗莎，她进家后不得不改名，以免被误认为是自己。我同情地说：可怜的佣人，连自己的名字都不能保留！想到这里，我沉默了一会儿，开始思考一些严肃的问题。我的思绪飘忽不定，但现在却能轻易地将它们记在脑海里。所以第二天，当我为一个不能保留自己名字的人寻找合适的名字时，朵拉这个名字立刻浮现在我的脑海中。在这种情况下，我唯一能想到的名字是基于内容的高度相似性，因为在我的病人的病史中，对她治疗过程产生关键影响的人也是在异乡做佣人的人，这次是家庭教师。

This little incident had an unexpected sequel years later. One day, when I brought up the case history of the girl I had called Dora in a lecture — the case history itself had been published long before — I realized that one of the two women in my audience was also called Dora, a name I would have to mention very often and in very many different contexts during the lecture. I turned to my young colleague, who was also a personal acquaintance of mine, and apologized, saying that I really hadn’t stopped to think that her own name was Dora, and I would be happy to replace the name I had given my patient by another in today’s lecture. Then I had to think of a name in a hurry, and was just telling myself that I must not set a bad example to my psychoanalytically trained colleagues by hitting upon the first name of the other woman present. So I was pleased when the name Erna occurred to me as a replacement for Dora, and I made use of it in the lecture. Afterwards, I wondered just where the name Erna had come from, and could not help smiling when I realized that the possibility I had feared in choosing a replacement name had in fact happened, at least in part. For the other lady’s surname was Lucerna, ending in ‘-erna’.

多年后，这件小事却有了意想不到的后续。一天，我在讲座中提到了那个我称之为“朵拉”的女孩的案例——这个案例其实早已发表——我突然意识到，听众席上的两位女士中，有一位也叫朵拉。这意味着在讲座中，我将在各种不同的场合频繁提及这个名字。我转向那位年轻的同事，她也是我的熟人，向她道歉，说我之前真的没想到她也叫朵拉，并表示很乐意在今天的讲座中用另一个名字代替我给病人起的名字。当时我得赶紧想个名字，心里想着千万不能因为用了另一位女士的名字而给其他受过精神分析训练的同事们树立坏榜样。所以，当我想到用“厄娜”来代替朵拉时，我欣喜若狂，并在讲座中使用了这个名字。之后，我一直在想“厄娜”这个名字究竟是怎么来的，当我意识到我之前担心的那个可能性——至少部分地——真的发生了时，我不禁笑了。因为另一位女士的姓氏是卢塞纳（Lucerna），以“-erna”结尾。

2) I wrote to a friend telling him that I had finished reading the proofs of the Interpretation of Dreams , and was not going to change anything else in the work ‘even if there turned out to be 2467 mistakes in it’. I immediately tried to account to myself for this number, and added my little analysis as a postscript to my letter. I think I had better quote exactly what I wrote when I had caught myself in the act:

2）我写信给一位朋友，告诉他我已经读完了《梦的解析》的校样，并且“即使最终发现里面有2467处错误”，我也不会再做任何修改。我立刻试图解释这个数字，并在信的附言中附上了我的简短分析。我想我最好还是把我意识到自己犯错时写下的内容原原本本引用出来：

‘So here, briefly, is another contribution to the psychopathology of everyday life. You will find in this letter the number 2467, given as a high-spirited, arbitrary assessment of the number of errors that might be found in the dream book. I meant it to suggest just any very large number, and so indeed it does. But there is nothing arbitrary or undetermined in the workings of the mind. You will also, and correctly, expect that my unconscious set to work in a hurry to decide on the number that my conscious mind was to produce. Well, I had just been reading a piece in the newspaper about the retirement of one General E. M. as master of ordnance. I take an interest in the man: when I was doing my military service as a medical student he was a colonel. At the time he fell ill, and told the doctors: “You’d better cure me within the week. I have work to do, and the emperor is waiting for it.” I determined then and there to follow the man’s career, and now (this was in 1899) he had come to the end of it, having retired with the rank of master of ordnance. I tried working out how long it had taken him, and supposed I must have met him in the hospital in 1882. That would make it 17 years. I told my wife, and she commented: “Then I suppose you’ll soon be retiring too.” To which I protested: “Heaven forbid!” After this exchange I sat down at my desk to write to you, but my previous train of thought continued, and for a very good reason. My calculation had been wrong, and I had a clear point of reference for that fact in my memory. I had reached my majority, I mean my 24th birthday, while I was under military arrest for going absent without leave. That was in 1880, and thus 19 years ago. So there’s the reason for the “24” in 2467! Now, take my age at present, 43, add 24 years, and the result is 67! Which means that when my wife suggested I might feel like retiring, my wishful thinking added another 24 years of work to my age now. I was clearly feeling vexed that during the whole period over which I had followed Colonel M.’s career I had not got very far myself, yet I felt a kind of triumph at the thought that he was now retired while I still had everything ahead of me. So I may legitimately say that not even the number 2467, which I brought out without any conscious intention, was not determined by my unconscious mind.’

“所以，简而言之，这是对日常生活心理病理学的又一次贡献。你会在这封信中看到数字2467，这是我随意估计的梦境记录本中可能出现的错误数量。我本意是想暗示一个非常大的数字，而事实也的确如此。但在人的思维运作中，没有什么是随意或不确定的。你也会，而且理所当然地，预料到我的潜意识会迅速行动起来，决定我的意识应该得出哪个数字。嗯，我刚刚在报纸上读到一篇关于E. M.将军从军械总监职位上退休的文章。我对这个人很感兴趣：我当医学生服兵役时，他是一位上校。当时他生病了，对医生们说：‘你们最好在一周内治好我。我还有工作要做，皇帝在等着呢。’”我当时就决定要追踪这个人的职业生涯，而现在（那是1899年），他已经走到了尽头，以军械大师的军衔退休了。我试着计算他花了多长时间，估计我是在1882年在医院里认识他的。那算起来就是17年了。我把这事告诉了妻子，她说道：“那我想你也快退休了吧。”我抗议道：“天哪！”说完这番话，我坐在书桌前准备给你写信，但我之前的思绪却一直萦绕在心头，而且原因很充分。我的计算错了，而且我记忆中有一个清晰的参照点。我成年的时候，也就是24岁生日那天，因为擅离职守而被军队逮捕。那是1880年，也就是19年前。所以，这就是2467中的“24”的由来！现在，以我目前的年龄43岁为例，加上24年，结果是67岁！这意味着，当我妻子建议我考虑退休时，我的一厢情愿的想法又让我的年龄加上了24年的工作年限。我显然感到懊恼，因为在我关注M上校职业生涯的这段时间里，我自己却没什么成就，但想到他现在已经退休，而我的前途一片光明，我又感到一丝胜利的喜悦。所以，我可以理直气壮地说，即使是我不经意间说出的2467这个数字，也不是我的潜意识决定的。

3) Since studying this first example of the explanation of a number apparently chosen at random, I have tried the same experiment many times, and with equal success, but most of these cases are so intimate in their content that they cannot be passed on.

3）自从研究了第一个解释看似随机选择的数字的例子后，我多次尝试了同样的实验，也都取得了同样的成功，但这些案例的内容大多非常私密，无法传播。

For that reason, however, I will add here a very interesting analysis of a ‘chance number’ that Dr Alfred Adler of Vienna heard from an acquaintance whom he describes as a Very sound source’. 1 ‘Yesterday evening,’ said this man, ‘I was reading the Psychopathology of Everyday Life [an earlier edition], and I would have finished the book there and then had not a curious incident prevented me. For when I read the passage claiming that every number we call into our conscious minds, apparently quite arbitrarily, has a meaning of its own, I decided to try an experiment. The number 1734 occurred to me. And now the following ideas came at a headlong pace: 1734 ÷ 17 = 102; 102 ÷ 17 = 6. Then I divided the digits of the number into 17 and 34. I am 34 years old. As I think I once told you, I regard one’s 34th year as the last year of youth, so I felt extremely gloomy on my last birthday. I had entered upon a very enjoyable and interesting period of development at the end of my 17th year. I divide my life up into 17-year sections. So what is the meaning of my division sums? I thought of the number 102, which is the number given to Kotzebue’s play Menschenhass und Reue [ Misanthropy and Remorse ] in the Reclam Universal Library series.

然而，正因如此，我在此补充一段关于“偶然数字”的非常有趣的分析。维也纳的阿尔弗雷德·阿德勒博士从一位熟人那里听到了这个数字，他称这位熟人是“非常可靠的消息来源”。 1 “昨天晚上，”这个人说，“我正在读《日常生活心理病理学》（旧版），如果不是发生了一件奇事，我本可以读完这本书。因为当我读到书中声称，我们意识中呼唤的每一个数字，看似随意，都有其自身的含义时，我决定做个实验。我想到了1734这个数字。然后，以下几个想法如潮水般涌来：1734 ÷ 17 = 102；102 ÷ 17 = 6。然后我把这个数字的各位数字分成17和34两部分。我今年34岁。”我想我曾经跟你说过，我认为34岁是青春的最后一年，所以在我上一个生日那天，我感到非常沮丧。17岁末，我进入了一个非常愉快且充满发展乐趣的时期。我把人生分成17年一个阶段。那么，我的这些划分意味着什么呢？我想到了102这个数字，它是科策布的戏剧《厌世与悔恨》（Menschenhass und Reue）在Reclam Universal Library系列中的编号。

‘My present psychic condition, as it happens, is one of misanthropy and remorse. No. 6 in the Universal Library (and I know a good many of the numbers in that series off by heart) is Müllner’s Die Schuld [ Guilt ]. I am constantly tormented by the idea that I am to blame for my own inability to become what I could have been. It also occurred to me that No. 34 in the Universal Library series is a story also by Müllner, entitled Der Kaliber [ The Calibre ]. I divided the word into “Ka-liber”, and it then struck me that it contains the words “Ali” and “Kali” [potassium]. This reminded me that I was once playing at making up rhymes with my 6-year-old son Ali. I asked him if he could find a rhyme for Ali. He couldn’t, and when he asked me for one I said: “Ali reinigt den Mund mit hypermangansaurem Kali’ [Ali cleans his mouth with potassium permanganate],” and we had a good laugh. Ali was a very lieb [sweet] child at this time, but recently I have been sorry to notice that he is ka ( kein ) lieber Ali [no longer a sweet Ali].’

“我目前的心理状态，恰好是厌世和悔恨。‘世界图书馆’系列的第六册（我对这个系列的很多册都倒背如流）是穆尔纳的《罪过》（Die Schuld）。我一直被一种想法折磨着：我没能成为我本可以成为的人，都是我自己的错。我还想到，‘世界图书馆’系列的第三十四册也是穆尔纳的作品，名为《口径》（Der Kaliber）。我把这个词拆开，读作‘Ka-liber’，然后突然意识到它包含了‘阿里’（Ali）和‘钾’（Kali）这两个词。这让我想起，我曾经和六岁的儿子阿里玩过编押韵诗的游戏。我问他能不能找到一个和阿里押韵的词。”他做不到，当他问我要的时候，我说：“Ali reinigt den Mund mit hypermangansaurem Kali’ [阿里用高锰酸钾漱口]”，我们都哈哈大笑起来。那时的阿里是个非常可爱的孩子，但最近我遗憾地发现，他已经不再是那个可爱的阿里了。

‘So then I asked myself, what book is No. 17 in the Universal Library? I couldn’t remember. However, I must certainly have known once, so I supposed that I had forgotten the number on purpose. I racked my brains to no avail. I meant to read on, but I was reading only automatically, without understanding a word, because that teasing No. 17 was on my mind. I put out the light and went on thinking. Finally it struck me that No. 17 must be a play by Shakespeare. But which play? I thought of Hero and Leander. Obviously a silly attempt of my will to distract me. Finally I got up and looked for the Reclam Universal library catalogue. No. 17 is Macbeth. To my surprise, I realized that my mind could dredge up almost nothing about the play, although I have paid it as much attention as other dramas by Shakespeare. All I could think of was: murderers, Lady Macbeth, witches, “Fair is foul”, and the fact that I had once thought Schiller’s version of Macbeth very good. No doubt I had wanted to forget the play. Then it occurred to me that 17 and 34 divided by 17 give 1 and 2. Nos. 1 and 2 in the Universal Library contain the text of Goethe’s Faust , and I once thought I saw many of Faust’s characteristics in myself.’ It is a pity that medical discretion did not allow us more of an insight into the meaning of this train of thought. Adler comments that the man did not succeed in synthesizing his ideas, which would hardly seem worthy of note if the rest of them had not produced something providing a key for the understanding of the number 1734 and the whole series of ideas.

于是我问自己，世界图书馆的第17号书是什么？我怎么也想不起来。但我肯定以前知道，所以我猜我是故意忘记的。我绞尽脑汁，却一无所获。我本想继续读下去，但却只是机械地读着，一个字也看不懂，因为那个令人困惑的第17号书一直萦绕在我的脑海里。我关了灯，继续思考。最后我突然想到，第17号一定是莎士比亚的一部戏剧。可是是哪部呢？我想到了《希罗与利安德》。显然，这是我试图分散注意力的愚蠢尝试。最后，我起身去查阅了Reclam世界图书馆的目录。第17号是《麦克白》。令我惊讶的是，我意识到，尽管我对这部剧的关注程度不亚于莎士比亚的其他戏剧，但我却几乎想不起任何关于这部剧的信息。我脑海里全是：谋杀犯、麦克白夫人、女巫、“美即丑”，以及我曾经觉得席勒的《麦克白》版本非常精彩。毫无疑问，我一直想忘记这部剧。然后我突然想到，17和34除以17分别等于1和2。世界图书馆的1号和2号藏书收录了歌德的《浮士德》的文本，而我曾经觉得我在自己身上看到了浮士德的许多特质。可惜的是，出于医学上的谨慎，我们无法更深入地理解这一思路的含义。阿德勒评论说，这个人没能成功地将他的想法融会贯通，而如果不是因为他的其他想法为理解数字1734以及整个系列的想法提供了关键线索，那么他未能将自己的想法融会贯通也就不足为奇了。

‘This morning,’ Adler’s source continued, ‘I had an experience that provides strong support for Freud’s theory. My wife, whom I had woken when I got up in the night, asked me what I was doing with the Universal Library catalogue. I told her the story. She thought it was all just hair-splitting, except — and this is very interesting — that she fancied there must be something in the idea of Macbeth , which I had so firmly rejected. But she added that if she thought of a random number she herself could associate no ideas with it. I said: “Let’s try.” She gave me the number 117. I replied at once: “17 refers to what I’ve just told you, and, what’s more, I was telling you only yesterday that there’s too much of an age difference between a woman of 82 and a man of 35.” For I had been teasing my wife over the last few days by pretending she was a little old lady of 82 - and 82 + 35 = 117.’

“今天早上，”阿德勒的消息来源继续说道，“我经历了一件事，这件事有力地支持了弗洛伊德的理论。我半夜起来的时候吵醒了妻子，她问我在用环球图书馆的目录做什么。我把事情经过告诉了她。她觉得这一切都是吹毛求疵，但——这一点很有意思——她觉得麦克白这个概念里肯定有某种东西，而我之前一直坚决反对它。但她补充说，如果她随便想一个数字，她自己也想不出任何与之相关的概念。我说：‘我们来试试。’她给了我117这个数字。我立刻回答说：‘17指的是我刚才跟你说的，而且，就在昨天，我还跟你说过，一个82岁的女人和一个35岁的男人之间的年龄差距太大了。’”因为过去几天我一直逗弄我妻子，假装她是一位82岁的老太太——而82+35=117。

So the man who could not work out the determination of his own number immediately found the answer when his wife gave him a number apparently chosen at random. In fact the wife had a very good idea of the complex that had given rise to the figure thought up by her husband, and took her own from the same complex, which they must both have shared because it concerned their respective ages and, as Adler indicates, the husband’s suppressed wish which, followed out to its conclusion, would have run: ‘The only right sort of wife for a man of 34, like me, would be a girl of 17.’

所以，那个无法确定自己命数的男人，在妻子给他一个看似随意选择的数字时，立刻找到了答案。事实上，妻子非常清楚丈夫心中那个数字背后的复杂心理，并从中汲取了灵感。他们必然都拥有这种心理，因为它与他们各自的年龄有关，而且正如阿德勒所指出的，也反映了丈夫内心深处压抑的愿望——如果顺着这个愿望发展下去，那就是：“像我这样34岁的男人，唯一合适的妻子就是17岁的女孩。”

Lest we should be over-inclined to dismiss such ‘parlour games’ as beneath consideration, I will add something I recently heard from Dr Adler: a year after the publication of this analysis, the man concerned was divorced from his wife. 2

为了避免我们过于倾向于将这类“室内游戏”视为不值一提，我想补充一下我最近从阿德勒博士那里听到的消息：在这篇分析发表一年后，文中提到的那位男士与妻子离婚了。

4) Adler gives similar explanations for the occurrence of obsessive numbers, and the choice of what are described as ‘favourite numbers’ is not without some connection to the life of the person who chooses them, and has a certain psychological interest. A man who admitted to a particular preference for the numbers 17 and 19 added, after a little thought, that when he went to university at the age of 17 he had at last attained the academic freedom for which he longed, while at the age of 19 he had gone on his first major journey and soon afterwards made his first scientific discovery. However, his preference did not become fixed until a decade later, when the same numbers acquired significance in his love life. In fact even those numbers that are used with particular frequency in certain circumstances, although apparently at random, can be traced back to an unexpected significance through analysis. For instance, it occurred to a patient of mine one day that when he was annoyed he was particularly apt to say: ‘I’ve told you that 17 to 36 times before,’ and he wondered whether there was some motivation for it. It struck him at once that he had been born on the 27th of a month, while his younger brother was born on the 26th of a month, and he felt justified in complaining that fate had deprived him of many of the good things of life in order to give them to his younger brother. He depicted this favouritism of destiny in his mind by subtracting ten from his own date of birth and adding that number to his brother’s birthday. ‘Even though I’m the elder brother I’ve been shortchanged.’

4）阿德勒对痴迷数字的出现给出了类似的解释，选择所谓的“最喜欢的数字”并非毫无关联，而是与选择者的生活息息相关，并具有一定的心理意义。一位承认自己特别偏爱数字17和19的男士在稍作思考后补充道，17岁上大学时，他终于获得了梦寐以求的学术自由；19岁时，他开启了人生中的第一次重要旅行，不久后便取得了他的第一个科学发现。然而，直到十年后，当这些数字在他的爱情生活中具有了重要意义时，他的偏好才最终形成。事实上，即使是那些在特定情况下频繁使用的数字，尽管表面上看似随机，但通过分析也能追溯到意想不到的意义。例如，有一天，我的一位病人突然意识到，当他生气时，他特别喜欢说：“我已经跟你说过17到36遍了。”他不禁思考，这背后是否有什么原因。他立刻想到，自己是每月27号出生的，而弟弟是每月26号出生的，他觉得自己有理由抱怨命运剥夺了他许多美好的事物，却把它们给了弟弟。为了形象地表达命运的偏袒，他把自己的生日减去10，然后加上弟弟的生日。“即使我是哥哥，我也吃了亏。”

5) I will dwell a little longer on the analysis of ideas connected with numbers, for I know of no other isolated observations that so strikingly prove the existence of extremely complex thought processes inaccessible to the conscious mind, nor of any better example of analysis in which influence by the doctor (through suggestion), something often suspected, can so definitely be ruled out. With his consent, I will therefore give an account of the analysis of a numerical idea produced by one of my patients. I need say of him only that he is the youngest of a large family and lost his father, whom he greatly admired, while he was a small child. In a particularly cheerful frame of mind, he thought of the number 426718 and asked himself: ‘Now, what do I associate with that? Well, first of all there’s a joke I heard: “If a doctor treats your cold it will last 42 days, and if you leave it untreated it will go on for 6 weeks.”’ This matches the first digits in the number: 42 = 6 × 7 . When he hesitated after producing this first idea, I pointed out that the 6 figure number he had chosen contained all the digits up to 8 except for 3 and 5. At once he went on with his interpretation. ‘Well, there are 7 siblings in our family and I am the youngest. No. 3 in order of age is my sister A. and No. 5 is my brother L. — they were both my enemies. As a child I used to ask God in my prayers every evening to remove my tormentors from this life. I think I was fulfilling that wish myself: I passed over 3 and 5, my nasty brother and the sister I hated.’ ‘So if the number refers to your brothers and sisters, what about the 18 at the end? There were only 7 of you.’ ‘I often thought that if my father had lived longer then I wouldn’t have been the youngest child. If there had been another “1”, then there would have been 8 of us, and being the elder I’d have had a younger brother or sister to boss about.’
